speechtext:
Mr. G. E. MoCRANEY moved:
That Bill No. 118 for the relief of Charles Isaac Alexander be placed on the Order Paper for consideration in the Committee of the Whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this Bill was considered in the Senate and passed. It was considered by the Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills of the House, and the preamble was rejected by a vote of 7 to 6 on Thursday last. On Monday of this week, I moved to refer the Bill back to the Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills, which was agreed to and the preamble of the Bill was rejected on a vote of 11 to 9. In view of the narrow difference of opinion in the Private Bills Committee, and in view of the fact that the conclusion appears to be at variance with the evidence, I think the Bill should have the attention of the whole House.

Twice this
matter has been before the Committee on Private Bills and has been rejected. I, for one, object to its being brought before the House. And, I raise the point of order, as I think I am entitled to do, that the motion cannot be brought forward at this time. If any case clearly indicates the necessity of provision being made by Parliament for the creation of a proper tribunal to consider divorces, it is this. It is the kind of case that should not be thrust upon this House for consideration. I am not a member of the committee, but at this stage of the session I am not disposed to question the conclusion of the committee which twice considered the matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I supported the motion to refer the case back to the Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills, for reasons which I then stated and to which I still adhere. At that time, I said that the very anomalous result which had bee* reached, indicated, as has just been pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett), the necessity for some change in the method by which such cases are disposed of. It occurs to me that the method which has been suggested more 138i
than once, that of having these Bills referred to a joint committee of both Houses, so that members of the committee having thd Bill under consideration shall hear the witnesses, might be a better method than that which is now in vogue. The Bill was referred back to the Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills, and that committee has again decided against reporting the Bill. . In the circumstances, while personally, had I been a member of the committee I should have voted to report the Bill, I do not think it is our duty to further deal with the question in this House. The rule has been in the past that the report of a committee upon a Bill should1 command the approval of the House unless; there are very cogent and convincing reasons to the contrary, and notwithstanding that rule, I supported the motion to refer the Bill back. But now that it has been twice considered by the committee, it seems to me that the Bill must be dealt with in accordance with the views of the majority of the committee, and that no good purpose would be served, under present conditions, by asking the House to undertake consideration of a question which, although it is within the judgment of the House, is nevertheless primarily within the judgment of the committee to whom the Bill has been twice confided. I regret therefore that I cannot support the motion of my hon. friend from Saskatoon (Mr. MoCraney).
If this Bill is knocked out it will be in my opinion a travesty on justice and it shows the absurdity of the Parliament of Canada dealing with divorces at all.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member, it seems to me, is exceeding his rights when he reflects upon Parliament in that way.

If Parliament throws
out this Bill it will deserve to be reflected upon. There would be absolutely no justice in such procedure, because probably not more than a third or a fourth of the membership of the committee was present. If this is to be the final judgment of Parliament on a Bill of this kind, then the sooner Parliament appoints a court to deal with divorce cases, the better it will be for the honour of the Dominion of Canada.
Motion negatived.

Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I rise to a
question of privilege. A leaflet has been placed in my hands which purports on the face of it to be published by the Federal Press Agency, 47 Slater Street, Ottawa, Canada, the central publication and distribution office of the Conservative party of Canada. The leaflet reads:
Laurier and Quebec.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier once declared that if the Empire was ever in peril he would be " the first to stump Quebec.' Well, the Empire was in peril-the greatest peril it has ever faced. Did he stump Quebec? Did he call for French Canadian recruits? Not a bit of it. His lips were sealed in so far as any appeal to his fellow-countrymen was concerned. Why? Because Laurier, now as ever, cares not a whit for the Empire. Vote Conservative, for Borden backs Britain.
It is very seldom, Mr. Speaker, that I trouble the House with anything which concerns myself personally, with anything relating to opinions, speeches, actions, or

omissions on my part, but the statement contained in this leaflet is so absolutely contrary to the facts that I think I am justified in calling the attention of the House and of the country to it. The question is asked:
Did he call for French-Oanadian recruits? Not a bit of it.
As to my action in that regard, I have only to call to witness my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Casgrain). I attended a meeting in the city of Montreal with my hon. friend, who was then a private citizen, but who, I understand, came, directed by the Government, just for the purpose of asking Freneh-Canadians to recruit. I addressed other public meetings in Montreal on the same line, and on every occasion I gave evidence that my heart was very much in this fight in which England is now engaged. I have addressed meetings wherever there was occasion to do so and I would have done more if more had been needed; but I had the testimony' of the Prime Minister himself and of the Minister of Militia that French Canadians had answered nobly to the appeal, and that they had done as much as any of their fellow countrymen of English or of other origin. This morning I have a letter stating that French Canadians are crowding the recruiting offices and are being refused because for some reason no more are needed. In the face of this I characterize this leaflet as a falsehood and a malignant libel and slander.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I beg to say from the
Chair that, while I would not regard this as a matter of privilege according to my understanding of privilege, it is quite proper that the right hon. gentleman should draw attention to this leaflet as he has done and deny it if he wishes to do so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The leaflet to
which the right hon. gentleman alludes did not come to my attention, but I would like to inform him that he is not the only person upon whom animadversions have been made. I recollect that last autumn, when I was working at my duties from 16 to 18 hours a day, and remaining at my post against the advice of my physician, organs of the Liberal party, or some of them, in the province of Ontario, were attacking me because they said that not one single patriotic word had emanated from the lazy lips of Sir Robert Borden since the outbreak of the war.
Was that in a newspaper?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, from a very well recognized organ of hon. gentlemen opposite and during a period when they claimed to be observing a truce. Further than that, afterwards, when I did go forth to deliver certain addresses in this country which contained, in the judgment of every man in this country, not one controversial word, the same organs which had denounced me for holding my peace charged me with conducting a political compaign.

speechtext: Sir GEORGE FOSTER moved the third reading of Bill No. 112, to amend the Canada Grain Act:

I notice that in the amendment submitted by the minister there is no provision for settling cases of shortages of grain from one elevator to another, that is from an elevator in the West to a terminal elevator at the head of the lakes. I would ask if the minister .proposes to make such a provision later on?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The legislation which is here proposed has been suggested, and in my opinion is rendered necessary because of a particular phase of the grain transport business having to do with shortages which occur between the elevators at Fort William or Port Arthur and elevators in the East, on the lake carrying route. All parties to this controversy have been heard by the Government or by my department, and they have all had their opportunity to make their representations. At the close of a session it is not advisable to bring in very important legislation affecting large interests and to pass it through the House. My warrant for asking the House to pass this is, as I have stated, that all parties have presented their cases and we have full information. The other suggestion of my hon. friend which would involve the settlement of all shortages from the place of production to the elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur is a very much larger question in its way, and, if anything, a more important question. We are taking this step at this time on a very important section, involving somewhat the same principle as his suggestion. We will see how that works out during the year and then be in a better position to decide what measures may be taken in that or some other direction in a succeeding year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am in receipt this morning of a letter coming from a prominent gentleman connected with lake navigation and the carrying of grain. He represents to me that this legislation has been hasty and is not fair to the navigation interests. I shall read the concluding portion of the letter:
Apparently the unloading elevators have taken the position, which I assumed they would
take, and I understand now that on Saturday the min'ster gave some explanation to the House stating that the shippers, outloaders, and the carriers are agreeable to having the amendment to the Grain Act put through and that only some of the eastern elevators object.
I feel it only right that I should explain the situation to you and point out that as a vessel manager I do not agree with this proposed amendment at all, as it is no way to remedy one evil by creating another, or correcting the evil unfairly at the expense of every one interested.
I have no opinion of my own to express on this matter, for it is a very technical subject, and I am sure that only a few of us can understand it; but I thought it well to bring to the attention of the minister this protest from a man who is very prominently connected with the lake commerce.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Of course it is very difficult for all parties to see eye to eye on a question of this kind. Tb# correspondent of my right hon. friend is probably objecting to the compromise arrangement which it is proposed to make, and in reference to which representatives of all the different interests were called together. My right hon. friend will see that this legislation gives the Grain Commission power to take what measures seem to them right in order to settle the shortages. So far as this letter is a protest, it is a protest against something which has fallen through and not a protest against handing over this matter to the responsible management of the Grain Commission who Teally know more about this than any of us, and whose interests in the question are, I think, not only very intelligent but very sympathetic.

I desire to move an
amendment to the motion for the third reading of this Bill, not for the purpose of dividing the House, but [DOT] for the purpose of getting an expression of opinion. I beg to move:
That the Bill be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole for the purpose of amendment by striking out the word "shipper" where it occurs in the sixth line of section 120 (a).
The purpose of the Bill is to authorize the Grain Commission to examine into any question of shortage; to make a finding in regard to that shortage and to enforce that finding. Now the only parties who can be responsible for the shortage are, first, the elevator operators at the western lake terminal; secondly, the elevator operators at the eastern lake terminal, and thirdly, the carriers between
219*2

those two points. One of those three must be responsible for the shortage. So far as I understand the matter, there is no way in which the shipper can be responsible for the shortage; and if the shipper cannot be responsible for the Shortage, power should not be placed in the hands of the Grain Commission to hold him responsible. I do not imagine that the Grain Commission would give a decision laying the responsibility on the shipper when it did not rest there, but I think it very undesirable that the legislation should contain the suggestion that the shipper may be held responsible when he cannot possibly protect himself against that responsibility. The shipper, whether he ships from an interior point or from a terminal elevator, ships subject to the weighing in and to the weighing out of the terminal, by officials of this Government over whom a shipper has not and cannot have any control. Neither has he any control over the carrier nor over the eastern receiving elevator. Therefore the shipper cannot be held responsible in any degree for the shortage in shipments through Fort William. When his grain is received into the elevator he gets credit only for the grain that is weighed in by the Government weighmaster, and from the time that the grain is taken in hand by the Government weighmaster the shipper has no control whatever over it. Therefore, the shipper should not be placed on the list of those responsible for a possible shortage in the weight between the shipping elevator and the eastern port of delivery.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I should like to point
out that this amendment is hardly in the proper form. It asks that the Bill be referred back for the purpose of striking out certain words instead of asking that the Bill be referred back for further consideration.

The hon. member for
Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) is dealing with lomet'hing that does not come within the scope of this Bill. The original shipper does not ship through the terminal elevators but to them and he is left entirely out of the question after the grain has been weighed in. From that point forward the shipment is by an entirely different party. There must be some' method I apprehend of determining the amount of grain that goes into a vessel at Fort William for instance, and I do not know any very good reason why the man who loads the vessel with grain there should not be held ac-

countable for the amount of grain he claims to put into that vessel. If he does not/put in the number of bushels that he charges up to the buyey, there, ought to be some method of determining that the proper amount has not gone into the vessels. If there is a shortage when the grain arrives at the eastern port, whether Montreal, Midland, Port Colhorne, Goderich, or any of the other numerous places in the east to which grain is shipped, it does not necessarily follow that it is the fault of the lake carriers or even of those who have control of the grain at the eastern port. The shortage might be accounted for by the fact that the proper amount of grain was not put into the vessel at Fort William or whatever the shipping point was. The people in the Prairie provinces and further west would have no concern in that shortage at all. They are entirely through with the grain as soon as it lands at the elevator at the head of the Lakes. I may be mistaken, but I think the idea the hon. member for Edmonton had in mind was that these people would still be responsible if a shortage was found at the eastern point of delivery. That is entirely distinct from the object of the Bill. This legislation is not intended to touch the question of any shortage that might arise between the loading by the farmer or by the small elevator man in the West and the large elevator at the head of the Lakes.

When this Bill was in committee additions were made to section 4, and I notice that in both 120a and 120b, which were added to section 4 the word " shippers" appears. In answer to my hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. Wright) who is a grain grower in the West, let me point out this. He ships down from his farm in Saskatchewan to Fort William 10,000 bushels of wheat; when it reaches Fort William the elevator man takes it in and gives him a certificate for 9,900 bushels, which is 100 bushels short; he sends down that certificate and the bills of lading to the elevator man who took it in at Fort William, and says: Ship this wheat to James Richardson & Son at Kingston; they weigh it into the boat and ship it to Goderich for account of James Richardson & Sons, and when it reaches Goderich they say that there are only 9,800 bushels-does the hon. gentleman think that he as a shipper should be held responsible for the loss of that second hundred bushels?

il93

The hon. gentleman
is conjuring up a thoroughly imaginary proposition.

That is exactly what is
done.

That is exactly what is
not done.
It happens very frequently.

I beg to differ from my hon. friend. Everybody knows that the farmer of the We3t does not ship to the terminal elevators and does not load a vessel with grain going down to the big elevators on the lakes. There are not many farmers in the West who can load a quarter of a million bushels of grain through the elevator. The weight of the grain is finally determined when it goes into the terminal elevator at the head of the lakes unless it may be that he is shipping a carload of grain direct all rail and it goes down to a mill in the East. But if it is the intention to provide some kind of a remedy for the farmer of the West who might be subject to shortage, I think the question will have to be dealt with separately. It should not be mixed up with the question of the transportation of grain in the Great Lake carriers. The grain loses its distinctive individuality and there is no method of identifying the farmer's grain after it has gone . into the lake vessel. It is all put in the hold of the vessel and it would be almost impossible to trace it through the terminal elevators at Fort William and away back to the loading platform of the farmer who originally shipped it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: As the hon. gentleman has already spoken he could not properly go beyond an explanation in reference to the question raised by the hon'. member on this side of the House.
I was only trying to touch the point raised by the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb). I had no intention of going into the question.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
While I see some force in the argument of my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) that in the general course of events it could not be that the shipper entered into the question as to the responsibility for shortage, still, one can conceive of a case where possibly he might do so. I do not look upon it as a case between the Western farmer and the elevator companies or lake carriers. The shipper is in another category altogether. He is
not an exporter on the one hand or a farmer on the other. He is a grain dealer usually operating on the grain exchange at Winnipeg. However, the question comes in here: the lake carrier seems to be of the view that the shipper is the man who should in general.be responsible. Whether they are correct in that view or not, they take that view and they press it very strongly. Consequently, if we are to relegate to the Grain Commission we should relegate the whole question and let them decide it. Although we feel that the shipper should in general be exempt from the question, still it is evident that when we are relegating to the commission we should let the commission decide that as well as the rest. We give them no directions at all. We simply say that if in any specific case you will find the shipper has gained an advantage where the grain has been overweighed out of the elevator you have a right to adjust it accordingly. If they agree with the hon. member for Edmonton that in any case he should not be responsible, they will not hold him responsible. Surely it is the duty of the House, when we are submitting the question to a tribunal, because we cannot bring the parties to the question together, not to tie the hands of the tribunal but to submit to such tribunal the whole question and not a part alone.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I do not know that I can say anything to reinforce what has been already said, and particularly what has been said by my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Meighen), but there are two main facts in connection with it. In the first plate, it is not, I think, pertinent to try to confuse the original producer of the grain, in the guise of the small farmer, or even of the comparatively large farmer, with the shipper. He is largely the shipper of the grain from the locality but very often sails to the street buyer or the track buyer and so he has no interest in the grain thereafter. In many cases he ships from the loading platform and in many other cases he sands in quantities through the local elevator.	He is the shipper in theSe cases, but the facts of the case are that when you come to ship out from the elevators at FoTt William and Port Arthur, the original farmer is almost entirely eliminated. The grain at that point has got into the hands of the intermediate and laTge buyers and they are the people who are the shippers from that point on. The farmer, away

back in the producing centre, has very little interest as far as this legislation is concerned. The other fact is this: We have in this measure worked out an arrangement. If this measure is thought to be wise, we are handing over the matter of the adjustment of this much vexed question to a body which has more experience than we have, and it is only right that we should give to them broad powers to make the adjustment between all concerned. It is true in a sense that the shipper has no mechanical interest in, or power over, his grain after it has been weighed out of the Government elevator and the weight has been adduced. That is true, but he is still the owner of the grain and he has chief interest in it. In the case of the ovsr-weighing of grain, where it would be to the advantage of the shipper he should not be eliminated from the adjustment. The third fact is that it must be borne in mind that we are simply relegating this question to the board which understands the matter and will take every one of these interests into consideration. If the shipper has no interest, and it will so appear to them, he does not come into the adjustment at all, but if there is an interest and it so appears to them, why should we limit their power to spread the adjustment over all the parties to the transaction? I trust that my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) will not press his motion. This is a small piece of legislation which has been very carefully thought over and discussed with the Board of Grain CSommissioners, and we have put it in about the best possible way we could. I should be disposed to think that the House would be well advised to just let it go through without proposing further amendments. At the same time it is quite Open to any one to press his views.
Have I the right to say a Word now in conclusion?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Certainly.
I do not wish to trespass on the House, but I thought it was my prerogative.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

Well, then, I will not say anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce

I do not wish to prolong the discussion at all. I wish to correct the impression that seems to have occurred to the mind of the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Wright), and' to that of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster),	that I was
particularly advocating	the	case of
the rural producer and outside shipper. speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. Ill, to enable Canadians on active military service during the present war to exercise their electoral franchise.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman please explain this Bill, we have had no information so far.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The purpose of this Bill is to enable Canadians on active military service, whether in this country or outside of Canada, to exercise their electoral franchise. Under the provisions of this Bill, every soldier, twenty-one years of age and a British subject, will be entitled to vote in the event of occasion arising for him to exercise that right. That vote he will be entitled to have recorded within the electoral district wherein he has resided for thirty days preceding his enlistment or enrolment. That is the general rule proposed with regard to the locality as to which this right to vote shall be exercised. There is, however, a proviso that where any soldier has a right to vote, irrespective of this Bill, in any particular electoral district, he shall vote in that electoral district, and, of course in that electoral district only.
To provide means, to enable the soldier upon active service to register his vote is the purpose of the great bulk of the provisions of the Bill. The system may be summarized as follows:	It is proposed that
upon this law being enacted, ballots should be prepared sufficient in number for the number of men who may be entitled to exercise the right under this Bill.
Prepared by whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Printed as we would
print ballots for any ordinary election. There would be prepared also a form of affidavit to be made by the soldier who votes under this Bill, and a form of certificate to be given by the officer, who, under the Act would receive the ballots. These ballots being printed, a sufficient quantity would be sent to the different officers commanding at the military bases in Canada, to the officer commanding the Canadian troops in Bermuda, and to the office of the High Commissioner in London, whose secretary is constituted the custodian of these ballots. In the event of a writ being issued for an election, the fact would be at once communicated to the different officers commanding both in Canada and in Bermuda, and
21'JG

to the secretary of the High Commissioner's office in London. In the two latter cases, it would probably have to be done by telegraph, and provision is made for it being so done. On the receipt of this information, it becomes the duty of the custodians of these ballots to make a distribution of them to the persons entitled to receive them. As regards the commanding officers in Canada and Bermuda, that distribution would be made directly to the soldiers under their command. With regard to the ballot for the soldiers overseas, on receipt of information of the issue of an election writ, it would become the duty of the secretary of the High Commissioner to see that these ballots are forwarded to the different officers commanding the several units wherever they may be found. The method provided whereby the soldier is to vote is that being furnished with a ballot, he shall mark the ballot in the presence of a commissioned officer, but shall so mark it that while the officer shall be in a position to know that it is the soldier ibimself who marks the ballot, he will not be able to know in what way he marks it; that is, he will not be able to know how the soldier votes.
Will the officer be sworn?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As the power is conferred on commissioned officers, the Bill does not propose to require an oath from the officer in regard to the matter. It was considered that we might entrust that duty to the officer in his official capacity. If, on consideration of the Bill, the sense of the House should be that it would be desirable that the officer be sworn particularly for the purpose, I do not know that there would be any material objection to that being done. The ballots having been marked in the presence of the officer, the soldier also would make an affidavit as to his qualifications and as to the place in which he had resided before his enlistment or his address in any electoral district in which he may have had a vote irrespective of this Bill. The affidavit is to be sworn before the officer and attested by the officer. The ballot and the affidavit will be enclosed in an envelope and sealed by the officer who will also endorse upon the back of it a certificate that the person who made the enclosed affidavit is known to him as a member of his company, platoon, or whatever the subdivision may be and as the person whose name appears, and that, to the best of the officer's knowledge, the statements in the affidavit made by the soldier are true, 
these	envelopes	will be	addressedand	forwarded	by mail	to the
Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. It will become the duty of that officer, upon receipt of these ballots, to distribute them among the different electoral districts in which the votes are to be registered. In what electoral district the vote contained in a given envelope is to be oast will appear, of course, by the attestation on the exterior of the envelope made by the officer. On the face of that will appear the address given by the soldier. It was suggested that the soldier should state the electoral district; but it was pointed out that, particularly in view of our recent redistribution, there might be confusion as to the exact title of the district. With the address given it will be a simple matter for the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to distribute the ballots to the several districts in which they should be registered.
Has the Government a complete list of the names, post office addresses and residences of all the men who have enlisted?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
But representatives of
both candidates are present at the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand that, and before I have finished my explanation it will be seen that representatives of both candidates will control, to some extent at least, tnese declarations of the soldiers. In principle, if the soldier swears to his qualifications, I think that we may at least give to him the same credence that we give to voters in certain of the provinces of this Dominion. It is not considered an insup-

erable obstacle to their voting that there is not in existence an exact list showing where their residences have been in the past or what their qualifications are. 1 -o not quite see that we should refuse to tne soldier- whose name is not on a list what we are willing to give to the citizen who is in the same position. It will appear on the certificate on the exterior of the envelope where the ballot ought to be deposited, and it will be the duty of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, having received this envelope sealed, to affix his own seal to it, and, putting together "in one parcel all the envelopes that belong to a particular electoral district, to forward the bundle, properly sealed by himself, to the returning officer for that electoral district. Upon the receipt of such parcel containing ballots of this kind, it will become the duty of the returning officer to notify the candidates or their representatives that he has received such a parcel of ballots and that he will proceed, upon the day fixed for the election, at a certain hour after the close of the polls, to open this parcel and to deposit the ballots contained therein. In that way the candidates or their representatives will be enabled to control the operations of the returning officers in regard to these ballots. The ballot, when marked by the soldier, is to be folded, as all ballots are, in such manner that it will not appear on the exterior how he has voted. The returning officer, having given the notice mentioned, is on the polling day to proceed to open the parcel in the presence of the candidates or their representatives, and, having submitted the exterior of the envelopes to the examination of the parties interested, if there be no objection, it is his duty to open the envelopes, withdraw the affidavits and submit them to the candidates and their representatives. These being found regular and satisfactory, he is to take the ballot from the envelope and drop them in the ballot box, ijust as the deputy returnng officer takes the ballot from any voter who presents himself at the poll and drops it into the ballot box. These ballots so dropped into the box will be counted and credited to the representatives of the parties for whom these votes have been cast.
What safeguards are there that the ballots marked by the soldiers will be the ballots returned to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The safeguards are, that that ballot is, in the presence of the soldier, inserted in an envelope sealed by his officer.

The Bill does not say
"sealed."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If it doss not say
sealed," but we can provide for that. Certainly the intention was that it should.

What puzzles me is
what absolute safeguard there will be.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If we are looking for
absolute safeguards, I do not think that we can find them. We have to trust men in respect to the voting that is done at home; and notwithstanding all the precautions that we take, a dishonest officer can act dishonestly and defeat the purpose of the law.
When there are scrutineers at his elbow, acting on behalf of both parties, he cannot very well act wrongly, but there are no scrutineers at the front.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are no scrutineers at the front, nor will the ballot be deposited in the box at the front. What we have at the front is the commissioned officer of the men who are voting. We are, therefore, confiding to the commissioned officers of our troops the confidence that we give to the deputy returning officers in this country; and if that is a risk that we should not take, we have to admit that we are taking it. But I do not think that it can be suggested that we cannot place the same confidence in our officers who are at the front that we put in the deputy returning officers who are selected by the returning officers to preside over the operations that take place at the polls.

Does the minister mean that the only difference in the way of safeguards is that the commissioned officer is substituted for the deputy returning officer, and that in all other respects the safeguards are as great in the one case as in the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is not the presence or representatives of candidates; that is true.

And the officers are not
sworn.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I said to the hon. member, if it is considered necessary that we should swear these officers for this particular duty, personally I would see no objection to its being done. It is not provided in the Bill. As the matter presented

itself to the minds of those who submitted the Bill to the House, it did not appear to be necessary. It seemed to us that the honest performance of this duty might have been entrusted to an officer in his capacity of officer, relying upon the traditional honour of one who is an officer and a gentleman.
We swear our own returning officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, and I am not suggesting that it might not be advisable to swear the officers.

Would the minister
think it perfectly safe to leave the handing of the vote to deputy returning officers without scrutineers of either party being present?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I wish to state frankly now that if the view put forward is that before the soldier votes we must surround his vote with all of the protections which surround the vote of a man in this country, this Bill does not attain that object. Those who submitted this Bill thought, however, that the right in the exercise of which this Bill seeks to protect the soldier was of such importance that we should be willing, providing we had reasonable precautions, to waiye some of the details of the operations that surround the voting at home.

The minister has stated that some certain provision was recommended by somebody in the committee. I would like to have it understood that this Bill has not been recommended by the committee. It was opposed by the minority of the committee and was not even recommended by anybody on the committee. Probably there is no difference between us on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Absolutely none. I
said when the Bill wa3 laid before the House that the committee was not making a recommendation, was not unanimous in submitting it to the House, that the minority of the committee did not approve either of the measure in principle or of the method provided in the Bill for giving it effect; and I did not say that the committee had recommended this. I said that those who did recommend it took this responsibility. I do not hesitate to say that, so far as I am personally concerned-and I think I speak in that regard for a majority of the committee -we do recommend this Bill to the favourable consideration of the House.
[Mr. Doherty. 1

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
You do not
do it very strongly.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do it just as I do everything that I do, I do it sincerely. The strength with which I may do it depends on the force that my representations may exercise upon the judgment of the House, but I am prepared to say that I put this measure forward with all the sincerity with which I have ever put forward any measure. I am prepared to admit that it may be open to criticism in its details, and I am of course prepared to admit that there may be gentlemen in this House who can suggest a better method of carrying out what is proposed to be carried out; but in so far as the principle of the Bill is concerned, I would be surprised to find that there was not a general consensus that if this thing can be, and I believe it can be, properly carried out, we should see to it that the soldier who has sacrificed so much in order to do our work and to carry Canada's honour through this struggle, should not be asked in addition to all his other sacrifices to make the sacrifice of his right to have his voice heard in the determination of the public questions of this country. I did not think it was necessary for me to endeavour to make any extra evidence of the strength of my convictions, because I fancied that was a conviction that was shared by everybody.

The minister gives the
votes to those who are voters as well as to those who are not voters.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; we endeavour to secure to the man who is a voter a manner by which he can exercise his vote. But we say that the man who is a soldier and a British subject engaged actively in the service of this country and of the Empire shall have a vote for that reason, even if there be no other reason why he should have a vote. Somebody has said that the men who are good enough to do our fighting are good enough to do some of our voting.

Why do you not leave
out those who are under 21 years of age?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In that regard I think it might be fair that we should make that requirement of a man being of age. I would not very strongly resist a suggestion in this connection.
Why leave out the men serving in the navy?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Because as far as we
could ascertain, their number is very few. However, if hon. gentlemen's only objection to the Bill is that we have left out the men who are serving in the navy, I am sure, speaking for the majority of the committee, we shall be most happy to include the men serving in the navy. The Bill was originally drafted in that way, but two things were pointed out: In the first place, that the number of men serving in the navy who were properly speaking Canadians was very small, and, in the second place, that the sea is very wide and whatever means we may have to make the ballot reach the man who is on land wherever he may be, we have not the same means of making these ballots reach the men who are in the navy, and may be at sea where they cannot be reached.

They would be
more easily reached than the soldiers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If that is the only difficulty in the way we shall be most happy to extend this provision so as to make it apply to the navy.
Have the Government been in communication with the military authorities of Great Britain as to how far they will be prepared to give facilities for carrying out this Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. If there is one
thing that never occurred to my mind as a thing concerning which we should consult any outside authority, even the Imperial authorities, it is the question of how far we should extend the Canadian franchise. That'is a matter that I think belongs to this Parliament to determine
We should have to get permission before the soldiers could vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are providing that under the law of Canada there shall be a right, and we are providing a method by which that right can be exercised. We have absolute confidence that if the exercise of that right would interfere with the proper performance of the military duties of any Canadian soldier, he would, in the face of the major duty that was incumbent upon him as a soldier, sacrifice the right that we are securing to him. We have no doubt that the Imperial authorities to whom we have handed over our soldiers will see to it that the exercise of this right on the part of our soldiers is not allowed to interfere-even if we concede that there is a danger that our soldiers might allow it to interferewith the due performance of their military duties. In this country, all of us sometimes find ourselves in situations where the performance of a duty, very much less important than the performance of the military duty of a soldier, makes it impossible for us to vote. But because that may happen, are we going to refuse to provide a method whereby the soldier who, at the time he is called upon to vote, finds himself in a position to exercise that right without interference with the performance of his military duties-are we going to say that that soldier shall not have an opportunity of exercising that right? We are not seeking to impose anything upon the War Office; we are not seeking to interfere with the control of the soldiers that Canada has given into the hands of the War Office. But we are saying that those soldiers are Canadians, and that as they are Canadians they shall have the right to register a vote; and we are taking pains to provide a means for the exercise of that right. How that can be an interference with the control of their military superiors, I must confess I am at a loss to see. Undoubtedly the military authorities will see to it that these men perform their military duties, and undoubtedly not one of our soldiers would for a single moment dream of dropping his military duty, if that were necessary, to avail himself of the opportunity of exercising the right that this Bill seeks to give him.	But his right	will
be recognized.	We are simply proproviding means whereby he may exercise that right. But if paramount and superior duties interfere with the exercise of that right, he will be in the unfortunate position of not being able to avail himself of the right- that we are recognizing to him; just the same as many of us in this country are sometimes prevented from voting by some duty, although that duty may not be so important as the military duty of a soldier. I am at a loss to see how the idea arises that, in recognizing to this man a right, and providing a method for its exercise, we are in any manner whatever interfering with the military control of the War Office and its officers.
Several British subjects in my riding are French reservists, and are now fighting with tne armies of France. Will the minister approach the French Government in order to let these men vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is a somewhat exceptional case, to which our attention has not been previously called.
Quite a lot of French reservists from Montreal are with the French army.
Will the minister give votes to British subjects who are prisoners of war in Germany?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We are giving them the right to vote, the same as we are giving that right to every other Canadian soldier. If they are detained by the enemy I am afraid that will prevent their availing themselves of the right to exercise their vote. iThe hon. gentleman seems to think that if it can be shown that any soldier will not be able to vote under this Act, we should in consequence not let any other soldier vote. It would be just as reasonable if somebody got up and said: We have our General Elections Act, but there may be a man sick in hospital who may be unable to rise from his bed to vote; what are you doing for him?
Arrangements could be made whereby the man in the hospital could vote. The ballots might be sent to the nurses.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman propose that that should be done?
I do not know, it is a very difficult question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then he ought to condemn the existing election law.

If it be possible, I am in favour of giving our soldiers the right to vote, but the difficulty is as to the means. Let me ask a question. A soldier who wants to vote conscientiously would want to be informed of the issues, but the ballot that it is proposed to send to him says nothing about the issues. The soldier has to vote for or against the Government, or for an Independent. Does the minister propose any method whereby campaign literature issued by both sides shall be forwarded to the soldiers, so that they may be informed on the questions at issue?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The idea of providing for electioneering among the soldiers never occurred to the committee.
The minister will find several of the officers engaged in electioneering.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We were not looking at this matter from the point of view of an electioneering device.
Qui s'excuse s'accuse.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The first suggestion of electioneering came from the hon. gentleman himself, and it is not surprising that I should repudiate it at once. He did not give me time to accuse myself, but went forward to suggest t)he accusation. I was going on to say that if the doctrine is laid down that, unless you can get an arrangement under which every soldier will be able to register his vote, you should not let any soldier vote, then the Bill might as well be dropped. We have an election law in this country under whose enactments large numbers of people who have the right to vote find themselves, by reason of certain circumstances, in a position where they cannot avail themselves of this right, and there will be some soldiers who will not be in a position to exercise this right-the prisoners of war in Germany, for instance.
Get the German commanding officers to assist you. That will be just as reasonable as this proposal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the hon. member was drafting the Bill, perhaps he would think the German commanding officer a suitable person for an election officer; but the majority of us do not think so.

Has the hon. Minister
thought of a different kind of ballot form, than that provided for in Schedule A of this Bill? Because the ballot form provided for in the Bill cannot most certainly meet all the different cases which may happen to occur. Let us imagine for instance a case where there will be three independent candidates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As regards the details, when we go into committee, I think hon. members will find that I have a perfectly

open mind and that I am quite prepared to accept any suggestions which will improve the machinery by which the purpose sought to he attained by this Act is carried out. The thing that is important is the purpose in view, and while we suggest this method of doing it, we do it realizing that it no doubt would be possible to improve it and we will he only too anxious to accept any suggestions in that direction.

Does the Minister of Justice know whether the Imperial Parliament is providing any such means to enable the English soldiers to east their votes? It may be that they will have to hold an election in England before it is necessary to hold one in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not aware that the Imperial Parliament is legislating upon this subject. As I said a little while ago, in regard to the other matter, I would be disposed to let the Parliament of Canada take the responsibility of determining what is best from the point of view of the exercise of the franchise in Canada, and leave it to the Parliament of the United Kingdom to exercise its own' judgment as to what may be a desirable course for itself.
Has there been any demand from the soldiers for this Bill?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would like to say, in regard to many of the questions, that while I am very reluctant to interfere, they do not seem to me to be exactly in order at this stage. The second reading of the Bill is simply the stage in which the principle of the Bill is discussed.
This is the principle, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is asking a question
in regard to what is taking place in another part of the world. The principle of the Bill is on the right of the soldiers to vote.

Surely it is important
to consider what is being done in the mother of parliaments?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I know, but the asking
of questions which would be more appropriate in the committee stage does not seem to me to be exactly in order. I have been reluctant to interfere or to interrupt hon. *members in putting these questions. 1 think hon. gentlemen should remember that we are simply discussing the principle of the Bill and that these details may be 139

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: considered when the House is in Committee of the Whole.
May I ask, Mr. Speaker, if you consider my question out of order?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would regard the question as rather out of order.

With every disposition to regard as important the suggestion of the right hon. the Prime Minister, may I ask a supplementary question in regard to what I have already said? Would not the minister consider it very unfortunate if a different view should be found to prevail in the mind of Lord Kitchener in regard to the facilities for voting at the front from that which seems to animate this Government? Would not my hon. friend think that it would be an unfortunate contingency should it arise?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not quite grasp
the seriousness of the risk. I am not supposing for a moment that Lord Kitchener, or any other British military authority, would want to interfere with the exercise of this right merely because in his opinion Canadian soldiers ought not to vote in Canada.
The military authorities are in absolute control of everything going on at the front.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, they are in absolute control and I was going on to say that I have no doubt that they will so exercise that absolute control as to see that anything that interferes with the soldier's paramount duty does not take place.
What is his paramount duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: His paramount duty-
It is to fight, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: His paramount duty is at the front, and his paramount duty is to bear himself like a man in the great struggle in which he is engaged, but I cannot see that it is inconsistent with the perfect performance of that duty, assuming that the conditions and circumstances permit of it, that he should give some thought to what may be good for Canada here at home and what may be good for her from the point of view of the determination of how she is to be governed. It seems to me that the two things ought to go hand in hand. The same spirit which animates the soldier to his duty in the fighting line should animate the citizen to do his duty in expressing consci-

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
entiously and honestly what he believes to be best upon the great question of the control of the affairs of his country and the great question of the preservation of her-in-terests all of which are involved in any general election. I cannot see that there is any inconsistency between the performance of these two duties. I have difficulty in quite seizing whence comes the suggestion that in voting there is something that involves a departure from the highest principles and the highest ideals. I put fighting and voting on the same level. They are both of them duties to one's country and I cannot conceive why it should be suggested that there is something derogatory in making it possible for a man to perform both of these duties at the same time. I cannot conceive why it should be suggested that we have to apprehend that Lord Kitchener will intervene to prohibit this and create an unpleasant situation. I have no doubt that Lord Kitchener and the military authorities will see that the opportunity we are giving the	soldier	to	exercise	this	right isnot	allowed	to	interfere	with	the performance of his paramount duty. It is not our idea that the soldier himself would wish it to be so. We are willing to trust him with this right without fear that, because he has it and we have given him the means of exercising it, he will, for the sake of exercising it, forget the great purpose for which he is where he is. But if the military authorities in one portion of the seat of war, or in another portion, or perhaps throughout the entire front, find that conditions make it necessary that the men should be placed in such a position as they will not be able to avail themselves of this right, I do not see that any unfortunate situation is created or that it will be unfortunate if they cannot, by reason of the call of a higher duty, avail themselves of the opportunity that we are putting before them. What we are doing is this: We are recognizing the right of the soldier to vote; we are endeavouring to prevent him from being called upon to sacrifice that right because he has gone forward to the front, and with all respect, I think there is no body in this world other than this Parliament that has any right to express any opinion upon the question whether that ought to be done or not. Whether it is consistent with the performance of military duty properly under given circumstances that a man should get time or opportunity to vote, is a question for the War Office, and one which I have no doubt it will properly decide; but I cannot for one mo-
ment suppose that Lord Kitchener or any other of the British authorities is going to take upon himself to determine merely as an abstract question whether or not we in Canada should so legislate that our Canadian soldiers shall have recognized to them their rights as citizens; and provide a means whereby they may exercise that right.

To clear up
this point and to give the minister an opportunity to clear it up, I may say that I have been told by a man who has been a soldier for years that it would be contrary to military discipline as practised in the British army for a soldier at the front to vote. If that is so, would it not have been wise for the Government to solicit that information before putting Parliament and the country to a political discussion upon the question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not aware whether there is such a rule as the hon member has suggested, but assuming that there is such a rule, I do not know that that would be a conclusive reason why we should say that a soldier shall have no right to vote, and that we shall provide no means by which he may do so. With all respect, I would think that under such circumstances it might perhaps be for those who made that rule of military discipline to consider whether they had not a duty in the premises, but that is a matter for their consideration. As I said before, it is for us to determine who shall have the franchise in this country, and to provide a method for those who should have it whereby, in conformity with the law of this country, they may exercise that right. If they be subject to other duties of military discipline which prevent their exercising that right, we at all events have done our part; the people of Canada have shown to the men who have gone forward to the front to fight for them that, so far as it depends upon the people of Canada speaking through their parliamentary representatives, every right which those men might otherwise have shall be guaranteed to them, and that in so far as the people of Canada can furnish them a means to exercise that right, they shall have that means. The responsibility for the rules of military discipline will rest

with those who make them, and we do not undertake to over-ride them. We have done our full duty when we provide under our law for the recognition and protection of the soldier's rights as a citizen, when we make it clear to him that we do not force him to add to all his other sacrifices the sacrifice of his right of franchise as a citizen. What may be the proper rule of discipline is for the military authorities to determine, and whether that rule of discipline should interfere with the exercise of the right of the soldier as a citizen, must of course, by force of circumstances and in the nature of things, be determined by the military authorities.
At one o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at three o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Before the House rose I had endeavoured to set forth, the principle of the measure and to give its outlines. I was led quite willingly into more detail than was strictly necessary by questions which I am very happy to answer. I would like to point out that the idea of soldiers on active service voting in an election, or a method being provided whereby persons who are not able, as soldiers are not able, to be in their own electoral districts at the time of polling, may be enabled to vote, is not new. They are both new, I think, in this country; but as long ago as the Civil War in the United States, we saw the right to the franchise of the soldier in the field recognized and an effective method provided whereby he could exercise that franchise. It is quite true that the circumstances were not identical with those surrounding our soldiers to-day, but it is also true that those circumstances offered greater difficulties to the exercise of the franchise than our own soldiers would labour under so long as they remain within Canada. In the course of the American Civil War no less than thirteen states of the Union provided a system whereby the soldiers in the field were enabled to vote, and under these provisions 150,000 votes were cast in the election of 1864. The method by which these votes were taken differs from that which this Bill proposes to provide. It was possible there to provide differently, because the conditions were different. An arrangement was made whereby the different units chose election officers, and these election officers held the polls and took the ballots in the ordinary way and these ballots were for-139i
warded. In some of the siates provision was made that a soldier was entitled to register his vote in any electoral district in which ihe had resided for a period of ten days anterior to his enlistment. As the House is aware, the elections in the United States, even for the presidency or other federal office, are under the laws of the different states, each of these states electing a certain number of men to represent it in the Electoral College. As between states provisions differ in detail, but, generally, the vote was taken in the way I have indicated, and these votes were gathered by commissioners or electoral officers. These electoral officers or commissioners, as is provided here, wrote certificates on the back of the ballots, and the ballots were then sent to the judge of the electoral district in which the vote was to be cast, and it was then cast and counted practically in the manner which the Bill suggests the votes of our soldiers should be cast and counted. There was also provision, as in our Bill, for qualified electors establishing their qualification by means of affidavit. Many of the states of the Union have provision whereby persons absent for other reasons than the fact that they may be engaged in military service are enabled t-o vote. One of the states makes this provision "with regard to soldiers in particular as a permanent law, but other states provide means by which any absentee can record his vote. I need not go into the matter further than to say that these measures do not differ, I believe, materially, from the system we propose. Provision is made for the enclosure of the ballot in the envelope and for its being forwarded; and, of course, where it is essential, in order to vote, that a person should be registered upon the list, provision is made for the establishment of the fact that he is so registered. In Australia, there is provision for a vote by absentees, and similar provision is made in New Zealand, Queensland, Victoria, and Tasmania. I may refer especially to the Tasmania law, where the machinery for the transmission of the vote is almost identical with that suggested here. Of course, it does not involve the intervention of military officers, because it is a law of general application under whose operation all persons who are absent from their electoral districts may exercise their franchise.
That vote is taken before such officers very much in the same way as we propose that the votes of our soldiers shall be taken; it
