The answer received from the Prime * Minister of N'ew Zealand was as follows:
In reply cable 28 your clerk House of Commons. Bill referred to passed and votes of all soldiers who left before general election recorded. Total votes, 10,000.
Were the votes of the soldiers taken before they left New Zealand?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, this Bill applied only to the soldiers who had left New Zealand. The law in New Zealand to which I refer, and which is referred to in these messages, was passed exclusively for the

purpose of enabling soldiers who had left New Zealand to record their votes. Saction 2 of that Act is:
Every member of any expeditionary force sent from New Zealand to serve in be war in which His Majesty is at present engaged, shall be entitled to vote in the manner hereinafter prescribed.
Then, in dealing with the appointment of electoral officers this point is further made clear:
Electoral officers may be appointed out of New Zealand for the purpose of enabling any person to record his vote under this Act who is a member of any expeditionary force sent out of New Zealand before the passing of this Act.
The soldi 3rs who had not left New Zealand could vote under the general law providing for absentee voting.
Is the minister able to state where the soldiers cast their votes?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have not that information, but wherever they were, they were outside of New Zealand, and wherever they were, they would have been entitled to vote under that Act. As long ago as 1864 provision was made in the neighbouring republic to enable soldiers in the field to vote. The	Government and the
Congress of the United States in that day did not fear that a soldier would fight less well because he also voted in the elections upon which the fate of his country might depend just as fully as on the result of a war. We have the further fact that in all the different states of the Union, and the different dominions of this Empire that I have mentioned, a system for the registering of the votes of people who were absent from their own electoral district has been in force and in operation, and, as I am informed, has given rise to no ground for complaint. We are after all not in the face of any very novel proposition. Large and important parts of the world, where the ballot is looked upon as of as great sacredness and of as great importance as we look upon it, have found it possible to devise a method by which to get an honest and a safe vote of persons who were not actually at home. Some of these countries have gone so far as to extend the advantages of such a method to people who were absent on their own private and personal business only, and I am not prepared to say that they did not do properly. But I do ask the House, should we hesitate to take the risk in respect to our soldiers that they have been willing to take in the interest of persons whose absence
was attributable only to their attention to their proper affairs. Should we not take the risk when it is a question of endeavouring to protect in the exercise of their right of franchise men who are absent from their homes and their country, for Canada's affairs, for the affairs of this Empire, and when their absence involves the risking of their very lives. New Zealand has solved the problem under practically the identical circumstances in which we are confronted with it. I may say that it is not the first time, that New Zealand has set a good example to the other countries of the world, and I fancy we would make no mistake in following her lead.
I think I have said all that I can say with usefulness or advantage in moving the second reading of this Bill and commending it to the House for adoption. Some query has been made as to the strength of my commendation. As I said in answer to that question the House must judge as to the strength with which I have presented it. For my own part I pretend to nothing more than to commend it with all earnestness and all sincerity. I believe that it is impossible to justify the questioning of the soundness of the principle. I have seen a good deal of criticism of it, but it has seemed to me that the criticism rested upon the assumption that everything that surrounded the exercise of the franchise necessarily involved ignoble and unworthy dispute .and strife. I cannot recognize the truth of that proposition. I cannot for one moment conceive that you are going to throw disorder and disunion into the ranks of our troops because you merely afford to each man, at his own option and in the exercise of his own liberty, an opportunity of recording his voice upon the question of how his country ought to be governed. I commend this Bill with all the sincerity and all the earnestness of which I am capable. I shall certainly be very glad of any suggestions that may serve to make it more workable, and to make it more effectually and safely attain the purpose in view. I commend it personally in no partisan spirit, and I have every confidence that it will be received and dealt with in no partisan spirit. I am satisfied that we ought to be able to all get together in a common endeavour to give to the men who are carrying to-day Canada's honour in their hands-the men who have possibly put many of us who are at home and will have every facility to vote, to the blush when we compare our conduct with theirs-the opportunity which Canada
COMMUlN*
extends practically to all her sons, to have each his say, and to make his voice heard in the determination of the great issues upon which the future of Canada depends. To my mind everything that tends to facilitate the exercise of his franchise by every man entitled to vote, ought to be encouraged. There is no doubt that, looking at this from the point of view of the right of the soldier, the question is one of very great importance, and I do not think we need look further than to the fact that it is intended to afford him protection in the exercise of 'his rights, to find ample justification for making an effort to enable him to exercise that right. But over and above the rights of the soldier, or of any individual, is Canada's right to have her people vote. The country has the right to see that every honest man within her boundaries should give to her the advantage of his advice and his opinion as to the manner in which her affairs should be governed and directed. We count that
50.000	of Canada's sons will be absent from us before this war is over. We are ready to look forward to the possibility of twice
50.000	men being absent from our borders before this war is over. Is it fair to ask Canada to lose the advantage of having those 50,000 or 100,000, or other thousands that may be added to that number, cast their vote and give their views as to what is best for her? * Ts it not presumable that these thousands of men are among the best that Canada has to give, and shall we lightly sacrifice the advantage to Canada of their participation in decisions that may be as fraught with importance to her future as anything that possibly is involved in this war? I say from the point of view of this country that we should strain every nerve to secure to her the advantage of the participation in any election that may take place of these, her noblest and her best sons.
In conclusion, I simply want again to say that I ask ultimately the acceptance of this measure, and that as to the details, they ought to be given the best consideration of which we are capable. I am satisfied that there are hon. gentlemen in this House who can suggest methods of working this plan out that will be an improvement on those that the members of the committee who do commend the Bill have been able to find. I would in a very special manner welcome the aid and co-operation of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), who said this morning that with the principle of the Bill he was quite in agreement. I know no man in this House who can give more

valuable aid towards the solution of such difficulties as the giving effect to the important principle involves, than that very hon. gentleman. This morning it seemed to me that there was on the part of some members a disposition to laugh at this measure. I would be sorry to suppose, that that disposition, if it did exist, would persist. I should not like to make any reference to the class of people of whom it has been said:	They came to laugh but remained
to pray. Still less would I flatter myself that any words of mine could influence the state of mind of any hon. gentleman. But I have absolute confidence that if hon. gentlemen of this House will give serious thought to the principle involved, they will realize that the matter is a serious one, and that it calls for our most earnest consideration. I have confidence that if this House gives to this Bill the serious consideration that it deserves, the Bill, whether it be perfect now or not, will leave this House a fairly perfect measure. I do not question that there are difficulties in the way of providing a suitable method, but I believe we have found a solution. I do not question that there may be a better solution.
I recognized at the very outset that there were difficulties in the way, but I was surprised to see that because I had said there were difficulties, some people inferred that it was impossible to find a solution. When it is a question of doing a thing that, ought to be done, difficulties only exist in order that they may be overcome, and I am satisfied that with the earnest co-operation of the members of this House, without distinction of party, we shall triumphantly overcome the obstacles that stand in the way of the realization of the proposal 'of this Bill; and that the Parliament of Canada shall not separate until it has seen to it that should occasion arise our soldiers shall have their right to their vote protected, and Canada shall have the assurance of the benefit of their participation in any election that may take place.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My hon. friend the Minister of Justice has expressed the. hope that all those who had anything to do with this measure would approach it in a spirit of candour. Speaking for myself, I will say very candidly-and I hope my hon. friend will believe me, for I am speaking as sincerely as he has spoken-that I shall approach this measure in no other spirit than that which he has prayed for. There is no one in this House, I am sure, who would be disposed to question this measure,

if the object of it could be attained consistently with the spirit and letter of our constitution. But I have to observe at once to my hon. friend that this measure is, I will not say revolutionary, but certainly very much more extensive than any we have to-day upon the statute book. This proposed legislation creates a new franchise.
I am fairly familiar, though perhaps not so familiar as he, with the legislation of 1864 in the United States during the Civil War. I am aware that bn that occasion several of the States of the Union passed laws to allow their soldiers in the field to cast their votes at the presidential election. I think I am correct in stating, however, that on no such occasion did any of those States create a new franchise. They simply provided that those who were electors in the States should be enabled to cast their votes in the field. But my hon. friend knows that the very first disposition of the Bill which he has brought down for our consideration is the creation of a franchise which does not exist to-day. My hon. friend gave the very inspiration of this legislation when, in the course of his observations, he stated that one who is good enough to take a share in the fight which is now going on, not only for the Empire, but for the whole of civilization, fs good enough to take a share in the auministration of this country. Let me observe at once that while these are glittering words they are, after all, nothing but words. They do not stand analysis, and the falsity of that phrasing of words is shown by the very first line of the first disposition of this Bill:
Every male British subject of twenty-one years of age or upwards serving in the military forces of Canada in the present war. . . who, when he was appointed to or enlisted or enrolled in such forces, . . . shall be entitled to vote.
My hon. friend stated that any man who takes a share in this fight ought to be allowed to cast a vote in the impending election, and to be given a share in the administration of the country, but my hon. friend is aware-the statement has been made on the floor of this House-that there are within the Canadian forces hundreds, nay, perhaps thousands, of Americans who crossed over to this country for the purpose of enlisting and who are to-day taking a share in the fight. It is a matter of history that when the war broke out in August last, thousands of Americans who were in Paris, impelled by the sacredness of the cause for which France was fighting,
at once gave up their life of luxury and took up the life of the soldier; and to-day these men are in the trenches doing their share in the fight for France, for England, for civilization. According to the dictum of the Minister of Justice, it is not only those who are British subjects who are entitled to take a share in the administration of this country, but all of our soldiers who are in the fight. If you maintain this principle, then, by a parity of reasoning, these Americans should also be given a share in the administration of the country. But no one would think of that, because it is inconsistent with responsible government as we understand it that those who are not subjects of the Realm should have the franchise, and so that class has to be eliminated. Again, hundreds of our fellow citizens, boys of our own flesh and blood of 16 or 17 or 18 years of age, have cast aside their prospects in life and risked everything in order to take a share in the fight which is going on. These young men did not wait until they were 21 years of age. My hon. friend does not contemplate giving them the right of suffrage, 'because the law is universal that the right of suffrage shall not be entrusted to those who are not of age. Therefore, it is not a truism to say, as was said by my hon. friend this morning, ithat he who is good enough to share in the fight is good enough to share in the administration of this country. We have laws and regulations, the result of the wisdom and experience of ages, which have determined that we may expect the blood and the sacrifice of the soldier, and yet that the soldier is not entitled to cast a vote in the administration of the country. That is so in this country; it is so in Great Britain; it is so in the United States. There are uniform laws governing the exercise of civil and political rights which no nation has yet contravened.
The first blemish I find in the measure of my hon. friend is that it creates a new franchise. If my hon. friend had been content with proposing a measure which would enable the soldier who is an elector to give his vote, it would have been less objectionable than this measure is. Sir, I need not recall to you the fact that in this country we have no Dominion franchise; we take the franchises of the provinces, but to-day we are creating a Dominion franchise for a certain purpose. The very example which my hon. friend has given of the American legislation of 1864, does not prove his case,

but is rather against it, because the law of 1864 was not passed by Congress. The several states of the Union which had the right to legislate with reference to the franchise passed the laws, and if such a law is to be passed in this country, it ought to be left to the provinces which have the right to legislate with reference to the franchise.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does the right hon. gentleman contend that Congress had any constitutional power whatever to pass such a law? We have.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
No doubt we have the power; the only question is whether we should exercise the power. It is not a question of power. I grant that we have the power to a certain extent, but I will show later on that we have no power to pass such a law as this. We have the power to pass a law which confers the franchise. We can discard to-morrow the provincial franchises upon which our elections have been carried on from 1867 to 1882 and from 1900 to the present day. But my hon. friend adds to the franchises of the provinces a new franchise especially for one class of His Majesty's subjects. The object of the Bill is to give to soldiers who are not in the country the right to vote. My hon. friend know as well as I do that there is in this country, and there will always be, a certain class of subjects who cannot exercise the franchise on election day. It was only a few days ago, when we were discussing a Bill-I think it was one of the electoral Bills-that the statement was made on one side and not contradicted on the other, that railway men-conductors, firemen and men of that class-cannot on election day cast their votes. The trains of the country must go on; certain duties have to be performed and the man who has to perform these duties cannot vote. Is there any difference in this respect between the railway man and the soldier? The railway man is not alone. The sailor, the fisherman, and the lumberman are very often not able to cast their votes. Within my own remembrance we have had three elections in winter time-in 1874, 1887 and 1891-and those whose memories go back to those days must recall that in many a constituency men who were voters could not register their votes because they were away in the bush doing their work as lumbermen. Between the soldier, the lumberman, the fisherman, the farmer and any other class, there is no difference whatever in this respect; all are subject to the same 
laws and all are equal before the law. We all certainly are proud of the soldier. But the soldier, in our economy, is no more entitled to favour than any other class of the community. The man who digs in the trenches of a railway is just as much entitled to favour as the man who digs in the trenches in France. The man who. farms, who fishes, or who lumbers has just as much right to his vote as the soldier. But we make a special provision for the soldier. What do we give him? We. recognize the duties which he performs for the country, we recognize the sacrifices which he makes, we recognize the dangers to which he is exposed and, therefore, if he is disabled, we provide to keep him for the rest of his days, and if he loses his life we provide for those who are dependent upon him. But when it comes to the matter of the franchise, all subjects of the King are on a footing of absolute equality.
There are in the Bill of my hon. friend provisions for the soldier who is at home and provisions for the soldier who is out of the country fighting in Europe. As to the soldier who is at home, there can be no necessity for any law. If he is in the country he can easily be allowed to vote where he is registered, and the military authorities would certainly give him leave to go wherever he had to go to record his vote. Therefore the measure applies only to the man who is serving out of the country-the man who has enlisted, and is no longer in Canada, but is in Bermuda or in Europe. This man is no longer under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Parliament. Every one of the 50,000 men who have left the country, or who will leave the country, is no longer under the control and jurisdiction of this Parliament; he is a part of the British Army; he is under the control of British authority; he is under the jurisdiction of the War Office, and the War Office alone has the right to pass legislation for him or against him. My hon. friend gives power under such circumstances, but to whom does he give the power? Who is to exercise the authority? My hon. friend is trying by an Act of this Parliament to impose a duty upon the officers of the British army. Let me say to my hon. friend at once that every line of his Bill, even after it has been sanctioned by the Senate, even after it has been assented to by His Royal Highness the Governor General, is so much waste paper. This Parliament has no rignt to pass any legislation to impose any duty upon the officers of the British army, and

my hon. friend has to some extent recognized this.
Before I proceed further let me go back to another radical disposition of this Bill by which the man who is going to vote is not going to vote as any man in Canada is going to vote: he is not going to vote for a candidate, he is not going to vote for a man, but he is going to vote for a party. This is the first time in British legislation, as far as my poor knowledge goes, that we have ever seen such a provision of law. We live under party government, but up to this time we have never carried party so far as to make it the object of an election. This is the first time, I repeat, as far as my information goes, and I believe that my information is absolutely accurate, that a voter in a British country will have been called upon to express his opinion, not upon a candidate but upon a party. Is that in accordance with the principle of British legislation? Although we believe in party, we Tespect the intelligence of the voter so much that we allow him to exercise his free judgment in voting upon the candidate rather	than upon	the party.
It is impossible to separate the party from the candidate and the candidate from the party; and in every election there are men who belong to one party who refuse to cast their vote in favour of the candidate of that party, because they are not in sympathy with him. I will give a case in point. In the election of 1911, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister carried the city of Halifax, hut a political opponent was elected at the same time with him. There was a dual contest: two candidates on each side and two to be elected, but it was not the ticket of one party or the ticket of the other that was elected, because while my right hon. friend the Prime Minister was at the head of the poll, his chief political opponent was next to him. What conclusion are we to draw from that? That a large proportion of the Conservative electorate did not believe in the other candidate and preferred to give their votes to the candidate of the other party. But why does my hon. friend not allow the ordinary machinery to be used, and why does he not permit the soldier at the front to vote for the candidate? The answer is that it is impossible to do so. For my part, I am not willing to create a new franchise, because I think that is absolutely wrong; but I am quite willing that the soldier who is a voter to-day should be allowed to vote if it is possible to provide means to
enable him to vote. As I said before, however-and I come back to this idea-the whole Bill is radically wrong in this, that you are trying to exercise legislative authority over those over whom you have no authority at all.
There is a curious provision in the Bill as to those who are to be the registering officers. The ballots are to be sent to the Secretary of the High Commissioner in London and he is to send them-where? This is where the impossibility of the thing is disclosed. Let me call the attention of my hon. friend to section 3, subsection 2:
If the corps is in Europe, the clerk of the Crown in Chancery shall notify by telegraph cable the secretary of the High Commissioner for Canada of the issuing of the writ, and the secretary shall thereupon send a sufficient number of ballot papers, affidavits and envelopes to the proper officer or officers, and such officer or officers shall give each volunteer entitled to vote a ballot paper, affidavit and envelope.
Where do you find any definition in this Bill as to who is to be the proper officer or officers? There are now over 30,000 of our soldiers in Europe, who are part of the British army, and the units which existed when they left Canada are no longer the units in Great Britain or France. Those
30,000	men may be found in 30 different regiments, in 300 different companies. Who, therefore, is the proper officer or officers to become the returning officer?
The difficulty is so great that my hon. friend has not tried to solve it; he has left this vague disposition in the Bill. When you have a permanent organization which is running its ordinary course every day, you can refer certain duties to the proper officers; but this is not a permanent organization. It is not even a temporary organization; it is no organization at all; it has to be made for the occasion, and there is no disposition in this Bill to say where the ballots are to go. How can the Secretary of the High Commissioner, who is entrusted with the duty, know where the ballots are to go, and how will he be informed as to where the 30,000 or 50,000 4 p.m. men are? He does not know unless he can know by the grace of the War Office, and he does not know to whom he should address the envelopes and documents mentioned in this subsection. Is the proper officer to be the general of the division or the colonel of the regiment or the captain of the company? Who is to have authority over there? The weak point in the Bill, to which my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) referred when he questioned the minister

upon it, is that you are imposing upon 20 or 30 or 40 officers of the British army duties in regard to which they have received no information and as to which they know nothing at all. This consideration, it seems to me, should show very forcibly to my hon. friend that, apart from the fact that we have no authority to give any instructions to officers of the British army, it is impossible to say where and how this Bill is to be carried out if it becomes law.
All the points in this Bill are more or less technical, but I come now to a consideration which is very practical and as to which the minister, when he was questioned, did not in my opinion give any satisfactory answer. Elections are felections, whether they are at the front or elsewhere. They mean passion in ithe voter and in those who are inspiring the voter. The right of election presupposes the right of selection; and, if you give to the soldiers who are now at the front the right to vote, you also thereby give to the Government or to the Opposition the right to canvass. You cannot expect that the soldiers are going to perform their duty as electors unless they are instructed upon the issues. There is in this country not only the broad issue of the war^tlie issue of the war is of course the supreme issue-but many other considerations which will and must influence the judgment of the electors, and the soldier has a right to be instructed upon them. If you give to the soldier who is today in the trenches the right to vote, you sanction also the possibility of canvassing him; you sanction also the introduction into the army of the canvasser. I do not know how canvassers would be received in the British army; but there is another more insidious means of canvassing which is possible: you can canvass by mail, and who knows that the trenches will not be flooded with the kind of literature of which I gave the House a sample this morning? This is not a vain idea on my part, because this literature is issued by a great party, and it can go wherever there is a vote to be reached; and according to this Bill, if it becomes law, there is a vote to be reached in the trenches of France as there is in this country.

speechtext: The House resumed, consideration of the motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice) for the second reading of Bill, No. Ill, to enable Canadians on active military service during the present war to exercise their electoral franchise.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It would be a mere truism for me to remind hon. gentlemen that the exercise of the franchise has always been surrounded with safeguards, not only to secure a correct expression of the opinion of the electors, but also to insure the due performance of their duties by the election officers and to establish a measure of absolute fair play between party and party. Our system of Government is a complicated one, but the supreme end that we should have in view is that there should be an honest expression of the opinions of the electorate, and that the will of the people should prevail. I do not means to say that the will of the people is always on the right side; but we must take the bad with the good. Though wrong may sometimes triumph; after all, the best system of Government that has yet been devised is that under which we live. The blemish, the fatal blemish, it seems to me, in the measure of my hon. friend is that it does not provide any of the safeguards which exist in this country when the people are called upon to give their verdict upon public questions, and which assure a correct expression of the will of the electors. There are in this Bill no such safeguards; and, if such safeguards are not provided, it is not because my hon. friend has been oblivious to the need of them. I am sure that he must have given more than one anxious hour to the consideration of this matter, and he must have found that it was not possible to provide for registering the votes in the trenches with the same attention and security as prevail in this country. If the Bill is silent upon this point, if it is a dead letter so far as this is concerned, it is only because it is not possible for the hon. gentleman to find safeguards which

would afford a satisfactory solution of his problem.
What safeguards can we have? I need not enlarge 'upon the formalities which are required in our elections to provide that we shall have a minimum of fraud. Our law goes far to prevent fraud and to get an honest expression of public opinion. For instance, the law provides that scrutineers may be present, and very few frauds can be committed when they are present. The returning officer may be a partisan; in fact, returning officers have been accused more than once in this House of being partisans. There may be partisanship even at the front. It is well known to us all that in the heat of elections men who are in ordinary affairs honest and respectable citizens will take , liberties with the law which they would never take in the prosecution of their own private business. The passion for party, the passion to win, makes men more or less callous upon such occasions. Is there anything which can justify my hon. friend in supposing that the same passions which rule on our side of the Atlantic will be powerless on the other side? Is there reason to believe that the instinct which moves a man on this side of the Atlantic to do the best he can, and even to go beyond the law, to obtain a triumph for the cause in which he believes, will not make its influence felt because the elections will be held under khaki instead of under worsted?
The only safeguard of which the Minister of Justice spoke this morning is that he trusts to the honour of the British officer. Sir, no man goes farther in his confidence in the British officer than I do. Everybody knows that nowhere in the world is honour more supreme than in the Tanks of the British army, especially among the officers. But, Sir, the British army is composed of men like other men, and even among them it is possible to find men who are not quite infallible. It will not do for us to believe that they are of different flesh from ourselves. Their education may be better than ours and their accent more refined, but after all they are of the human race, and we must presume that human frailty affects them as it affects others. So we must assume that there will be offences. What provisions are made in respect to this matter? Let us see how the Bill provides that the vote is to be taken:
The volunteer may thereupon make the affidavit in form B before any commissioned officer in the Canadian military forces, and,

after making the affidavit, mark the ballot paper as a vote for the Government or the Opposition or for the independent candidate, in the presence of the said commissioned officer, but in such a manner as not to disclose to the officer how he is voting, and shall fold the ballot paper so that it cannot be read and shall then place the same, together with the affidavit, in an envelope upon the back of which shall bo endorsed a certificate in form C.
Then that is to be transmitted to the returning officer. These are all the precautions taken, and they are no precautions at all, I submit to the consideration of the hon. minister himself that, taking the vote in this way, there and then you open a wide door for violation of the law and for fraud against the electors. Who is going to insure that the vote of the elector which is put in the envelope shall he the vote that comes to the returning officer? Who is going to insure that the envelope shall not be tampered with-that the vote shall not be tampered with? Such things have been known before. The law guards against such things now, but there is no such safeguard in the Bill. Let this Bill become law, and, I repeat, it opens the door wide for fraud and violation of the law.
My hon. friend suggests that we must trust the honour of the British officers; but he himself does not altogether trust the honour of the British officers, because, "foreseeing a violation of the law, he has imposed penalties upon wrong doers. I direct attention to section 9 of the Bill:
9.	Any person who wilfully and without lawful excuse:
(a)	causes any delay In the transmission or delivery to the returning officer of any envelope with the certificate endorsed in accordance with the provisions of this Act, or
(b)	opens any such envelope, or
(c)	shall attempt to obtain or communicate any information as to the party or person for whom any vote is given in any particular ballot paper used under the provisions of this Act, or
(d)	prevents or endeavours to prevent any volunteer entitled to vote hereunder from voting, or
(e)	makes any untrue statement as to his name or corps for insertion in a certificate, or
(f)	signs a certificate containing any untrue statement, shall be liable upon summary conviction to a fine not exceeding two hundred dollars and costs, or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months, or to both fine and imprisonment.
The hon. gentleman who fathers this Bill has foreseen that offences of this kind might be committed under the operation of this proposed legislation, and, by providing for a violation of the law, he gives answer to his own assertion that he would trust the honour of the British officers. What is the worth of this enactment of penalties? How

will the commission of such offences as are contemplated be prevented? My hon. friend knows that these penalties cannot be enforced. The offenders cannot be tried in this country, and in all probability they *would not he tried in Great Britain. They will be tried, perhaps, in France, perhaps in Belgium, perhaps in Germany, because it is possible that when elections take place our troops may be in Germany. This provision with regard to penalties is there only for show; it is not there to serve its professed purpose.
There is another objection to which the attention of my hon. friend was called this morning, and to which I think he did not give a satisfactory answer. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) asked my hon. friend whether the Government had communicated with the War Office with regard to this measure. What was my hon. friend's answer? He said that the Government had not communicated with the War Office; he presumed that it would be a matter of indifference to Lord Kitchener whether the Canadian soldiers were or were not allowed to vote, or what were the issues between the Government and the Opposition in this country. It is true that to Lord Kitchener and the War Office it would be a matter of indifference as to what the issues were between the Government and the Opposition in Canada, but what is not a matter of indifference to Lord Kitchener and to the War Office is the discipline of the army over which Lord Kitchener presides. Does my hon. friend suggest that it is a matter of indifference to the army that one section of it should be allowed to vote on a certain question, and that the rest of the army should not be allowed to vote? Is it a matter of indifference to the War Office and to the British authorities that such an example should be set in the army? If the Canadian soldier were allowed to vote, would the commander of the army be indifferent to the spirit manifested in the portion of the army which was not allowed to vote. That is a democratic age, and while I am a strong democrat, nevertheless, I think, that democracy must be subject to the law. The principle of manhood suffrage is far more extended in this country than it is in many other countries, perhaps more so even than in Great Britain, and if this proposed Bill becomes law there will be introduced into the army a new spirit which has not yet been found to be consistent with public opinion in Great Britain. This is a very important consideration, and it is one in regard to which, I venture to say, the commander of the army may have an opinion to express. Certainly it was the first duty of the Government, when they contemplated such legislation as this, to confer with the British authorities and to ascertain whether or not they would sanction it.
But the matter of discipline is not the only consideration. How would the operation of such a law affect the movements of the army? Spring is advancing, and we have reason to believe that as spring advances the allied armies will pounce upon the German army and drive it from France and Belgium to the Rhine, and from the Rhine to the very heart of Germany. We know too well that this cannot be accomplished in a day, in a month, or perhaps in one season. Battles are imminent, and in these modern times battles are not fought in one day or two days or three days, as they were in the time of Napoleon; under modern conditions battles last for weeks. Yet it is proposed that the Secretary of the High Commissioner shall send his ballots and his envelopes to the commanders or officers in charge, in order to obtain the votes of the Canadian soldiers. It is possible that this might be done when an important movement of the army would be taking place. Perhaps the Canadian forces would be engaged in battle, and one section of the army would have a vote and the other would not. This is not a vague supposition; it is a supposition which is quite within the bounds of possibility, and it is in respect to this that the Government would have been wise if they had consulted the British War Office before thrusting upon them the responsibility which will be imposed upon them if this Bill becomes law. Looking upon this measure dispassionately and without prejudice; looking upon it from the standpoint of duty not only to ourselves, but to the great cause in which we are engaged, we must come to the conclusion that it is ill-conceived in its principle, ill-conceived in its practice, and, still more, ill-conceived in its dispositions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am somewhat surprised at the tone of the right hon. gentleman's remarks, because, when this matter was first broached in the House, I heard, if I am not mistaken, a strong expression of opinion from his chief lieutenant in favour of the principle of the resolution placed on the Order Paper by the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Fripp): that the men serving abroad in the expeditionary forces of Canada ought not to be denied

the right and opportunity to vote. The right hon. gentleman has taken very strong ground against the measure. I did not underestimate the difficulties of working out a proposal which on the one hand would provide proper safeguards and on the other hand would not deny to the soldier the right which he would have possessed if he had remained in Canada; and therefore I moved that the resolution which had been placed upon the Order Paper by the hon. member for Ottawa should be referred to a committee then engaged in the work of considering amendments to the Controverted Elections Act. They have since had this subject under consideration and have made the report to the House which is embodied in this Bill.
I take very strongly the ground that men who are risking their lives in order that the liberties and institutions of this land shall be preserved ought not to be penalized by being deprived of the right and opportunity to vote. My right hon. friend does not seem to have much regard for that principle and he urges upon our attention arguments and illustrations of a somewhat singular character. I am not absolutely sure, comparing one part of his speech with another, as to whether he objects to the Bill in its entirety or whether he is prepared to support a measure which will give to those men who would be entitled to vote if they were in Canada the right and opportunity to vote although they are at the front. From one part of his speech I would gather that he was in favour of that measure of justice; but from another part I would gather that he was absolutely opposed to it. Will my right hon. friend inform me as to what I am to understand in that regard?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I certainly am in favour of no extension of the present franchise; but I would give those who have the right to vote an opportunity to do so if it were possible to provide the machinery for it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
A great deal of my right hon. friend's speech goes by the board because his argument tended to destroy that position altogether. He argues that any such measure must be absolutely unworkable, that you cannot provide proper safeguards, that the men would be so engaged in military 'duties that they could not vote. He says that Lord Kitchener will not permit them to vote. But having made these arguments intended to destroy the Bill, he then changes front and admits that men who are on voters' lists in Canada and

who could therefore vote if they were here ought to be entitled to vote although they are at the front. It is difficult to understand just what is my hon. friend's position. I maintain that the gallant men who have gone to the front and who have thus shown their willingness and determination to risk and if necessary to sacrifice their lives for their country are entitled to vote whether they are on the list, or not; and I say further that according to my apprehension they are entitled to vote, whether they have arrived at the age of 21 years or not. We all know that an arbitrary age must be fixed in our statute, and the age of 21 years is fixed; but we also know that some men at the age of 17 or 18 are as well developed physically and mentally as other men when they attain the age of 35 years. Those men under the age of 21 who have gone to the front to fight for their country have shown the possession of a mental * and physical development which ought justly to entitle them to vote if any man is entitled to vote while absent from Canada on the patriotic duty of fighting for his country.
My right hon. friend further argues- and this goes absolutely against his contention in reply to a question from me a moment ago-that our soldiers at the front ought not to be permitted to vote because there are men in Canada carrying on their ordinary avocations who, owing to the conditions under which they earn their livelihood cannot vote. He puts that forward as an argument in the hearing of every hon. gentleman in this House. That argument, if it means anything at all, confounds the very admission he made to me not five minutes ago, because it would exclude those whose names are on the electoral lists as well as all others. I venture to believe that there is a distinction to be found between men engaged properly and legitimately, in their own interest, jn ordinary business avocations in Canada and those who have abandoned all considerations of business and of interest and have gone to the front to sacrifice their lives' if necessary for the preservation of our institutions and liberties. I venture also to believe that the fathers and the mothers, the brothers and the sisters of these men fighting and risking their lives at the front will not consider the question in the coldblooded way in which my right hon. friend regards it.
My right hon. friend goes on further - and I will only touch very lightly the

points that he made, because most of them are matters of detail which can be better discussed in committee than on the second reading of the Bill-he goes on to say that our soldiers in France, being beyond the limits of this Dominion, cannot properly be authorized to vote under any law passed by this Parliament. Again he used an argument which confounds the admission made by himself only a few minutes ago, that the men upon the lists in Canada should be permitted to vote if at the front and that we should make some provision for that purpose.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I said if
you could find the provisions, but I am not able to see yet how it can be done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It would have been better in that case for my right hon. friend to have given us his assistance in framing the measure rather than to have devoted something like an hour to arguing that no such provision was possible. I venture to think that the men in the trenches in France, if we authorize them to vote under a provision made by the Parliament of Canada, are entitled to have their votes east at a general election in this country; and I know of no constitutional or other reason which would forbid them. Therefore, I pass by that argument of iny right hon. friend, because he adduced no reason which commends itself to my judgment in support of it.
Then he argues that it is absolutely and entirely improper and objectionable to permit the men at the front a vote not for a particular candidate but for a particular party, and he declares that in no British country, so far as he was aware, had any legislation of the kind ever been proposed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Except New Zealand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My right hon. friend, did not, I think, except New Zealand.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I excepted it a moment ago.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The principle which the hon. leader of the Opposition condemns has been acted on in New Zealand; and it is well to place on the Hansard the exact provisions of the New Zealand Act as they have been furnished to me by the Minister of Justice, in order that the country may be informed of what has been done in another progressive British dominion along the lines we are
proposing to-day. The New Zealand Act is in these words:
An Act to enable.tile members of the expeditionary forces to exercise their votes at the next general election of members of the House of Representatives and licensing poll.
Be it enacted by the General Assembly of New Zealand in Parliament assembled, and by the authority of the same, as follows :
1.	This Act may be cited as the Expeditionary Forces Voting Act, 1914.
2.	Every member of any expeditionary force sent from New Zealand to serve in the war in which His Majesty is at present engaged shall be entitled to vote in the manner hereinafter prescribed at the next general election of members of the House of Representatives, and also at the licensing poll taken simultaneously with such election.
3.	(1) With respect to the votes to be given by members of any such force at the next general election of members of the House of Representatives the following provisions shall apply :
(a)	The vote of each such member shall be recorded on a voting paper in the form in the schedule hereto by striking out the words indicating the parties for whom he does not wish to vote.
(b)	Every vote given as aforesaid for any party shall be counted as a vote for the candidate who has been selected in the manner hereinafter prescribed as the candidate representing that party in the electoral district in which the voter resided immediately before joining the expeditionary force.
(c)	Such selection shall be made-
(i)	In the case of the Government party,
by the Prime Minister;
(ii)	In the case of the Opposition party, by the leader of the Opposition; and
(iii)	In the case of the Labour party, by two members of the House of Representatives (as now constituted) who shall be appointed as selectors by resolution of the said House on the recommendation of a majority of the Labour members of the said House.
(d)	If there is no candidate selected as aforesaid as representing the party for which the vote is given, the vote shall not be counted.
(e)	Every selection made under paragraphs (b) and (c) hereof shall be gazetted not later than five days after nomination day, and shall be given effect to by returning officers at the election.
(f)	A voting paper in the form in the schedule hereto shall be supplied by an electoral officer appointed for the purpose by the chief electoral officer to every member of the said forces who applies for the same.
(g)	When the voter has marked his voting paper as aforesaid he shall enclose it in an envelope addressed to the returning officer of the electoral district in which he resided immediately before he joined the force, and having sealed the envolope, shall deliver the same to the electoral officer, who shall forthwith forward it to the chief electoral officer at Wellington.

(2) For the purposes of this section " Government " and " Opposition " mean respectively the Government and Opposition in office on the passing of this Act.
4.	With respect to the votes to be given at the licensing poll taken simultaneously with the said general election, the following provisions shall apply:
(a)	The vote of each member shall be recorded on the voting papers and in the manner prescribed by the Licensing Act, 1908.	.
(b)	A voting paper on each of the issues submitted at the licensing poll in the forms prescribed as aforesaid shall be supplied by the electoral officer aforesaid to every member who applies to vote under the last preceding section, and shall be dealt with in the manner provided by paragraph (g) of that section.
(c)	In the event of the form of the voting paper prescribed for the taking of the licensing poll on the issue of national prohibition being altered during the present session of Parliament, then the votes at the licensing poll under this Act on that issue against national prohibition and for national prohibition respectively, shall be counted as if they bad been given for national continuance or for national prohibition or otherwise in accordance with the tenor of the altered form of the voting paper in which the issue is submitted for the determination of the electors at the general election.
5.	Not later than seven days before the day fixed for the general election the chief electoral officer shall forward to the returning officer of each electoral district and to the returning officer of each licensing district all Envelopes addressed as aforesaid to that returning officer.
6.	At the counting of the votes at the satd general election and licensing poll the returning officer shall open all envelopes so sent to him, and shall, subject to the foregoing provisions of this Act, deal with the voting papers contained therein as if they had been issued pursuant to an absent voter's permit.
7.	No person Who has exercised his vote under this Act shall be entitled to vote again at the general election or licensing poll.
8.	Electoral officers may be appointed out of New Zealand for the purpose of enabling any person to record his vote under this Act who is a member of any expeditionary force sent out of New Zealand before the passing of this Act.
9.	The Governor may, from time to time, by Order in Council, make regulations prescribing anything necessary for carrying this Act into effect.
10.	The validity of the election at the said general election in any electoral district or of the licensing poll taken in any licensing district shall not be questioned on the ground that anything has been done irregularly or omitted to be done under this Act, or that for any reason whatever It is found impracticable for any member of any expeditionary force aforesaid to record his vote.
11.	This Act shall be deemed to be repealed on the completion of the said general election:
Provided that such repeal shall not affect any proceeding in relation to the said election or to the sa'd licensing poll.
