I venture to submit that in that Act the legislature of New Zealand has made provision for a more complicated condition of affairs than that for which we are endeavouring to provide in this Act. They have empowered the members of the expeditionary forces of New Zealand sent overseas to vote not only at the parliamentary election, but also upon other issues of a very special character. I venture also to think that in the provisions of the New Zealand Act there are not to be found any greater safeguards than those which we have provided. But if, in addition to the safeguards which already appear in this Bill, there are any other safeguards which can be suggested by any hon. gentleman on the other side of the House, we shall be very glad to consider and, if reasonable, to accept them. The very fact that under the New Zealand Act 10,000 men, as I am informed, have cast their votes overseas indicates that legislation of this character is not only effective, but has been found to be thoroughly practicable in actual operation.
My right hon. friend has called attention to the possibility of canvassing, and of inflammatory literature, if one may so term it, being circulated among the men in the trenches, and of passion being thus aroused. Whatever else Lord Kitchener is likely to do, I should think it exceedingly likely that he would put his foot down on anything of ithis nature. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice went very fully into these matters this morning, and pointed out that there are two duties for the soldier, one of which, the duty to vote, he will he entitled to perform under the provisions of this Act, and the other his military duty, which it is incumbent upon him to perform under the engagement that he took when he volunteered to fight and if necessary to die for his country.	He stated most
clearly and distinctly that under the conditions which confront the Empire, the military duty must take precedence. But he argued that, if opportunity could be afforded, the men at the front should also be permitted to give their voice in the determination of questions which will affect the Government of this country in the future.

So in respect of all that has been urged in regard to the control of the War Office, we are perfectly willing, and I think the country will be willing, to let the matter be determined in that way.
Then my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) went on to argue, and he did argue, that we must anticipate all kinds of fraud and attempted fraud and corruption among the men at the front. I for one dissent from that view in the strongest possible terms. I venture to think that the men and officers who, at- this juncture, are risking their lives for their country may well be trusted by the people of Canada and the Parliament of Canada to vote honestly and without any attempt at fraud or deception. And it did not seen to me at all desirable or appropriate that my right hon. friend should dwell so much on the possibility of fraud in this connection. I believe that these men who have gone to the front have been actuated by a sense of duty, and I decline to believe that a man who to-morrow may have to risk his life in facing the foe, the sternest of all the duties that a soldier has to perform, will to-day have his mind intent on practising electoral corruption and violating the provisions of this Act. These men, I think, c n be trusted to vote honestly, and I believe that the omcers can be trusted to record their votes honestly. Those in this country whose kinsmen are facing the foe in the trenches will not be inclined to join in the belief and expectation of my right hon. friend, that the just recognition proposed by this Bill, and the refusal to penalize soldiers who are fighting for their country will result in attempted fraud and dishonesty by the gallant men so engaged in tnat great patriotic duty.
Why, although we have had the most elaborate provisions in our election laws, they have proven insufficient repeatedly in this country whenever they have not been backed up by the honesty of tne men who were constituted and appointed to enforce them. Even in Canada we have known that no legislative enactment can be so carried out as to prevent fraud unless we appoint men who are honest; and if we have men who are honest we need no legislative enactment to ensure that an honest result shall be obtained. I recall that with all our safeguards and legislative provisions, a deputy returning officer and a poll clerk went forth in one of our western provinces, pretended to journey into the north 100 or 120 miles, but went in reality only 20 or 140
30 miles, where they sat down under a tree, filled in 150 names, deposited as many ballots, and came back with the story of a unanimous Liberal vote in that remote part of the constituency. It is impossible to prevent fraud absolutely by legislative enactment. It must depend in the final analysis upon the honesty and integrity of the men who are to carry out the law. I differ from my right hon. friend because I have sufficient confidence in the officers and men who are willing to sacrifice their lives at the front to believe that if this Act is passed its provisions will be carried out honestly and as Parliament intended.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to say a few words upon this matter as dispassionately as I know how. I should be glad personally if no words I uttered evoked the slightest applause. I would rather speak to the calm and deliberate judgment of hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House. I have a very strong opinion, which I think I can put with great brevity, about this measure as well as the grounds upon which I found that opinion. I think it is contrary to the spirit of the British army and almost of the British Constitution itself. I regret extremely that a measure of so provocative a nature should be brought in by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), and should have been supported by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden). I recall no case in seven years' experience of Parliament where a minister introducing a measure has had his measure so completely turned inside out as it was by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), and I recall no case in seven years' experience oi Parliament where the feeble effort of the minister were so lightly supported by what I almost thought the unpalatable effort of the right hon. the Prime Minister. I was brought up in a school of politicians who told me that it was dangerous to impute motives and I have always tried to follow the instruction, but it is extremely difficult in this case not to suspect a motive anyway. I think I could prove a motive, if I might do so, on the part of the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Fripp), who has occupied the boards in connection with this measure. When he was speaking I addressed to him the question: Has my hon. friend in his mind any machinery by which he 5 p.m. hopes to have the soldiers at the front seized of the issues upon



which the election will be fought? My hon. friendis a somewhat young Parliamentarian and lh.is answer gave his whole case away. He said that there is one issue in regard to which the soldiers will be seized. My hon. friend spoke with the approbation, and under the smiling countenance, of the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers), whom I suspect very strongly as being the originator of this measure and, if my hon. friend's words had any meaning at all, they meant that there was one issue upon which he wished the soldier to vote, and he was persuaded that the soldier would vote upon his side of the issue. I give that for what it is worth as lending, colour to the suspicion which I confess I myself entertain.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: What was that issue?

My hon. friend will forego his right of cross-examination for a moment. There is nothing that surprise me more in this House than the eagerness with which hon. gentlemen opposite go to the United States, New Zealand, or anywhere but Britain for an argument to support a bad case. They are the British party-
Hear, hear.
They are the upholders of British institutions-
Hear, hear.
They say they are the British party-
Hear, hear.

Yes, but nothing that is done in Britain meets with their approval. In the last election they were the antiAmerican party,' but wlhen they want to justify a procedure in regard to voting which is anti-British they immediately go south for the approval of the United States, and if they have that they think the whole thing is settled. Failing to settle it by the United States, the Prime Minister reads a whole Act that has .-een introduced in the little colony of New Zealand with less than a million people. I do not want 10 detract from what is done in New Zealand, but I venture to think there is not a man in this House who would have a more acute difference with nine-tenths of the legislation that is passed in New Zealand than the Prime Minister. Why, New Zealand is the hot bed of socialism. Just imagine the leader of the great Conservative party, supported by the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) who, if he has one point stronger uian another it is oppo-

sition to socialism, going to New Zealand to get support for a nostrum like this. The Minister of Justice, in reply to a question I put to him, said that he thought the last thing we should do would be to go to the War Office in Britain to find out what legislation we should enact in Canada upon such a subject as this. He and I just differ one hundred per cent upon that conclusion and I will tell him why. Having regard to this particular measure, it was the first thing he should have done and for a very practical reason. If the war authorities in Great Britain, who have been admitted to be the supreme court in this matter, both by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice and my right hon. friend the Prime Minister should proceed to overrule the measure, in the name of goodness, what is the use of passing the measure at a time when we all want to get home and when the session has lasted too long now in the peculiar circumstances in which the British Empire finds itself? The best that can be said for the Government is that they are introducing a measure which is going to be useless because it will I should suppose be overruled by the military authorities in Great Britain. That is a very strong reason why the Government should have known exactly the attitude of the militray authorities of Great Britain before they proceeded to introduce a measure which I have already described as of an exceedingly provocative nature.
Why did they not overrule the Parliament of New Zealand?

Perhaps my hon. friend is better able to speak in regard to the Parliament of Ne*y Zealand than I am. I cannot discover as yet where the New Zealand soldiers voted. Does my hon. friend know if they voted in the trenches?
I am satisfied when I know they voted.

I personally would oppose this measure because when men are gathered under arms for the purpose of war, they are and have always been recognized in the old country as men apart, and there has always been the most acute distinction drawn between the civilian population and the army. The army has been kept from interference in politics; the civilian population has been kept supreme just because it is the master, and the army is not allowed to interfere. The army is the executive arm of the civilian authority for certain specific purposes. I think that is

a distinction which goes to the very root of British practice, British thought, and the British constitution itself. It is on the surface of things that the moment men are gathered under arms for the specific purpose of war, their minds ought to be left intent upon the supreme duty of saving the country, because they have no less duty on hand, and the Government or the politician who puts anything in the way of their full discharge of that duty is guilty-perhaps unwittingly-of putting an obstruction in the way of the prosecution of that war in which we are all engaged. So much for the principle.
To dream of men voting at the front is to dream of men having their discipline upset and having their minds taken away from the only work on hand for them-and so they recognize it aslhave the very best reason for knowing. It is the only work they think of day or night-the only work they care for. I supposed, however, that my hon. friend the Minister of Justice would have done what I thought was the first thing he should have done-and tried to find out the mind of Lord Kitchener on the subject. Need any one of us be in any doubt what his mind is? We all read at the time-although the Government had evidently forgotten it, the speech which that extraordinary man delivered in the House of Lords, after he accepted the position of War Minister. In that speech he was most careful to guard himself from being suspected of being concerned in the general politics of the Government which he had joined. He explained that he had taken up his duties for three years or for the term of the war, and that he had taken those duties upon him as a soldier. Then he used the sentence, which if the Government gives it the consideration which is due to the utterances that proceed from Lord Kitchener at the present moment, ought to lead them at once to withdraw this measure. He said:	"As a soldier I
have no politics." That is his attitude without a doubt, because Lord Kitchener always uses language that is full of meaning and very easily understood. He emphatically divested himself of political beliefs and of any desire to interfere in politics. My objections to this measure of the Government is that it proposes to place the duty upon all the Canadian soldiers who are under the command of that great man, of taking a course of conduct and following a rule of conduct diametrically opposed to the rule which he has laid down for himself. Is it necessary to argue this any further?
140*
When he said: "as a soldier, I have no politics," it is recorded that the House of Lords, a body which is usually very calm in its expression of approval, applauded vociferously, and his attitude was at once endorsed by the applause of a body which I suppose some hon. gentlemen opposite almost worship, or did worship until it was curtailed so mightily of its power a few years ago.
The Minister of Justice asked us to suggest a better method than that proposed and I am going, in all seriousness, to suggest a better method of dealing with this question. The idea of having the soldiers vote while they are assembled for the purpose	of war has behind it	another idea, and the Government should entertain neither the one idea nor the other. The soldiers can vote only if there is an election, and I want to tell the Government something very plainly, without the slightest passion-and I think I shall find some endorsement in remarks which I regret very much not to have heard. I was absent from the city at the time my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce delivered his very moderate and able speech on the Budget; I was absent when he delivered that patriotic peroration, in which he told the House and the country that we should have only one thought. The Government ought not to have any thought of an election while the soldiers are assembled for purposes of war. I say this, if the House will believe me, without the slightest thought of what is going to happen to my party, and still less of what is going to happen to myself. I suppose there is not a man in this House who, so far as personal ambition goes, attaches less interest than I do to the question whether or not he will ever be back here again after the next general election. From the point of view of the best interest of Canada, from the point of view of the best interest of the Empire, and from the point of view of the successful prosecution of the greatest fight for the greatest object that ever engaged the highest civilizations of the world against what we believe to be lower and despotic civilizations, the Government have enough on hand to do what I have given them credit for doing in the main-seeing this fight through to a finish, without thinking of elections. That, however, is a matter between them and their consciences. What I have said I have said upon the point, and I do not think the moderate men of this country will view the measure before us with favour. They will not view it with

favour upon its merits, and they will view it with still greater disfavour because of the consideration upon which I have now dealt for a moment, that is, that the Government are wondering, if we can judge appearances, when it is going to be a good time to spring an election.
I do not want to make a contrast between this Government and the Government of Great Britain. But everybody knows that the thought has seriously occurred to that Government that they should extend their term so that they can do +he soldiers are doing-stick to their job and see it through. I rather think my right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden), judging from his general constitution, would want to stick to his job and have a voice in the settlement of affairs after the war.
He will be there.

I could not enter into that without differing in opinion and giving good reasons for it, and I do not want to do that. I -have the best reasons for knowing, and for stating, that the soldiers at the front are not thinking about votes, and not thinking about elections in Canada. I had, only yesterday, correspondence which informs me that men of our own first troops to go into the fight are feeling, to the last man amongst them, the strain of the campaign, and that not one of them feels himself as good a man physically as when he went into the trenches. I have had this information further, that the horror and the suffering which they are looking upon are leading them to wonder whether there is such a thing as Christianity in the world and what the end of all this business is to be. I can imagine this Government-I do not want to touch upon anything controversial-going to these soldiers at the front and saying: Some of our friends did not take good care to give you boots, but we are coming to give you votes. What do you think would be the attitude of these men, devoted to what they believe a holy cause of warfare, animated by the thoughts I have mentioned? I can imagine no man among them worthy of admiration-and I believe they are all such men-who would not turn to the Government and say: We are devoted to the sacred cause of repatriating the Belgians; we are devoted to the sacred cause of human freedom; we are going through untold sufferings and untold horrors to prosecute that cause to a successful issue-in the name of God and of all goodness do not add to these horrors

and these sufferings the horrors of the Public Accounts Committee.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I had not the honour of being a member of the committee to which was submitted the motion of the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Fripp), and as a result of whose deliberations the Bill now before the House comes up for consideration. I do not feel competent to discuss, nor do I think it would be proper to discuss at this stage, the several clauses and the various provisions of the Bill; but it is a circumstance of happy augury that those who on the floor of Parliament so far in this debate have opposed it, have opposed it not because of any defects in the machinery, hut firstly, lastly and all the time, on the ground that the very principle of the Bill is wrong. They are opposed to soldiers being given the right to vote, and opposed to the right of citizenship being vouchsafed to them as well as the rights they enjoy as soldiers. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) is very deeply grieved that any such Bill, involving, as he says, a controversial principle, should be launched on Parliament this session. What reason had we to believe that this Bill involved a controversial principle? The principle of this Bill was under discussion on the 22nd of February last, on the motion of the hon. member ruary last, on the motion of the hon. member opposite spoke on that motion, and neither of them opposed the principle of the Bill. The Opposition was represented on that occasion chiefly by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). Did he take up the cry of the hon. member for Red Deer this afternoon, that it was a sacrilege to have a soldier vote; or that a soldier, because he is a soldier, must not vote, because to vote is to be a politician? Was that his attitude? No. Speaking for the Opposition Re said he believed in soldiers voting, and he hoped that machinery to that end could be provided. " I agree with all that has been said," said the hon. gentleman, " as to the wisdom of having our volunteers exercise their franchise"; and I quote from page 364 of Hansard of the 22nd of February. Later in hie speech he elaborated that in these words:
I do not wish to be too emphatic in the matter, but I see almost unsurmountable difficulties in the way of our trying to apply this principle to our volunteers, particularly to those outside our own country. As to those who are in Canada. I think the modus operandi might be worked out without very much difficulty.

The attitude of the Opposition then was: There will be difficulties to be surmounted in hedging about the method of voting sufficient safeguards, and the machinery will not be easily evolved; but we are one with you in extending the franchise to the soldier, and in giving the soldier all the rights of citizenship and not a part of them. Why, then, had we any reason to anticipate that this Bill involved a controversial principle? This principle was acceded to by hon. gentlemen opposite before it was submitted to the committee. As to the efficiency of the machinery provided, as to the different clauses of the Bill, these may well await discussion until we get into Committee of the Whole.
The hon. member for Red Deer is exceedingly exercised because he claims it is against the fundamental principle, which is acknowledged by British statesmen; that the soldier must have no politics. And he quotes the words of Lord Kitchener, that as a soldier, he has no politics. But does that mean that because he is a soldier he is no longer a citizen? While he has no politics as a soldier, is he to have no political rights as a citizen? ,

The hon. gentleman will not dispute that I carefully spoke of soldiers assembled for the purpose of war, exactly as I understood Lord Kitchener to speak, when he spoke of having taken special duties upon himself for the time of the war.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
says he referred to soldiers assembled for the purposes of war on the battlefield; but the very man who used these words was not on the battlefield. Lord Kitchener, who gave that dictum was at that very time a member of the Cabinet of Great Britain. He assumed that position as a soldier, and he stated, that as a soldier, he had no politics. Did he wish to give the doctrine to the country that no soldier under his command, whether at home or in the foreign field, was to have the right to vote, or to give expression to his views on politics? Does the hon. member for Red Deer think he meant that? If so, where does his leader stand, who, to-day, in this House, said he was in favour of a soldier voting on the battlefield, providing he had the right to vote at home.
Lord Kitchener is my leader, and good enough for my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
In matters of war, Lord Kitchener is good enough for me, but in the House of Commons I acknowledge the leadership of the leader of the Government.
I am glad to see that, at last, the hon. member for Red Deer repudiates his leader.
We have no use, the hon. member says, for anything British; the actions of the British Government do not satisfy us. He has never seen us, he said, accord with, anything done in Britain. I remember one occasion upon which the opinion of the British Government was given on a matter of which they should know something; on a matter upon which they should be to us the highest authority; on a matter in respect of which they gave their opinion to this Parliament in the most explicit and decided manner. I remember that their authority was repudiated by hon. gentlemen opposite, and in the most violent language by the hon. member for Red Deer himself. The hon. gentleman spurns the example of New Zealand. The example of that little country which, he says, is socialistically mad, whicn has a population of less than one million-he has no use for. But it is only a year since he stood up in the House and castigated hon. gentlemen on this side of the House because they did not follow, in the most pitifully copying manner, the example of New Zealand. Not that there was anything to criticise adversely in the action of New Zealand on that occasion; we do not and never did say that, from their standpoint, they did anything wrong. But it was an example which did not come into question then at all, and, even though it did not come into question, the hon. member for Red Deer proposed that we should follow that example against the advice of the Admiralty of Britain. The hon. gentleman say-s that the British example is not good enough. When did the action taken by New Zealand cease to be a British example? Is New Zealand not a member of the family of Britain? Is New Zealand not the first British country to whidh, this question ever appealed, the first British country to decide the issue and to determine whether or not the soldiers have a right to vote? The British nation was on a previous occasion at war during election time. One hundred years ago, when Pitt fought against Fox in the British House of Commons, it was necessary to hold elections in time of war. But at that time they did not have manhood suffrage, as they (have to-day, and I doubt

really whether at that time very many of the men who were fighting the battles of Great Britain across the English channel would have had the right to vote had they been at home. The question which we are now considering did not present itself to Britain then, nor has it presented itself to Britain since. No election was held during the South African war, Which occurred about fifteen years ago, and there is no British example as against the position taken by this Government.
The hon. member, I presume, does not want to misrepresent the facts. The South African war lasted fully a year after the election of 1900, which took place during that war.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I accept the correction of {he hon. memebr for Red Deer; I understood that the election was held after the war was over. But if he is correct, let him never more stand in the House of Commons and plead the example of Great Britain against an election being held in time of war.

There were
different stages of that war; the guerilla warfare lasted for a year and a half. It is perfectly true that Mr. Chamberlain went to the country in the year 1900 with the cry "the war is over"; so that to have an election he had to contend that the war was over. John Burns remarked at the time that the war was over-it was all over the shop.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have tried to get the exact viewpoint of the hon. member for Red Deer, and if I have caught it in this case, it is this: that it is all right to have an election during the progress of guerilla warfare, but if you can apply any other adjective to the war, then it is wrong to have an election. There were stages of the war, and the British election was held a year before the end of the war. That is the reason why the hon. gentleman objects to an election now.
Before the signing of peace.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The British election was held a year before the signing of peace, according to the hon. member for Red Deer.
Something like a year.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Something like a year before, so that if the hon. gentleman is loyal to British example, and if he believes that we are within a year of the termination of the war, he will cease to oppose an election.

It is an historic principle of British jurisprudence that the civilians must rule, not the soldiers; that the civilian must be supreme and not the military authorities. In this respect British institutions differ radically from those of Germany, and in the expression of that principle I agree with the hon. member. But is it to be argued that upon that ground soldiers should be deprived of the franchise? Is that the interpretation put upon that principle by the British Government?
No.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If soldiers must not be deprived of the franchise, then why not vote for this Bill?
Does not my hon. friend see the distinction between the soldier fighting in the trenches and the soldier who becomes a civilian after the war is over and he is at his own home?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I see it very clearly, and will explain to the hon. member for Red Deer where that puts him. The civilian must be supreme, not the soldier, and the hon. gentleman means the soldier at home. The hon. gentleman is quite content that the soldier at home, the parade soldier, who is not fighting, shall be supreme and shall dominate the civilian, but he is determined that the soldier who fights shall have nothing to say at all. What is at the bottom of the theory in Britain that the civilian must control the affairs of state and that the soldier must not gain ascendancy over him? It is this: The ascendancy of the soldier means a military autocracy such as they have in Germany, and that is what is to be feared. But is there any reason why the ascendancy of the soldier who is not at war should be any more dangerous than the ascendancy of the soldier who is at war? What is the difference? What have we to fear from the vote of a man on the battlefield because he is a soldier, any more than we have to feaT from the vote of the man at home, who is a soldier and who refuses to go to the battlefield? It must be plain .to the right hon. leader of the Opposition-because I am sure that he struggled hard to keep within the pale of reason in the speech that he delivered- that all that has been advanced in favour of his position by his lieutenant from Red Deer is so much vapour.
It is argued also that we should have asked the advice of Lork Kitchener before we adopted the principle that in so far

as we can give power to the soldiers on the battlefield to vote. We should do so. Lord Kitchener t>r Sir John French as head of the service, has the command for the time being of our soldiers on the battlefield, and I do not dispute the truth of the assertion that, if he wishes, he can prevent the operation of any provision for carrying out this proposed legislation. He can refuse to the soldiers authority to vote, even though we, in so far as we are able to give it, are ready t,o extend to them that authority. But is the fact that Lord Kitchener has the right to exercise his jurisdiction any reason why we should fefuse, within our province, to exercise ours? If, as the hon. member for Red Deer says, this legislation will -be vetoed by Lord Kitchener, let me ask him why he takes up the time of the House in an attempt to defeat it here? He does not know what the attitude of Lord Kitchener will be, any more than I do. I assume that Lord Kitchener will extend to this country the same courtesy that, he extended to New Zealand; I know of no reason why he should show less respect for the opinion of the Parliament of Canada than he shows for the opinion of the Parliament of New Zealand. If the hon. member for Red Deer knows of any reason why he should, I shall be pleased to have him give it to me.
Where did the New Zealanders vote?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The New Zealanders
voted while under the jurisdiction of Lord Kitchener, and while away from their own country.
Where?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: They voted in a foreign land.
Name it?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Name the country?
Would it be any different if they voted in Belgium or France or Egypt?

They did not
vote in either Belgium or France. Are any of them there?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman tell me? I do not know where they voted.

My hon. friend ought to
know.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I know enough for the purposes of my argument, that they voted outside the jurisdiction of the New Zealand authorities and within the jurisdiction of
Lord Kitchener. Will the hon. member for Red Deer tell me where they voted? They voted on whatever battlefield or at whatever other place they were at the time the election was on, and that is where the soldiers of Canada would vote should there be an election that would demand the exercise of the franchise while they are at the front.
The right hon. leader of the Opposition has the greatest dread of election campaign literature getting into the trenches. No vote could be taken when there would be less to fear from the invasion of campaign literature than such as is contemplated by this Bill. The men are under the command of the British authorities and to their wisdom and to their good sense we can safely leave such questions as that, feeling certain that nothing will be permitted by the British authorities that will interfere with the efficiency of a soldier as a soldier on the battlefield.

In regard to section 4, my hon. friend says that the voting, the marking of the ballot, is to be under the supervision of a British officer. What is meant by those words?
The volunteer may thereupon make affidavit in form B before any commissioned officer in the Canadian militaj-y forces.
Does that mean a British officer?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: They are all British officers.
This is limited to a Canadian officer, a commissioned officer in the Canadian military forces. Does that not mean a Canadian officer?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It means a Canadian officer who by service abroad becomes a British officer.
The hon. gentleman said a British officer.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
He undoubtedly would be a British officer. What I referred to was the paramount jurisdiction of the war authorities to control in every way the admission of any kind of literature to the men at the front. They have that control in the war office and they will exercise it by such officers as they select. We may safely trust to them that the soldier would be protected from any undue influence in the exercise	of	his	franchise.
The hon. member for Red Deer was careful not to be cross-examined. He was willing to give his evidence so long as he

was subjected to no cross-examination. He quoted from the speech of the hon. member for Ottawa, endeavouring to assign to his words some motive which he said was behind the Government in introducing this legislation. He asked the hon. member for Ottawa if the soldiers at the front would know about the issues. He refused to tell the House what the hon. member for Ottawa answered. The hon. member for Ottawa answered that there was one thing about which the soldier at the front would know and that was how they were equipped by the people of Canada and the Government of Canada for the purposes of war. If we are to follow hon. gentlemen opposite, if we are to take seriously their activities within the last few weeks, we must come to the- conclusion that the question of the adequacy of the equipment is going to be one of the foremost questions in any campaign that may be waged, so that on one issue launched by hon. gentlemen opposite they should surely not be afraid to take the opinion of those who would best know the facts and who would not have to be bombarded by literature from one side or the other. The right hon. leader of the Opposition is afraid that campaign literature wiL get in. His lieutenant from Red Deer is afraid they will not know the issues. The one fears the subject for one reason and the other fears it for an exactly opposite reason. I apprehend that there is no reason to fear it for either reason. Should there be an election it is well that the soldier, while he exercises his functions as a soldier, should not be deprived of the exercise of his functions as a citizen. That is the purpose of the Bill and that only; and it has at all times been a cardinal feature of British parliamentary and political life that a soldier or a citizen had the same right, and that a soldier, by becoming a soldier, has not in any way his functions or his rights as a citizen, reduced.

A difference arose on a point of fact with regard to where the New Zealand soldiers voted. I Have consulted with some military members of the House, and my hon. friend asserted that they were under the jurisdiction of Lord Kitchener. These military members inform me that their impression is-they have no documentary evidence-
Oh, oh.
My hon. friends who laugh do not believe in any impressions. They have the impression that they voted in Wellington before leaving New Zealand.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
My authority was the
cablegram read by the Minister of Justice, which the member should have heard.
Which did not say where they voted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The statement of the
Prime Minister was that the men voted under the Bill that was read, and the Bill has no application except to the soldiers outside of New Zealand.
Has the Minister of Justice a copy of the Act as it finally passed or simply a copy of the Bill that was introduced in the New Zealand Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have a copy of the proposed Bill. The question 'asked of the Prime Minister of New Zealand was whether the proposed Bill giving the soldiers a vote had been passed, and the answer was to that question:
Bill referred to passed and votes of soldiers who left before general election recorded. Total votes, 10,000.
So, while I have only a copy of the proposed Bill, the question asked of the Prime Minister of New Zealand was whether the proposed Bill was passed and he said yes, the proposed Bill was passed.
Does my hon. friend think that language contains the meaning that the vote was recorded after they left?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
And votes of all soldiers who left before general election recorded.
So that they left before the general election and the Bill itself recognized that they had then left, because it is a Bill to enable the soldiers who had left to vote.
If they had not, the vote could be recorded anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Those who stayed at home would have their votes recorded under a totally different Bill. This was a Bill exclusively passed for men who when the Bill was passed had already left New Zealand. The Prime Minister of New Zealand was asked if that proposed Bill passed, and he said yes. He was asked if the vote was taken, and he said: Votes of all soldiers who left before the general election recorded.
It does not say when.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Certainly, unless it is assumed that, being asked a perfectly clear

question, the Prime Minister of New Zealand chose to give an ambiguous or misleading answer. It seems to me that it is perfectly clear that when he was asked whether a proposed Bill which only had application to soldiers who had already left the country when the Bill was proposed, had passed and whether the vote was taken, and he answered that the Bill had passed and that the votes of soldiers who left before the general election had been recorded-

My own impression is that they voted before they left, otherwise they voted by marconigram. When he gets the facts, my hon. friend will find that they voted before they left New Zealand. I would assert that.
Is it not a fact that the Bill that t)he hon. member speaks of was passed authorizing these men to vote previous to leaving New Zealand?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Absolutely the contrary.
The Times, that I took for my authority, certainly so stated.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know what The Times stated- But I do know that the Bill was applicable only to soldiers who had already left the country; for any soldier who tvas still iin New Zealand at the time of the election did not need that Bill at all in order to vote; he could vote under the ordinary law. The Prime Minister of New Zealand was asked whether the New Zealand Parliament had passed the proposed Bill to enable men who had left to vote. He answered, Yes. He was then asked, was the vote taken? By that I cannot conceive that the Prime Minister understood anything except, was the vote provided for in that Bill taken? If the question does not mean that, it has no meaning at all. He answered, Yes; and further stated that 10,000 votes had been recorded.	[DOT]

Would my hon. friend allow me to see the telegram that was sent to the Prime Minister of New Zealand, and the answer. I think it was most unfortunate that my hon. friend did not impress upon the Parliamentary Counsel to find out in his cable to New Zealand whether the Bill was passed as introduced. Many Bills are introduced in this Parliament and every other parliament in the world in regard to which it would be quite correct to say that they had passed, even though they had been amended. What I would assume might be correct, from the cablegram of the Prime Minister of New Zealand, is that the Bill as it finally passed allowed those soldiers who were to leave New Zealand to register their votes for or against the Government. That might well be the case, for the Government expected a general election. Then when the election came on the votes would be counted by the returning officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It would be possible to conceive of all these things were it not for the fact that so far as the soldiers still in New Zealand were concerned, no B:ll was required at all.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. The Bill had absolutely nothing to do with any soldiers except those who had left New Zealand when the Bill was introduced, and for the simple reason that under the general law the soldiers still in New Zealand were already entitled to vote. I have asked the question, was the Bill that was introduced passed? The question that I did ask was, was the proposed Bill passed? What distinction does the hon-gentleman make between the proposed Bill and the introduced Bill? I think my question was perfectly clear, and the answer to that question was, yes.

I am sorry that I cannot think the minister has made it absolutely clear that soldiers3 votes were taken after the soldiers had left New Zealand. My hon. friend says that it would have been of no advantage to have the enactments which I say might have been made, for he says the existing law allowed votes of soldiers to be taken if the soldiers were in New Zealand at the time of the election.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The votes of anybody.

Now it is entirely possible that this New Zealand Bill may have provided that soldiers going abroad could, before they left, mark their ballots either for or against the Government, and that when the election came on the returning officers entered the votes accordingly. My hon. friend who sits behind me says that he is satisfied from a statement in the Times that that was done. It might very easily have been done. In New Zealand they were expecting a general election. The soldiers were going to leave the country, and the Government might very well have provided that before the soldiers left they should be given an opportunity to register their votes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Why did they make the Bill applicable only to soldiers who had left?

We do not know that the Bill passed in that form. My hon. friend may be guessing with absolute accuracy, but it is not always safe to guess that a Parliament has passed a Bill in the form in which it was introduced. My hon. friend has often seen himself amending his own Bills. That is not at all an unlikely thing to happen to any Bill.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I was about to make some reference to the provisions of the Bill which I think should properly be considered on the motion for the second reading, and in that connection I might ex-press my thanks to the Minister of Justice for suggesting that I might be able to give some assistance in amending the Bill in case its principle should be approved of. Let me say to the minister that like my hon. friend from South Renfrew [Mr. Graham), I am in favour of giving soldiers the right to vote providing it can be done in such a way as not to interfere with the proper performance of their duties and also provided that it can be surrounded with the proper safeguards. In speaking of this Bill, I am inclined to think that it has not been prepared with sufficient care to merit the respectful consideration of this House. I cannot think that the Minister of Justice has had his heart in this measure at all. He protested, Mr. Speaker, with eloquence and in the most sincere tones, that he was sincere about the measure. He protested three or four times and each time with a little more strength. I rather thought that the hon. gentleman was seeking to convince himself as well as to convince this House of his sincerity, else why did he protest so much?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My sincerity was questioned.

My hon. friend has heard the story of the maiden who, when she protested so much it excited a considerable degree of suspicion. Just let me call my hon. friend's attention to section 4:
4. The volunteer may thereupon make the affidavit in form B before any commissioned officer in the Canadian military forces, and, after making the affidavit, mark the ballot paper as a vote for the Government or the Opposition or for the independent candidate, in the

presence of the said commissioned officer, but in such a manner as not to disclose to the officer how he is voting, and shall fold the ballot paper so that it cannot be read and shall then place the same, together with the affidavit, in an envelope upon the back of which shall be endorsed a certiflca'e in f rm C, which certificate shall be signed by such officer.
Now, let me read the certificate:
t hereby certify that the document contained in this envelope was written in my presence by (here insert name and rank and name of corps in which voter is serving), and according to the best information at my disposal I believe that the statements made in the affidavits are true.
That is the whole of the endorsement that is to be upon the envelope. The envelope is sealed. What then is to be done?
The envelopes containing the ballot papers and affidavits shall then be sent by post to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, who shall keep a record of them, place them in a package carefully sealed and marked on the outside " Soldiers Votes" and forward them by registered post to the returning officer of the electoral district in which Such election is to be held.
That is the whole direction. Would my hon. friend just pay attention to the language of this section? I would like my right hon. friend the Prime Minister to consider it also and see whether there is any meaning in it or whether it does not indicate the preparation of the Bill in the most slovenly way possible and in a manner which indicates that the Minister of Justice has really not had his heart in the measure and has really not given any attention to it. There is to be nothing endorsed upon the envelope except the certificate of the officer that the envelope contains the affidavit, etc., of so and so, simply giving the name of the corps in which he is' serving, not giving his residence, not giving the electoral district in which he has the right to vote. Then the officer has to send all these envelopes to the Clerk of the Grown in Chancery, the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery has to keep a record of them, he is not to open them, he does not know to which district any one of these voters belongs, he has to endorse on the outside "soldiers' vote" and he has to forward these envelopes by registered post to the returning officer in the electoral district in which such election is to be held.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Who has to do that?
The Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. Where is the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery going to send them?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is manifestly an error in the printing of the form. I plead

guilty to not seeing to the correction of the printed form, but it was intended that on the back of the envelope there should be endorsed, in addition to the name and the corps, the address given by the soldier in the affidavit.
Possibly that should be on the certificate?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: On the certificate, so that from the certificate the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery might know where to send the envelope of the man who claims to be entitled to vote.	.

Well, then, the section is wrong, because it says that the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery "shall forward them by registered post to the returning officer of the electoral district in which such election is to be held."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Certainly, because it is supposed that the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, having the address of the man, will be able to determine exactly what his electoral district is. It was first suggested that we should put in the electoral district, but it was pointed out that the soldier might not know the electoral district in which he was entitled to vote. For instance, in the city of Montreal, a soldier would know perfectly well where he had resided, the street and number, but he might not know precisely which of the electoral districts it was in, and to avoid the possibility of doubt about that, we substituted the address of the place where he had lived. It was intended-it is a mere omission in the form -that the address should appear on the certificate on the back of the envelope, and from that the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery will easily be able to ascertain what the electoral district is, and see that the envelope goes to the right electoral district.
Of course, I did not know what errors the minister had made or what omissions there were; I was merely speaking of the Bill as we have it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is entitled to speak of the Bill as it stands. Of course, a matter of that sort might more properly be dealt with in the committee. It could hardly be held as touching upon the principle of the Bill.

I think it does, because we have to point out the difficulties that surround the carrying out of the proposed measure. It was stated here that British officers could be trusted to see that the private marked his ballot paper, that we
could safely rely upon their fairness, and that we need not be anxious to have any precautions taken. As was pointed out, this Parliament would have no right to impose any duty upon a British officer, and apparently the Minister of Justice has had that in mind, because, while in subsection 2 it is left to the discretion of the High Commissioner for Canada to determine what * officers these ballots shall be sent to, and while there is nothing in the Bill to state who the officers shall be, it is provided by section 4 that the ballot must be marked in presence of a commissioned officer in the Canadian military forces.
That absolutely excludes a British commissioned officer because a British officer is not a commissioned officer in the Canadian military forces. The officer must be a Canadian officer and is it possible that my hon. friend and those on the committee who assisted him in framing this Bill had in mind that there are in England to-day some officers of the Canadian forces, who, as some English newspapers asserted, ware selected because of their political claims rather than of their military fitness? Is it possible that the minister has in view some officers who are still in England, who have not been sent to the front, whom General Alderson has no thought of sending to the front, whom he deems incapable of taking proper command and in whose

Mr. MEIGHEN': Do I understand the hon. gentleman to argue that the officers who did not receive appointments under General Alderson and who returned were political appointees?
Yes, quite a number of them.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The only one whom I happen to know, and who I understand led back the officers who were not appointed by General Alderson, was a Liberal who was defeated in the local elections in Manitoba.

That might be. I was not speaking particularly of those who came back to Canada; I was speaking rather of those who remain in England, whom General Alderson has not sent to the front and whom, if rumour is true, he will never send to the front. Is that why the minister has given this wide discretion

that these affidavits may be made before and ballots marked in presence of any Canadian commissioned officer in the military forces? Is that why he has not limited it to officers who are in command of the forces, because it must be apparent to the House that under this any commissioned officer, who has gone over to England and who may or may not be serving with the forces at the front may be appointed by the High Commissioner for the purpose of taking these affidavits and receiving the ballots. I do not hesitate to say that, in respect of some of those officers at all events-and they are rather well known to members of this House-I woiild desire to see some safeguards placed around the marking of the ballots and their being returned to Canada. I am not at all afraid to say that, and gentlemen who realize whom I have in mind, I think will be disposed to agree with me.
It is provided not merely that ballots shall be given to those soldiers who ask for them, but that any quantity of ballots may be sent to the High Commissioner and any quantity distributed. We have no safeguard whatever provided in this Bill as to the ballots being marked by those who are entitled to vote, or as to the ballots which are so marked finding their way back to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. That is a fundamental objection which I find to the Bill in making provision for soldiers who are out of Canada voting at a Canadian election. The hon. member for Bed Deer (Mr. Clark) has pointed out in language much stronger and clearer than any I can employ what, from a military standpoint, from the standpoint of the interest of the Empire and from the viewpoint which Lord Kitchener is likely to take of the matter, seemed to me an insuperable objection to having the vote taken at the front. It may be asked of me, how, in case I think it would be desirable to give soldiers the right to vote, I would have provided for it. I would have provided for it at the session of Parliament which was held in August before the soldiers went to the front, and I would have made provision for those who were going away to vote by marking their ballots before they left the country. In that way the matter might easily have been accomplished, and proper safeguards would have been thrown around the voting, and that is the way in which for the most part I believe the New Zealand Government has provided

for voting. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice read a despatch from the Prime Minister of New Zealand, in which it stated:
In reply cable 28th from your clerk House of Commons Bill referred to passed and votes of all soldiers who left before general election recorded, total votes 10,000.
My hon. friend, as I thought, led the House to believe that total of 10,000 must be made up of soldiers who had actually gone to the front before they had recorded their votes. An examination of the Bill, a copy of which I have before me, does not show that, because it provides that electoral officers in New Zealand shall receive the votes of the soldiers. It is true it provides that the New Zealand Government may appoint electoral officers outside of New Zealand, but for the purpose of taking the votes not of those who had not left New Zealand before it had passed, but of those who had left New Zealand before it had passed, therefdre showing that in the opinion of the Parliament and Government of New Zealand, it was' only .to meet the case of soldiers who had left before the Act had passed that they thought it desirable to allow this provision, but soldiers who might leave after the Act went into force must register their votes in New Zealand, and if they did not do so, they could not do it after they had gone abroad. Therefore, if I am right in this-and I will endeavour to show the House that I am right -it is possible that the whole 10,000 votes recorded were recorded in New Zealand after the Act passed, but before the soldiers departed from New Zealand to engage in the war.
Let me call the attention of the House to the provisions in the New Zealand Bill. By paragraph (f) -of subsection 1 of section 3 it is provided as follows:
A voting paper in the form in the schedule hereto shall be supplied by an electoral officer appointed for the purpose by the chief electoral officer to every member of the said forces who applies for the same.
The Act is speaking here evidently ol electoral officers in New Zealand, not of people who might be appointed out of New Zealand.
By paragraph (g) it is provided:
When the voter has marked his voting paper as aforesaid he shall enclose it in an envelope addressed to the returning officer of the electoral district in which he resided immediatley before he joined the force, and having sealed the envelope, shall deliver the same to the electoral officer, who shall forthwith forward it to the chief electoral officer at Wellington.

This provision is entirely for soldiers who were then in New Zealand and before they left that country.
Then, we find by section 8, a provision for the polling of votes of members of expeditionary forces sent out of New Zealand before the passing of the Act:
Electoral officers may be appointed out of New Zealand for the purpose of enabling any person to record his vote under this Act who is a member of any expeditionary force sent out of New Zealand before the passing of this Act.
I think it must be clear to the minister that he is in error in stating to the House that this whole ten thousand votes must have been of soldiers who were out of the country at the time they marked their ballots. On the contrary, it provides for the marking of ballots by soldiers who leave the country after the Act was passed. These men are to vote in New Zealand. And it distinctly provides, contrary to the terms of this Bill, that any soldier who leaves the country after the Act is passed must register his vote before he leaves or he will not be allowed to register it at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman allow me a word? He says I was mistaken, and he reads section 8 to prove it. But section 2 provides for all expeditionary forces sent from New Zealand to serve in the war, and they have the right to vote. There is further information on this point which I give now so that the hon. gentleman may know just upon what I rely. If he will turn to the London Times of the 12th December, he will find the following, dated Wellington, N.Z.:
According to the latest parliamentary returns, 38 Government, 30 Opposition and 8 Labour members have been elected, Including Social Democrats. As the Labour members support the Opposition, this makes the parties equal. But the votes of absentees and of members of the expeditionary forces have not yet been counted, and they may affect the result in several cases where the vote is close. There are about 10,000 voters in Egypt and Samoa, and 2,000 are encamped in the Dominion.
The figure of 10,000 in Egypt and Samoa, my hon. friend will notice, tallies exactly with the number of voters mentioned in the telegram of the Prime Minister of New Zealand.
But if the hon. minister will follow the Times 'he will find that up to the 24th of September these 10,000 votes were not yet returned to New Zealand.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But that does not say that they were not registered in Egypt and Samoa.

That does not answer the criticism I made. What I pointed out was that my hon. friend sought, it seemed to me, to convey the impression that the New Zealand Act only applied to soldiers who were at the front. For he said they already had an Act relating to absentee voters which would apply to the case of others. That to which I wish to call his attention, and which I wish to emphasize, is that the New Zealand Act is intended to give to soldiers the opportunity to vote before they leave for the front; and it expressly provides that if they go to the front after the Act passes they must vote in New Zealand or they will not be permitted to vote at all. In that respect it is different from the present Bill, because this Bill provides that members of future contingents that leave for the front need not vote before they go-indeed there is no provision, as I understand it, for their marking their ballots before they go-but that while they are at the front, any 'Canadian commissioned officer whom the High Commissioner for Canada, Sir George Perley, chooses to appoint, may take the ballots to them, have them mark the ballots, make the ' necessary certificate and send the ballot back to the returning officer. In that respect this Bill is entirely different from the Bill which was submitted to the New Zealand Parliament. The quotation from the New Zealand Bill shows that in the opinion of that Government and that Parliament it was not desirable to give the < vote to soldiers at the front engaged in actual warfare, but, they apparently thought that, because they were providing for soldiers who left in future registering their votes before they went away, ex necessitate but erroneously I think, that they must provide that those already abroad should be allowed to vote in the way proposed. Thereafter, however, any soldier who left for the front lyithout marking his ballot before leaving the country could not be permitted to vote.
Now, I submit that we cannot with very great safety follow the example of New Zealand in this matter. We know that they have some other provisions of a most novel character in their election law, provisions which we have never sought to adopt in this country. They make provision, for instance, for the voter who is absent upon his ordinary business being allowed to vote. In this country we should not think of such a thing, because we realize that in carrying

on the elections here it is desirable to have safeguards surrounding the depositing of the ballot which could not be thrown around the recording of the votes of absentees. The Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) made the statement that we could safely follow New Zealand because it is a British country. But we are in the habit of following as far as we can the example of the Mother Country. The people of Canada reanze that the example set by the Parliament of the Mother Country in most matters is a safe one to follow. It is a significant fact and one to which we should give great weight in dealing with this question that, though Great Britain (has been engaged in many wars, yet never has it occurred to any one that it would be desirable to have a Bill passed by the British Parliament such as is now before this House. The Solicitor General said he doubted if there were any soldiers at the front in Britain's wars, who, if they had been in England would have had the right to vote. I doubt that statement very much. We know that it has been the glory of England that her young men of wealth, as well as those without wealth, have always been willing to go to the front. He knows that always many men of wealth who had commissions in the army have been ready to go to the front. It would seem to me most extraordinary if that statement of my hon. friend could be supported. The hon. gentleman said that during the Boer war the British Government had no thought of an election. The hon. member for . Bed Deer (Mr. M. Clark) called his attention to the fact that an election was held while the Boer war was in progress. Instead of answering the hon. member for Bed Deer, the Solicitor General with that cleverness shall I say with that smartness-which I have sometimes seen in the police court when the police court lawyer turns and makes a flippant remark to the crowd of unwashed on the back benches to provoke laughter, said, " Well, you must not talk any more about not having elections during the war."
My hon. friend, instead of answering the hon. member for Bed Deer, sought to turn the point in a flippant manner in order to provoke the laughter of his supporters. I do not think that that was very creditable on the part of the Solicitor General; I should have thought that he would answer the question of the hon. member for Bed Deer. If there were any answer to be given, my hon. friend was capable of giving it; the

only inference that we can draw is that no reasonable answer [DOT] could be given.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister, and, I think, the Minister of Justice, referred to the fact that 50,000 Canadians are or soon will be fighting the battles of the Empire, and suggested that it would be outrageous if they should be compelled to make the sacrifice, in addition to risking their lives in the defence of their country, of losing the opportunity of voting in connection with questions which may affect the future government of this country. It has been pointed out that there is one way in which that condition need not be brought about. This Parliament will not have run its five years until very late in the autumn of 19X6, and there can be one or even two sessions of Parliament before it will be necessary for the Government to go to the country. What question of great importance looms up to-day which would cause the Government to feel that they can properly advise His Eoyal Highness to cause this country to. be plunged into the turmoil of an election contest? What reason is there why all these questions-questions respecting the navy; questions respecting the general administration of affairs; questions respecting the responsibilities for the scandals with which the atmosphere of the whole of this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific is tainted-should be put before the people at this time? Is there any reason why this deplorable state of affairs should be brought about? Hon. gentlemen pretend that when we make suggestions of this kind, we are indicating that we fear to meet the electorate. Let me say to hon. gentlemen opposite that so far as hon. gentlemen on this side of the House are concerned, our political success or failure is a matter of little importance to us as compared with the desirability, while this great war, which is shaking the Empire to its very foundations, is in progress, of not diverting the attention of the people from the serious questions relating to the war to the petty consideration of the triumph of one political party or the other. More than that, I believe that if hon. gentlemen, without reason save that of a desire to secure party triumph, throw this country into the turmoil of an election, that is the feeling which will be expressed by the people. In the session of August last, when Parliament was called for the purpose of considering measures which it was desirable to pass by reason of the war that had broken out, if the Government had then thought it de-

sirable to 'give the soldiers the right to vote, that was the time to have passed this legislation and to have made provisions, with proper safeguards, for the recording of the votes of the soldiers. In the various villages and towns where the soldiers were massed, opportunities could easily have been given for the marking of the ballots by the soldiers in. the presence of scrutineers, and these ballots could have heen kept, to be used when the election should take place. But the Government did not do that.

What about the soldiers
who, having voted, were subsequently killed?

The hon. gentleman asks a question which he might well ask of the Minister of Justice. Suppose many hundreds of soldiers are killed between the time they mark their ballots and the time the ballots reach the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery; what would happen then?

Their vot~s would be
counted.

Then my hon. friend
asserts that the votes of dead men would be counted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The votes counted
would be the votes of men who had voted during the course of the election, not the votes of men who had voted months or years previous to the election.

That does not make any difference, because the Minister of Justice is providing not for voting for a particular person, but for voting for the Government or the Opposition, and the merits of either party might not change very much in the .course of a few months-although, again, they might. I raised a question this afternoon when the Minister of Justice was speaking and I think it is a question which is worthy of consideration-as to the merits of the proposal to have soldiers vote while they are at the front. The casting of one's ballot is one of the most serious acts which a citizen can perform. It is a sacred right; it is also a sacred duty. To enable the elector to cast his vote intelligently and conscientiously, it is desirable that he should be informed upon the issues which are presented in the country. How is it possible for soldiers who have been for several months at the front, out of touch altogether with Canadian affairs, intelligently to vote
upon the different questions which will necessarily influence the electorate when the election takes place? The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce told a Toronto audience the other night that they must remember that politics is not all boots and binoculars. Politics is not all boots and binoculars, yet the question of the scandals connected with the purchase of supplies for the war department, the question of the purchase of boots and binoculars and horses, the question of the employing of members of Parliament to make these purchases, the question of the excess prices *which were charged-all these are matters which, to a large extent, will necessarily be considered by the electorate. What does a soldier at the front, who has been absent from the country for four or five months, know about these questions? It may be said: What does he care to know about them? Well, he will care to know about them if he wishes to cast his ballot in the best interests of his country and to perform his duty intelligently. I think it was the Minister of Justice who said that Lord Kitchener may be relied upon to prevent the soldiers from getting campaign literature. I do not know, however, that Lord Kitchener would be able to control that, if the partisan pamphlets were sent through the mails. T do not know that he 'would be aware of what kind of literature was being sent; besides I fancy that Lord Kitchener has something else to do. The officers who are at the front, Sir John French and others, have too much to do to pay attention to the letters or literature which might be sent to the soldiers. I am afraid that if this measure passes in its present form and the soldiers who are at the front are given the right to vote, you will find that at the time when all the best thought that a soldier can give to anything should be given to fighting the foe. there will be hostile camps among the soldiers, Liberal officers will be canvassing Liberal or Independent or wavering soldiers, and Conservative officers will be canvassing for their side, each endeavouring to explain to the soldiers his view of the issues which are before the people of Canada. Is that desirable? Of course that raises the whole question as to whether among the men who are at the front and whose first duty would be to devote all their time and attention to fighting in the interests of their country, it is desirable to introduce political contests and political partisanship and feeling. I do not see the same objection to

providing that soldiers who are going to the front shall be allowed to mark their ballot before they go. If the Bill had proposed to go only that far I would have been glad to support it and to give whatever aid I could towards perfecting the measure, towards surrounding the marking of the ballot of the soldier with every possible safeguard. But so far as those already gone are concerned, the Minister of Justice has lost the opportunity. Instead of bringing this measure in as I have said, in August, as he ought to have done if in the opinion of the Government it was desirable to pass a measure of this kind, he has waited until some 30,000 or more of our young men have gone to the front and he has lost the opportunity of giving them a reasonable and fair opportunity to cast their ballots. If, however, at this late date, the minister amends his Bill so that it will apply only to those who are hereafter to go to the front and give them an opportunity to mark their ballots before they go, then I will be heart and soul with him and will assist him in throwing safeguards around this measure, as I believe safeguards can easily be thrown around it. You can make provision and supply safeguards for soldiers voting in this country before they go to the front, but you cannot after they have gone to the front. Then too the same objection would not obtain as to introducing politics in the trenches. With soldiers voting here you can have scrutineers and proper arrangements made without great difficulty, and in that way I think there would be no complaint on the part of anybody. As my right hon. friend pointed out in those cases where the marking of the ballot is done in Canada you would have control over the officials whose duty it was to see that the ballots were properly marked, marked in secret and forwarded to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. All that could be provided for and persons who might commit violations of the law could be punished. But here you propose to send ballots to Belgium, France and, as my right hon. friend said, possibly even to Germany, to send ballots broadcast and place them in the hands of people who may commit wrong and who cannot be punished. You give an opportunity for the commission of any crime of forgery, any crime of substitution of ballots, outside of this country and by persons over whom the Canadian courts would have no jurisdiction. With reference to the franchise, as my right hon. friend in the unanswerable objection which he made to this Bill in its present 
form stated, this Bill gives a new franchise. It practically repeals the Provincial Franchise Act, under which the elections in Canada are held. The provincial Acts provide that a man must be resident in the province generally for a period of 12 months. This Bill provides that a man who happens to be a British subject, but who had lived previously in the United States, if he happened to be in Canada even while recruiting was going on, even while he was arranging to join the militia, even for 30 days, shall have the right to mark his ballot. What knowledge would a gentleman from the United States, who had come here to join the Canadian forces to fight for the Empire, have of the issues on which the Canadian people are divided? What reason is there in giving to those men who have not been citizens of Canada, who have not been permanent residents of Canada, who happen to have been in the country for 30 days, votes, when we deny them under ordinary circumstances to men whose residence has been as short as that?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: How could such a man have a vote under this Bill when he had only been 30 days in Canada?
Every male British subject-

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: How would he get to be a British subject if he had only beeD in Canada for 30 days?

In the United States there are thousands of British subjects' who have no interest in Canada whatever, but who have come to Canada, and they have been here 30 days before joining the Canadian forces, and have gone to serve the Empire. They go because they are British subjects. After the war is over they will go back to the United States. But what reason is there in giving to these men, who, even though they may be true British subjects, are strangers to Canada and strangers to the issues on which our people are divided, the right to decide as between the two parties, or to vote upon the issues which are dividing the Canadian people? The reason why the legislatures of the different provinces have required a considerable period of residence, is that a man who wants to cast his ballot may be interested in and informed upon Canadian questions, and may therefore vote intelligently on the issues before the people. In New Zealand there is no alteration in the franchise; no man can vote under the New Zealand Bill except a man who had a right to vote independently of that Bill altogether. It makes no change in the franchise, as this Bill does.
It is a manhood franchise there.
Manhood franchise? But manhood franchise requires probably a certain period of residence in the country.
Registration only.

At all events, all provinces of Canada have required a certain period of residence in order to entitle a man to be registered as a voter. We have manhood suffrage in this country, and we require that there shall be a certain definite period of residence before a man may be registered as a voter.
For these reasons I am opposed to the Bill in its present form. I desire to be understood that, so far as I am concerned, I would support a measure which would provide that soldiers, before they leave Canada for the front, would be enabled to mark their ballots so that if an election came on during their absence the ballots would be cast by the returning officers under proper supervision.
