I would not have the Bill absolutely without safeguards as this Bill is; I would see that reasonable safeguards surrounded the voting. If that provision was made and the Bill was limited to that, I would feel that I could heartily support it; but in its present form I cannot support it. There is another objection to this Bill. Unlike the New Zealand Bill it is not limited to a general election. It is to be permanently attached to the Dominion Elections Act. It provides that ballots may be cast in a by-election, so that if at any time between now and the next general election there should be a by-election all this performance would have to be gone through, just as if it was a general elee-' tion. I do not know whether the Government mean that, but that is one of the provisions of the Bill; and in that respect it differs most materially from the New Zealand Bill, which provides " that this Act shall be deemed to be repealed on the completion of the general election." This provision in regard to by-eleotions certainly seems to me to be contrary to reason, and on this ground alone, if on no other, the Bill ought not to commend itself to the House in its present form. I have the right to assume that when the Government brings down a Bill applying to byelections as well as general elections, they mean what the Bill says. If they do not mean it, of course the Minister of Justice will tell us so; and no doubt the Bill will then be changed simply to meet the case of the general election.

I was a member of the committee that was charged with the responsibility of preparing the Bill that is now submitted to the House. It does appear to me that the discussion that has taken place, during the last few moments at least, has overlooked the object for which that committee met, and the object that it had in view in endeavouring to provide votes for soldiers. The question it seems to me is a very simple one. Shall a portion of our population that is absent from Ganada for a great cause be deprived of its franchise? Put in another way it is this: Shall thousands of our citizens who are exercising the highest obligation of citizenship be deprived of its highest privilege? In other words it is this: Shall those who are offering their lives as a willing sacrifice for us who remain at home be deprived of the right of expressing their view as to how we who remain conduct the affairs of our common country? Put in another way it is this: shall men who offer their lives for their country be punished by being deprived of their highest civil right? Now, considering these questions from any standpoint it seems to me there is only one answer; and in considering the -answer that must be given to any one of these questions I submit that we must have regard to the constitutional conditions under which we live. No less a man than Lord Morley of Blackburn, in one of his admirable essays pointed out that it would never be possible for the residents or citizens of the overseas dominions to fight for Britain in a cause in which they had no special interest; and, strange as it may seem, he took as an illustration the possibility of citizens of overseas dominions fighting for the neutrality of Belgium. The very illustration that he took for what he said might not happen has happened; and today 'Canadians, New Zealanders, and Australians are fighting side by side with the regular troops of Great Britain for the maintenance of the neutrality and integrity of Belgium-a living demonstration of the lack of prophetic vision on the part of that great man.
Under our present constitutional system we had nothing to say directly as to whether we should engage in these hostilities. Our citizens who are offering their services are in no sense conscripts; they are under no obligation to render their ser-9 p.m. vice to the Empire. They are volunteers, and to that extent they are citizen soldiers, offering their ser-



vices on the plains of Europe for the maintenance of a common democracy. -That being so, the simple question is this: Shall citizen soldiers be deprived of the exercise of their civil rights, merely because as citizen soldiers they have offered their services on the fields of Europe? That was the question that was before the committee. We discussed it, and dealt with it from various standpoints, and there seemed to be in the mind of that committee hut one answer to that question, and it was this: That a citizen of Canada, who is only a soldier by sentiment, by loyalty, by patriotism, and by a high regard for democracy and the cause of humanity, should not be deprived of the right to use his franchise merely because under extraordinary conditions he happens to be absent from this Dominion. I do not say that the committee was unanimous in arriving at that conclusion, but no member of it stood up and said: I say the principle is wrong. On the contrary every member of the committee felt that it was his bounden duty to give effect so far as it was possible, to the principle that a citizen of Canada who is absent from our shores under such extraordinary circumstances, and on so great and glorious a mission, should not he deprived of his civil rights. Having arrived at that conclusion, the next question that confronted the committee was: How shall we give effect to that conclusion? I will admit at once that it is not an easy thing to give erfect to such a conclusion. That is the reason why the committee considered the matter at such length; that is the reason that they had recourse to precedents from other countries; that is the reason that they studied the legislation, for instance, of the States of the neighbouring republic; that is the reason that they studied the legislation of New Zealand. Why, Sir, during the last year there has been passed in many of the states of the United States legislation that will enable absentee voters to vote on election day, regardless of the cause on which they might be absent; and postal voting has been established in some of the King's Dominions, not in the republic to the south of us but in the King's Dominions, the principle being that mere temporary absence from the country should not deprive a man of the exercise of his franchise. No hon. gentleman opposite will deny that the whole trend of legislation to-day, so far as the exercise of the franchise is concerned, is to make possible the exercise of that franchise by every 
man who is entitled to exercise it under the laws of the country in which he lives. That is the whole trend of democratic legislation. If you look at the last American Year Book, to which I had occasion to direct the attention of the committee during the discussion of this measxire, you will find that in various states provision is being made to meet that very point; namely, that some provision should be made whereby the man who has a right to vote, but who is temporarily absent on election day, should be able to declare whether he favours or opposes particular Bills, or parties, or governments, or legislation. That being so, we endeavoured to find some method by which a well-recognized principle of democracy might be maintained in all its strength, and whereby our fellow Canadians not temporarily absent in the ordinary sense of the term, but absent for the greatest cause for which Canadians have ever gone away, should be given every chance of sharing in the Government of this country. That is all.
What do we propose? First of all we propose that every British subject of the age of 21 years shall have a vote. Why? It is the universal law in this Dominion that every British subject of the age of 21 years shall have a vote. In Ontario, Alberta, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, British Columbia, Quebec, in all the provinces, the same provision applies. Instead of making a new franchise we are endeavouring to recognize the fact that in each of the provinces men of that type have votes, and because of the fact that this legislation is for a Dominion franchise, we made the broad declaration that every British subject of the age of 21 years shall have a vote.
My hon. and learned friend from St. John has just directed attention to the fact that there is an extraordinary provision in the Bill whereby residence of a British subject for thirty days prior to enlistment shall constitute residence necessary to vote, and he directed attention to the fact that in the New Zealand Bill no such provision appears. Surely my hon. friend is not serious?

What I said was that
in the New Zealand Bill the franchise was not altered in regard to residence.

My hon. friend did
hardly say that.
Yes.

He went a step further. What does section 2 of the New Zealand Act say? It says:

Every member of any expeditionary force sent from New Zealand to serve in the war in which His Majesty is at present engaged, shall he entitled to vote.
I do not attach any importance to what they do in New Zealand. It is merely a precedent, because there happened to be a general election. It became necessary to preserve the rights of the citizens to vote and in order to preserve that right they passed that legislation, but I do not attach any importance to what they have done in New Zealand in so far as Canada is concerned. The problem we had to deal with was a problem of our own and we only refer to New Zealand in so far as its action throws any light upon the question. It is merely referred to by the Government as showing what others have done. We have different conditions.
We have endeavoured to preserve the provincial franchise. We felt that any man who is a subject of the King and Emperor, who had come to this country and resided in it for thirty days, who would ordinarily have acquired the franchise and who, instead of extending (his residence for three months or six months or twelve months, was still in theory a Canadian citizen while serving under the colours in Flanders or in France, should have the vote. We provided that if he had been for thirty days in Canada he should have a vote provided that if that man had a _ vote in any other portion of Canada he should vote just where he had that vote in accordance with the provincial list and not otherwise. We have made no new franchise, we have endeavoured to substitute no new Act for the existing Acts, but we merely say that we will recognize existing rights. The provincial franchise must be exercised. But the committee felt that a British subject who had lived thirty days in Canada, although having ihis residence insofar as the fact is concerned with the colours in France or Belgium, should be given the franchise. At one time we discussed the possibility of preparing a list, but many difficulties were pointed out, and that idea was abandoned. Then the committee submit to Parliament a measure by which they say: We shall send ballots forward for the purpose of enabling our citizen soldiers to express their will at the polls. If you admit that we should answer the question as to whether they should have a vote in the affirmative, and if it be answered in the affirmative, and that we should preserve as far as possible the existing franchise, the next thing to be done was to see that they exercise that 141 i
franchise under proper safeguards. That was discussed, and it was concluded to adopt the very simple method provided by the Bill. It is proposed that we shall prepare the ballots and send them forward. They will be distributed among the men, they will be placed in an envelope with an affidavit, because we must have some safeguards. This envelope will be sent back to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery and the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery will send the envelopes to the various electoral districts where the ballots will be counted. We felt that there should be legislation to provide against the very difficulty that the Minister of Justice has pointed out, namely, uncertainty as to the result of the elections. We said that if these ballots reached the returning officer after the polling day they should not be counted. We felt that the uncertainty that prevailed in New Zealand in consequence of the manner in which the soldiers' votes had been transmitted after they had been cast in Egypt and Samoa caused a great deal of difficulty and we said that if the votes of the soldiers reached the returning officers in the various constituencies in Canada after the day of election they should not be counted. Then we provided that some time during election day, but after the close of the poll, so as to obviate the possibility of there being some knowledge in the mind'of the electors as to how the poll was going, these ballots should be counted and placed in the ballot box and added to the general results. I do submit that that is fair, that it is a recognition of the obligation on the part of the Canadian people and Parliament assembled to give some countenance and support to the very proper claim that was made by the soldiers that went from my constituency to myself that they should be enabled to cast their votes if a general election should happen during their absence, and that they should not be obliged to lose their civil rights because they exercised the higher obligations of citizenship.
What complaint can be urged against that? Two complaints are urged against it. One is that it opens the way to fraud, and another is that you have not the safeguards that should surround the exercise of the franchise. Living as I do in western Canada all I can say is that under the legislation we have before us Canada's soldiers cannot do anything in the way of fraud comparable with what I have seen. I am not saying that in a cavilling spirit. That happened in the last general election in the province of Alberta? In one constituency

the ballot box was opened and the votes taken out and to this day the offender has not been punished. Would you sooner trust the British officer, one of our fellow Canadian officers, who has before him the grim responsibilities of his position with death staring him in the face, to do the decent, honest thing, or would you rather trust a returning officer where a ballot box was opened, as in Medicine Hat last election? Which would you rather have, which would the people of Canada sooner have, which would any reasonable man sooner have?
Then my hon. friend goes a step further and he says: Why, surely, you would not permit a British subject who has come in from the United States and has only been thirty days in Canada to vote in Canada? Oh, no! Come with me to the province of Saskatchewan. At the last general election you could have seen thousands of aliens voting as they were told. And that is not all. Come with me to any poll in the province of Alberta where we have naturalized Germans and Austrians and tell me whether you would prefer the vote of a British subject who lived thirty days in Canada to that of the naturalized alien whose instincts and sympathies are still with what he calls his fatherland.
Come with me and tell me whether or not you would sooner trust the Briton who has lived thirty days in Canada than the authors of the splendid pamphlet that I hold in my hand that is now printed on one side in German and on the other in English upon a printing press controlled, I believe, by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), commending: Canada first; down with participation by Canadians in the wars of the Empire; preserve Canada for the Germans and the Austrians and all those other foreign people who come here and make it their home; but never mind Britain, because she and her King can take care of themselves. Would you trust those naturalized foreigners or would you trust the thirty-day resident British subject who came from the United States in order that he might offer his life as a sacrifice for your safety and mine? I commend my hon. friend from the old loyalist city of St. John (Mr. Pugsley) to go back and ask his electors whether they would prefer to see the franchise for this great Dominion of Canada exercised by the men who had journeyed over from Massachusetts or Vermont or Maine and lived here for thirty days that they might fight for our country and Empire or the men I have mentioned. Bet him go and ask the descendants of the 'founders

of St. John. I leave it to the electorate of St. John to deal with my hon. friend as they will.
After dealing with that as I have stated and after having arrived at the conclusions which I have mentioned, we found it necessary to surround the franchise with such safeguards as we could suggest, and I think the safeguards in the Bill are adequate for the purposes intended. In the province in which I live all that is necessary for a man to do to exercise his franchise is this: He walks into a polling booth and the returning officer says: " What is your name?" "John Jones." "Where do you live?" "Well, just west of Edmonton," or "just west of Calgary." "Where?" "Oh, not far from Edson," or " not far from Morley." " Well, your name is not on the list." " That is all right, partner; let's swear." That is the way the thing goes on. The man puts his hand upon the Bible, and he swears that he is a British subject; that he is 21 years of age, and that he has resided one year in the province of Alberta and three months in a particular electoral district. He gets the ballot; goes out; fills it up; comes in and puts it into the ballot box, and you may seek in vain for John Jones next day. The place that knows him knows him no more, and the place that knew him knows him no more. Yet you are going to tell me that the 12,000 electors from the Province of Alberta that are now fighting or getting ready to fight for this Empire, some in Europe and some in England and some in Canada, cannot vote, but that this John Jones can vote. Out in yonder trenches the man goes up and swears an affidavit before his commanding officer, and we have the record of that man from now until the time that he is discharged or until he offers his life for his country. His name is there; it is enrolled upon the records; we know him for all time; his history will bj the common heritage of us all. We know that man, but who knows anything of John Jones who came in on the train and put up at a hotel? Yet he must vote, but my friends from Calgary cannot vote; my hon. friend's friends from Edmonton cannot vote. Why? Because my hon. friends opposite say that there are not sufficient safeguards when the soldier makes his affidavit. He marks his ballot and next morning perhaps he is offering his life for his country. His ballot is put into an envelope and sent back, but it cannot be counted because there are no safeguards! I am sure my hon. friend from Edmonton

will not support any such doctrine as that which my hon. friend from St. John advocates. I am sure he will not permit himself for a single moment to go back on his old and dried and true friends who are now fighting in Europe and who would like to have a chance to vote, any more tb#n I shall go back on those who have voted both for and against me and who in the trenches have a desire to vote. The safeguards which are thrown around the voting by the men in the trenches are better than the safeguards as regards voting in the province of Saskatchewan or of Alberta are to-'day or to-morrow.	[DOT]
Oh, my hon. friends perhaps will say: It is going to interfere with military operations and Lord Kitchener will veto the measure. In any event, it will not be Lord Kitchener that will veto the measure; it will be Sir John French or whoever is in command of the British forces. Assuming, however, that by virtue of military exigencies and necessities, our soldiers cannot vote, does that lessen the obligation of their fellow-Canadians to give them the Tight to vote if they want to?
I do not for a single moment say that our soldiers will vote, 'but I know that some of them want to vote. I do not say that they will have the opportunity to exercise the franchise that they would like to have, because it may be that the military exigencies and necessities of the war will prevent them from doing so; hut I would be recreant to my duties and this House would be recreant to its duties and to the trust reposed in it by its Canadian fellow-citizens thousands of miles from here, if we did not afford them the opportunity to vote if they wish to do so. When men tell me that some one is going to veto something or that something is going to interfere with something else, that does not interfere with or lessen the right of this Parliament to do its plain and obvious duty. I do not for a single moment doubt that if an election came at a certain date, there might be great difficulties; but we have not said on what day the soldiers shall vote. As soon as it is known there is going to be an election, the ballots will be transmitted to Europe and circulated, and although it may be that some of the soldiers will say: I am not going to be bothered about an election, and they will throw the ballot away, there may be ten men out of a company of a. hundred who want to vote. I intend to use such power and influence as I have to give those ten men the right to exercise the franchise if they so desire. Why should there be any
magnifying of the seriousness of the situation? Why should there not be a common desire on the paTt of this Parliament on both sides-Government and Opposition- to	say:	We are going	to give
the men an opportunity to vote, and we will make this measure as perfect as possible. When I think of the labyrinths of the mind of my hon. friend from St. John, I am sure he can devise safeguards to throw around this voting, and may I say that with his large experience and great knowledge of the law, it would be his manifest duty, as coming from the old loyalist city of St. John, when we are sitting here in committee, to give that splendid talent of his to make perfect this measure and to see that his fellow-citizens shall have the right to vote if they so desire. This is not a provocative nor a contentious measure; this Bill enanated from the committee as quite the opposite and we discussed it in the most friendly and amicable manner possible.. iSome hon. gentlemen opposite say that it is absolutely impossible to carry this legislation into effect. I say nothing is impossible to a Parliament that desires to achieve a given result or end, and although the measure may not be as perfect as it should be, that does not deter me from using my influence to have something placed upon the statute-book that will make possible the end which we have in mind and which should be effective. My hon. friend says:	I am in favour of
letting the soldiers in the country have a vote, but once they go out of the country, I am not. Is a soldier who is garrisoned at Halifax who comes from Alberta in any better position than a soldier who comes from Calgary who is garrisoned at Bermuda? Is a soldier who came from Edmonton and is now garrisoned at, let us say, Winnipeg, in any better position than the soldier who came from Edmonton and is now garrisoned at Alexandria, Egypt, or on Salisbury Plain or in Tidworth barracks? .
If we admit that, let us go a step further. Is such a soldier in any worse position if he happens to be with the second division, or brigaded with certain British regiments at some point in France? You say:	the
difficulties are multiplied because these men are in the trenches, but men do not stay in the trenches all the time; they go to their base. Suppose there are two hundred of them-a -double company with a major in charge, the major sees to it that these two hundred men are handed their ballots. In due course each makes his affidavit before the commissioned officer who is authorized

to administer the oath, and the ballot is put in an envelope, the officer certifying that the man entitled to vote had actually marked that ballot. That ballot comes out to Canada and in due course finds its way to Oalgary. Is there any difficulty about that? Why magnify these difficulties and go into mock heroics about the dangers of the trenches? Why discuss these sanguinary differences between two contending armies, when the vote is not being cast there at all? Why not look at this reasonably as practical men? It does seem to me it is possible to be done. Why innoculate this discussion with talk about scandals in boots?
If this Government were desirous of covering alleged scandal about improper equipment, do you suppose they would be so anxious that the men who wear the boots should have the vote? If this terrible condition exists that the hon. member for St. John city imagines-and it is pure imagination-does he think for a moment that the soldier wearing paper upon his feet instead of boots would vote for the Government? You would think the hon. gentleman would almost exhaust his energy in giving that soldier the right to vote. Either the hon. gentleman does not believe the boots are bad, or else there is something else behind all this to cause him to prevent the soldier from having the vote. What is it? Why does the right hon. leader of - the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) desire that the soldiers should not have the vote? Why does the	hon. member
for St. John city take the same view? Why do hon. gentlemen opposite generally offer such opposition to mis legislation? It must be that they remember that the soldiers have memories. It must be that they recollect that the men who are fighting for Canada at this time bear in mind the political history of their country. Their knowledge and recollection will induce them to mete out to the right hon. gentleman and those who sit beside him that measure of justice *which these recollections would entail. No doubt some of these gallant soldiers in the trenches have read the utterances of some of the hon. gentlemen opposite. They cannot fail to have taken note of the noble sentences that decry British diplomacy and look forward with joy to the day when, so far as Canada is concerned, it shall be no more. They cannot fail to remember having read in text books of elections in this country that Canadians would never fight for Britain in Britain's wars, Canada not being

interested. Remembering these sentences that have fallen from the lips of stalwart leaders of their party, peradventure, these hon. gentlemen opposite think: If we give these men the vote, they may remember this against us. I wonder if that is the reason. Far be it from me to suggest that to be the reason, because I know that hon. gentlemen opposite are dominated by a higher spirit of patriotism than that. There must be another reason. I fain would know it. But, after having listened to the speech of the right hon. leader of the Opposition and of that great legal luminary who sits to his right, I fail, absolutely fail, to ascertain that reason. There is a mystery about it, and I would like to see that mystery solved. No doubt many other people in Canada would like to see it solved. Why should a simple little rail that offers our fellow-Canadians the franchise cause all this trouble? One would think that hon. gentlemen opposite would be falling over one another in their support of this measure. Their statements will be read in the morning with great pain, and I am sure it will cause many an anxious moment to Liberals in the country that I come from when they find that their brothers are denied the franchise by the acts of hon. gentlemen opposite. And many a wife who has given her husband to the war will sorrow and he exceeding sad to know that her husband, because he is in France fighting for Canada, cannot vote in the next election. I wonder how the hon. member for Edmonton is going to feel when these two thousand men from his constitutency learn that he voted against this measure.
I cannot understand hon. gentlemen oppo- _ site to-night. Their conduct is really passing strange. And i do not think anybody will be able to understand on what principle they have arrived at such conclusions as they have expressed here. They talk about boot scandals, and yet they will not trust the soldiers to judge their own boots. They talk about (horse scandals, but the only horse I have seen ridden around here is one that, I think, will not accomplish much- the scandal horse. They are disappointed because the Government has called for a full inquiry; because there is no blockers' brigade, because there is no dark lantern brigade; and, to fill up their cup of bitter-enss-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman is not confining himself closely to the Bill under discussion.

Possibly I (have wandered far from the subject because the hon. member for St. John city was discussing scandal, and, as he is an expert in that matter, 1 wished to remind him of certain things. I had almost.thought (that perhaps the soldiers would remember the sawdust wharves and other things of that sort.
That is thoroughly nonpartisan.

The hon. gentleman says the wharf is non-partisan. In that, I think, he is altogether right. The committee in the preparation of this Bill did not have in mind an immediate election, and that I can say with all certainty. The hon. and learned gentleman who presided over the committee, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), brought to (bear upon the measure every consideration he could to make it fair and workable, and the other members of the committee did not prepare the Bill with regard to an immediate election. The hon. member for Bed Deer said that this measure emanated from the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Bogers). If all the work of the Minister of Public Works is as good as this-and I do not think he appeared before the committee-he has every reason to be proud of this handiwork in trying to give his fellow-Canadians at the front a chance to exercise the franchise. The committee had regard to what had been done in other colonies and dominions. Members may not have been altogether forgetful of the fact that challenges had been issued from the other side as to the possibility of an election. After these challenges I received letters from soldiers from my own constituency who were leaving for the front and from those who had already left, pointing out that it was said we were going to have a general election.
They had heard that the Opposition had said that we dare not have an election, and they expressed a desire to have an opportunity of recording their votes. I do not doubt that they desired to have a vote in order to vote against the party that dared challenge us to have an election at this time. All I have to say to the hon. member for Bed Deer, when he talks in high-flown and heroic terms about an election at this time, is that if he would make an attempt to have his own party refrain from making challenges about elections and from talking about elections and appeals to the people, he would be accomplishing a great deal more than he is doing by offering his advice
as to whether or not we should have one, while at the same time sending out ammunition in the shape of campaign literature.
In my town that ammunition is all in shape, ready to burst the moment the word is given. This partisan shell has a time fuse; just what time has been fixed, I do not know, but it is ready to be exploded at the proper time. A friend of mine, writing to me the other day, told me all about this. Our people have not any of this campaign ammunition in readiness, so far as I know; perhaps we do not need any.
I have pointed out the considerations that influenced the committee in endeavouring to arrive at a conclusion in this matter, and I have pointed out the safeguards with which we have endeavoured to surround the exercising of the franchise under the conditions proposed. I am not unmindful of the fact that any election law that may be placed on the statute book caii be circumvented and broken by crooks, but it remains for hon. gentlemen opposite to insinuate . that the officers who are offering their lives, and who may face death the next day, are going to do a fraudulent, dishonest and dishonourable thing in giving effect to this legislation. I do not believe it, and I do appeal to the members on the other side of this House for once to forget partisanship, provoeativeness and contentiousness, and to unite with us in putting upon the Statute Book a measure of which Canada may be proud. It is not enough that those who go to the front to fight for us should make us proud of them; we who remain behind to legislate and to deal with the great problems which surround us every day should make these men, when they come back from the trenches, proud of us. I do not believe that Canadians should be deprived of the privilege of exercising their civil rights merely because freely, voluntarily, without conscription, without restraint, without coercion, without in any sense being requested or asked so to do by legal authority, they have offered their services to their King and Empire. Twelve thousand soldiers from the province of Alberta ask that this measure of justice shall be given them. Twelve thousand men, their brothers and sisters, their wives and other relatives, ask that this measure of justice shall be given them. Even if the legislation is not surrounded by all the safeguards that you would wish, they ask that we place upon the statute book something which will enable the men who are offering their lives as a sacrifice to-day to exercise their rights,

for or against this Government. Let us do this thing, in the name of justice, of equity, of fair play, of that righteousness which exalteth a nation, of that spirit which pervades those who are offering their lives as sacrifices for us. That is what animated the committee, and the legislation, I do submit, is as fair and reasonable as it possibly could be, having regard to the circumstances and to the difficulty of the task which the committee undertook to perform.

I
am sure that if there had been any doubt in the minds of hon. gentlemen of the House as to the character and purpose of this Bill, the speech of our hon, friend has set that doubt at rest. We understand now beyond any question that this is a political measure, for partisan purposes, and for partisan purposes only. I do not wish at the moment to follow my hon. friend in the course of his devious remarks. I shall confine myself rather to the argument that preceded his. I wish at first to draw attention to the difference that exists between the conditions surrounding the bringing forward of the/New Zealand Bill and those surrounding the bringing forward of this proposed legislation, I wish to point out that there is no comparison between the conditions surrounding these two Bills. In the ease of the New Zealand Bill, an election was compelled in the immediate future by effluxion of time; in the case of this Bill, no election is compelled in the immediate future by effluxion of time. There was a definite reason why the New Zealand legislature should take some action in regard to the votes of soldiers; there is no reason why this Government at this time should take such action, unless it be the intention of the Government to bring on a general election during the course of this war for the purpose of enabling its followers to make addresses throughout the Dominion of Canada of the kind and character that my hon. friend has just favoured us with. If the right hon. the Prime Minister calls a general election and turns his followers loose on the platforms of this country with such talk as my hon. friend has engaged in here to-night, how far is that going to urge Canada to do her full share in the matter of rendering assistance to the Empire during the course of this war? I ask the Prime Minister whether, if Canada is to do her part, this is not a time when Canadians should be united; when there should be 
as few differences introduced into the public mind as possible? We are bound to assume, from what we have heard to-night, that he has it in mind, without cause or justification, except the probability of securing a partisan advantage, to throw a general election upon the country and to set Canadians against each other-as my hon. friend the hon. member for Calgary has himself said; against me and against my friends-at a time when men should be looking forward only in one direction, and that to the giving of whatever assistance they can to the Empire.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I should like
to say to my hon. friend, since he has ap-appealed to me, that the question of a general election will stand on its own merits when the time comes. There has been no decision either to hold an election or not to hold an election; we have been too busy with other things. But I desire to tell him this:	that, including the vote of want of
confidence which his leader moved and which he supported, in their every move during the past six weeks in this House, hon. gentlemen on the other side have been actuated purely by a desire to obtain partisan advantage at the expense of that unity which the hon. gentleman so greatly lauds at the present time. Any man who has followed the course taken by hon. gentlemen in this House and in the committees of this House during the past six weeks, knows absolutely the truth of what I have just said.
We do not know anything of the kind.

I may be permitted to deviate for a moment from the course of my remarks to follow what the Prime Minister said. The only occasion on which the course of the Government has .been challenged in this House at this session was on the occasion of the Budget, on the occasion of a reversal of the fiscal policy of Canada; and I ask him if he considers that in a country under representative institutions and under responsible Government, if we held views different from those advocated by himself, we would have been doing our duty to the country if we had done less than we did. I cannot imagine that unless my hon. friend is taking the position that he has been elected the Czar of Canada-
The Kaiser.

I beg pardon; yes, the
Kaiser, and that there must be no differ-

enee of opinion and no expression of any difference of opinion when once the mind of the Government has been made up. If that is the condition it is most extraordinary, and I for one had never understood that to be the position, even as the Prime Minister himself understood it or ever thought of enforcing it upon the country.
I would say this to him, if I may be permitted, that if he thinks that the excuses he has given here to-night will excuse him before the people of Canada if he throws this country into the turmoil of a general election when he does not need to while this war is on, he mistakes the opinion of the people of this country and mistakes it very seriously. However, from what has passed here to-day, while the Prime Minister has said that he has not decided yet to hold a general election, we are bound to assume from what he has said that a general election while the war is on is entirely within the range of possibility or even of probability; and I am entitled then to conclude that this legislation is introduced distinctly with that object in view.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.

That it is, in its nature and essentially, partisan legislation introduced for a partisan purpose fn order to further the interest of purely party politics.
Let me say further in regard to the Hew Zealand case, where provision is made for the taking of a vote for the election of members of the Legislaure and where the vote is not cast for the individual member, but cast for or against the Government or the Opposition or Labour party. But there was another vote provided for, a vote on the great question of prohibition. Provision is made for the taking of a vote on prohibition at the same time as the vote on the general election. It was necessary, I understand, under the arrangement that had been made that these two votes should be taken at the same time. I am pre-* pared to argue that instead of the Dominion of New" Zealand providing as they 'did for the taking of the vote of soldiers during their absence from the country for the sake of getting tne soldiers' vote, ,they made the provision for the purpose of getting the definite opinion of the people of New Zealand in regard to the question and principle of prohibition; and that if it bad not been for the submission of the question of prohibition there is no reason to believe that the Government of New Zealand would have
made a provision that would have called for a declaration on the part of a voter that he votes for or against the Government as an exercise of his franchise; because it is not an exercise of his franchise. I think the difference in these two points is sufficiently important to emphasize, first that the vote in New Zealand was primarily ordered for the purpose of deciding the prohibition question, a question that had not to do with men but only with principles and, secondly, that the election had to be held. In the case of Canada the election does not have to be held for another period of about 18 months. There is this further difference, that New Zealand is a small country with a comparatively small population, a compact country with a compact people of like race and language and interests and ideas from end to end of the dominion. It is more reasonable that the voters of New Zealand should satisfy their aspirations as to the expression of their political views by voting merely for or against the Government or Labour party than that this should be done by the people of the Dominion of Canada, spread over the width of a continent, of many different provinces, including many different races of people and many different conditions of life. There is no way that the elector of the Dominion of Canada can express his views in regard to the government of -this country to the satisfaction of ;his aspirations in Icontrolling the affairs of the country unless he votes for a man, unless he votes for somebody as well as for something; and when the hon. the Minister of Justice or the other members of the House who have spoken in support of this Bill, suggest that by the passing of this Bill they are giving to our soldiers who are or will be in Europe the opportunity to exercise their franchise on an equality with their fellow-citizens in Canada, they are simply stating what is absurd on its face. It is not, however, in regard to that feature of the voting that I wish to speak. It is not the provision for the voting of the soldier who is in Europe that I wish to criticise; it is the provision for the voting of the soldier who is in Canada. The other feature of the question has been already very fully dealt with. I find that in this Bill the seldieT who is still in Canada, who surely should be entitled to exercise bis franchise just as any other citizen of Canada, and should have the same safeguards thrown around the exercise of that franchise, is compelled to cast his vote just as the soldier who is in Europe. He does not vote for a candi-

date, he votes for the Government or for the Opposition as the case may be, although he is living right in Canada, and his vote must run the gauntlet of people holding the same view in regard to election proceedings, as my hon. friend from Calgary has told us, are so numerous in Western Canada. The fact that these people-for they are the same people-are in uniform does not necessarily change their character or their intentions or their views, but it does in a large measure give them immunity from those restrictions, or, in case of necessity, immunity from those penalties, to which civilians "acting in the same way would be subject.
My hon. friend from Calgary has alluded to the fact that there are 2,000 soldiers in barracks in or near the city of Edmonton with whom I shall have to reckon when election day comes. I shall be glad to reckon with these 2,000 soldiers, as I certainly will have to, if I could be sure that when these men vote they will vote on election day, and vote for candidates that are offering in the several constituencies, and that their votes will be taken by officials, who will be subject to the, ordinary procedure of the courts and not enjoy immunity in any degree, as they certainly will under the provisions of this Act. In other words, I want the 2,000 men to vote, but I want to be sure that their votes will be counted the way they want them to be counted; and I am not sure of that under the terms of this Bill. I want to say-and -if I go outside the rules, Mr. Speaker, I am sure you will check me-I say, on the statement of the hon. member for Calgary, and on the statement that I have given here to-night, that this Bill is for the purpose of stealing the election, and that that [DOT] is all it is for. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, whether this Government has the right to turn 2,000 voters loose in my constituency without proper check as to scrutineers, as to qualifications, or as to any other restrictions except what are contained in this Act? 1 say that it is a piece of electoral villainy that has been -planned and produced in this Act.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must remind the hon. member that it is not permissible for a member to impute improper motives. No rule is more clear than that, according to the rulings of both English and Canadian speakers.

I desire to bow to your
ruling, Mr. Speaker, and beg to withdraw the assertion unreservedly. I have no doubt that I trespassed on the rules of Parliament,

although I was speaking according to my own belief, and I think quite within the actual facts of the case. That is the condition prevailing under this Bill 10 p.m. as it applies to the case to which my hon. friend from Calgary has himself alluded. My hon. friend. from Calgary has in effect threatened me here in this House with what will happen to me at the hands of these men if I dare to oppose this Bill. Mr. Speaker, there have been some strange things done in the Parliament of Canada; there have been some strange things done in Canadian politics; but I venture to say that no stranger thing has been done than the production of a Bill such as this, backed by a threat such as that. I agree that every citizen of Canada who is entitled to vote should vote whenever and wherever the opportunity can be given or found that will ensure that his vote, when given, shall be counted as he intended it to be counted; and if the Minister of Justice will produce a Bill that will give our Canadian citizens in France or in Flanders or in Germany or wherever they please, the right to express their views and to east their votes for the candidates standing in the Dominion election, and if provision is made that that vote when cast shall be counted as it was intended to be counted, that Bill will have my hearty support. I do not object to the voting of the soldiers; but I object to the counting by the Government.
I say that it is-well, I will not say what I was going to say, but I say that if the soldiers are to mark their ballots in Belgium and our friends here in Ottawa are to count them without any more restrictions or provisions for an honest count than are contained in this Bill, the soldiers will certainly not be getting what some of the speakers here to-night have held out as being given to them. I am not going to tell the House, for my hon. friend from Calgary has told us to-night how corrupt are the election transactions in the province that he and I come from, _and how much more corrupt they are in other provinces. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to take the hon. gentleman at his word. Only take him at his word, and then read the provisions of this Bill, and say what chance there would be for the man who voted in Flanders of having his vote counted against the Government in Canada. Why, this Bill is an inspiration! Fifty thousand votes. to be collected and distributed throughout the various constituencies of Canada wherever they will do the most good! The possibilities are magnifi-

cent,, and no doubt they appeal to the brilliant imagination of my hon. friend from Calgary. I could easily imagine how industriously he worked on the terms of this Bill when I heard how enthusiastically he supported its provisions. Why, there would be nothing to an election with a Bill such as this in the hands of the Government. Will I deny that the electoral proceedings in my hon. friend's constituency are as corrupt as he said they were?

The hon. gentleman is mistaken. It was a Liberal returning officer, under the auspices of a Liberal Gov-eminent, that opened this ballot box, not in the constituency of Calgary but in the adjoining one of Medicine Hat.

I do not wish to put on a variety entertainment in this House, following the lead of my hon. friend from Calgary, but I may say for the information of the House, seeing that he has been so very personal, that I was informed by the gentleman who had charge of the Liberal side of the campaign that, after my hon. friend was elected to this House from the constituency of Calgary, they sent out letters to 2,500 addresses on the voters' list, persons who 'had presumably supported my hon. friend, and they never got any replies.
The lists were prepared by the Liberals.
What was the majority?
The majority was 3,000.

My hon. friend knows
whereof he speaks when he speaks of electoral corruption in Alberta.
No man has suffered more from it than myself.

I think that after hearing my hon. friend the House will bear me out when I make the suggestion that the hon. gentleman has suffered more from himself than from anybody else. My hon. friend made allusion to a paper which he held up and which he intimated was printed on a press owned and controlled by myself. It does not make any difference to the House, I presume, whether I owned or controlled the press or not, but for the information of the House I may say that I do not own or control the press nor have I had any control over it for some months past. I did have some interest in a German paper published in Edmonton, and I think my hon. friend had an interest in a German paper published in Calgary.
No.

I understood he had, but that the finanieal results were something like the financial results in Edmonton, and that ultimately the connection ceased. It certainly did in my case, and I presume it was the same in his.
That is right. It was a Liberal paper in which I had $200 worth of stock, subscribed under misrepresentation and I lost every dollar.
So I lost mine.
The honours are easy.

Yes. I have laid the
burden of establishing the position of the Government on the speech which the hon. member for Calgary delivered to the House.
I am sorry I cannot restrict my allusions to the hon. member for Calgary. I said in the beginning of my remarks that this Bill was evidently intended as a partisan measure, introduced with a view to an impending election and that it was brought forward by the Government for the express purpose of unduly and improperly affecting that election. Is this Government above.suspicion in matters of that kind? Is it unfair to make such a suggestion? I see mat my hon. friend from Bruce (Mr. Clark) nods his head. Does he say it is?

I- am curious to
know whether the hon. member thinks that the ballots that are marked in Flanders, in France, or in Germany will not be counted properly.

My hon. friend from Calgary has complained vociferously in regard to the mishandling of ballots in elections and I say that these same people will be the people who will handle the counting of the ballots from Flanders. I have no more reason to believe that that count will go straight than the count that my hon. friend has spoken of, assuming that what he said was true.

He was speaking of
elections controlled by Liberals.

That brings me about
where I wanted to get. This election is being controlled by Conservatives, it is being controlled by this Government, and inasmuch as it is going to be controlled by this Government, it is going to be a square election and these men are going to have their ballots counted properly-is that what I am to understand?
That is it.
What have we before the country to lead us to believe that the country is going to get a square deal at the hands of this Government?

It will be controlled
by British officers.
By what officers?
British officers.

If my hon. friend will
show me something in the Bill to say that it will not be controlled by Canadian officers perhaps there may be something in his argument, but we heard to-day that it was to be controlled by Canadian officers, and certainly it is only reasonable that it should be Canadian officers. I do not know that Canadian officers change their character very much because they become officers or because they are resident in Flanders instead of Canada. I am only taking the case as the hon. member for Calgary has put it. My hon. friend from Bruce must settle it with the hon. member for Calgary if he has any fault to find with my remarks. What right has this country to expect a square deal at elections or in anything at the hands of this Government? If this Government and party on the other side have any principle which they stand by, which they vociferate, it is the principle of loyalty to Britain. Is that right? How have they shown their loyalty to Britain? They have borrowed $50,000,000 from Britain for the purposes of war. What have they done with it? How have they used it? As soon as Parliament rose in August last, from end to end of Canada, the evidence is plain, their jackalls" were turned loose, they were told to "go to it."

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am afraid the hon. gentleman is forgetting that it is the principle of this Bill that is under consideration at present.

My hon. friend from
Bruce asked me a question. I was desirous of elaborating the point, and I wanted to show why the Government could not be trusted to count these ballots honestly. If I may proceed with all moderation; from the purchase of motor trucks to the purchase of hospital supplies, it is on the records that there has been nothing but graft and corruption from beginning to end. Is that loyalty? That is the kind of patriotism we are getting at the hands of this Government; that is the kind of

honesty that we have' been getting at the hands of this Government. If this Government cannot be trusted to buy bandages for sick soldiers at an honest price and of an honest quality, can they be trusted to count the votes cast in Flanders? I think not. If they cannot be trusted to buy boots that will keep the soldiers in fair condition, if their manufacturers supply leather doubled in order to make it strong instead of honest single leather; if they are able to charge from thirty cents to fifty cents per pair more for the boots supplied than they are worth, according to sworn evidence, and if the Government allows them to do that, is that the Government that is going to give us an honest count of these ballots? I say, no, and we do not expect it. The Government who sent their members of Parliament out to buy horses are the honest patriots who are going to count the votes of the soldiers in Flanders.

Mr. WILLIAM F. NICKLE (Kingston): At this particular time I doubt if I should have made any remarks upon the principle of this measure, had it not been for the extreme, and to me as an easterner, the violent language of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver).
Might I ask if the hon. member was offended by the language used by the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) ?

right to vote, 'but who could only vote provided they could return to the place whence they came. Where would there be discipline then? The men who came from Vancouver might be in Halifax; the men who came from Winnipeg might be at Petawawa, and are all those men to be returned to their homes? If that were so, then for a month the military camps of Canada would be in a turmoil.
Section 159 provides that even though a man were not on the electoral list he should be entitled to vote provided his not being on the list resulted from the fact that he was engaged in active service when the list was prepared. In other words, the man who has been in active service abroad, on returning to Canada would be entitled to go to the deputy returning officer and swear in his vote. The man in Canada who had not gone abroad, though his name were on the list and by the provision of the Ontario law, there is a form of registration that would permit many men to go on the list by virtue of a friend making the necessary affidavit that he is a British subject, and has been twelve months in Ontario, and three months in the district-could qualify and vote. But the men who have actually faced the enemy, the men who have been in the shadow of death, are to be deprived of their votes, being unable to vote in person because of the miles of water between England and Canada. That struck me as radically unfair, and the question pressed itself upon me: how are these men to vote? There were various ways by which it might be done, and a number of ways were suggested in the committee. In the opinion of the Minister of Justice the way provided in this Bill is the best that can be devised and it seems to me a fair and reasonable solution of the difficulty.
I cannot see eye to eye with the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) who insinuates that men who are fighting in the shadow of eternity are going to do corrupt and iniquitous things. I know nothing about his western' electoral methods, but I do know there are honourable officers at the front, men who would discharge their sacred duty- for so it is-of performing with honesty their part in the electoral machinery of Canada and who would, when required, see to it that the soldiers who came before them had the opportunity to mark their ballots as they desire without fear and free from intimidation. And these bal-

lots, having been marked and properly enclosed in an envelope, would be- sent forward to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, without interference and without irregularity. I am satisfied that once these ballots reach that officer there would be no difficulty whatever in elaborating plans that would prevent any irregularity in regard to the votes being received by [DOT] deputy returning officers and counted. If the hon. member for Edmonton is sincere, and if he is willing to facilitate the measure, why does he not admit the principle, and, then when the Bill comes to Committee of the Whole it will be a simple thing to insert a provision that when the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery sends the ballots forward to the deputy returning officer, notice should be sent to each candidate of that fact, and the ballots should be on receipt sealed with the seals of the candidates, and not opened until both candidates or their agents are present to see them counted. There is no difficulty in working out the machinery if you want to work it out, but there is great difficulty if you do not want to secure results.
I believe hon. gentlemen opposite are not sincere in their opposition to this Bill. I am one who has not always supported the party to which I belong, but I do believe that in a great measure of this sort, where recognition is being given to a class of people who are willing to risk their lives for a principle which they hold dear, we should set to one side party politics, get down to realities, and try to draft a measure that would prevent fraud, and that the men who are at the front would realize that there is no politics in being a soldier, but that every soldier, being a volunteer and a free man, should have the right to exercise his franchise, and that in joining the King's colours he did not take from himself that which we all hold most dear, the right to express himself by his vote on the conduct of his country's affairs.

My hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Nickle) spoke of himself as one who has not always been in accord with the policy of his party and yet was in favour of this Bill. I feel it incumbent on me, being one who has not always been in accord with the policy of his party, to declare myself as absolutely opposed to this Bill. I am not opposed to it because it is introduced by this Government; I would be equally opposed to it if it were introduced by the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier)

were he Prime Minister. My reasons for being opposed to the Bill may not be exactly those expressed thus far in the discussion.
I do think the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) has been too inflammable. if I may use that expression, during this session of Parliament. He began the session with a threat that if we on this side of the House dared-he did not use the word "dare," but that was the effect of his suggestion-to criticise the policy of the Government, he would carry the attack into our ranks and show that we were no better than they. I do not think that that made for unity of purpose at this particular crisis of the affairs of the Empire. To-night he has reiterated that proposition, saying that he had no knowledge at present that there would be an election in the near future, but the action of the Opposition tended to show that they were carrying a chip on their shoulder and rather wanted to have an election. The effect of an election upon me personally is not of the slightest interest; but in its effect upon the people of this country I think an election during the progress of this war would be a catastrophe. I would suggest to the Prime Minister that if he wants to go down in history as one of Canada's greatest statesmen, and one of the Empire's biggest men, he should now declare that during the progress of this war, so far as he is concerned and so far as his leadership of the Conservative party goes, there will be no election until this war is over. I can assure him that a proposition of this kind, emanating from him, will make for him more friends in the province of Ontario than any other course he could pursue, for the people of the province of Ontario, at least ninety per cent of them, irrespective of politics, do not want an election-of that I am absolutely certain. What were we on this side ito do or to consider? Last fall we heard threats and talk of an election.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would remind the hon. member that the question before the House is the second reading of a Bill and not the question of an election.

Mr. Speaker, I will keep as close to the subject of debate as I can, and if I encroach upon the rules in the remarks I am making, I will go no further, except to say this, that, unless there is to be an election before another session of Parliament, there is no necessity for this Bill. If there is to be another session before an election, then, next session, if it is thought necessary that the soldiers abroad should have votes,
let us get together and devise some scheme whereby they can have votes under all safeguards, which parties on both sides of the House will agree to.
The fact that this Bill is introduced at the present time and that the term of this Parliament will not expire until September, 1916, would lead one to believe that an election will take place before another session of Parliament is held. We are led to believe that there will be an election this summer, and that that is the object of the Government's bringing forward this legislation. That being the case-and we can draw no other conclusion-why am I opposed to this Bill? Because it is founded on sentiment, not on sense, and, if worked out at all, it will be worked out in absolute ignorance on the part of the voters, and with an entire absence of good results. Sentiment enters into the actions of most people, but in a case of this kind it seems to me that we should be governed by something more than sentiment.
It has been urged that we would be well advised if we should follow the example of New Zealand in the matter of legislation of this kind. I quite agree with the hon. member for Edmonton that the New Zealand Bill was passed for quite another purpose. The New Zealand elections were announced early in November last, and the elections were held on December 10. On December 24, notwithstanding the fact that the parties in the. New Zealand Legislature were pretty evenly divided, the votes cast by the soldiers had not been returned to New Zealand. If the soldiers who voted in Egypt were given the privilege of voting in order that they might decide the political situation, surely the votes would have been returned to New Zealand long before they were. Whether or not they have yet been returned, I do not know. The London Times gives the bald fact that about 10,000 New Zealanders voted in Egypt, but on December 24 those votes had not been returned to New Zealand, so that they were of no use in deciding the political contest between the parties in that Overseas Dominion.
The people of Canada during the past winter have been striving unitedly and energetically to raise an enormous patriotic fund. Every person in Canada, from one end of it to the other has been striving to the best of his ability, energy and influence to assist in the establishing of a patriotic fund to support the families of the brave men from Canada who have gone to the front. That work is still going

on, and will continue until this cruel war is over. Let us assume that there is an election in June, as there may be, or that there is to be an election before the war is over, as there is likely to be, judging by * the fact that this Bill has been introduced. Suppose that in a close constituency one representative is returned by the vote of the resident people, and at five o'clock on the eve of election day the residential vote declares a certain man elected. That night or the next day the vote of the soldiers is counted, and that count reverses the verdict.
How can it be counted the next day?
It is counted after the poll is closed; it cannot be counted before.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: All votes are counted after the poll is closed.

All votes are counted after the poll is closed, but the vote of the soldiers is not counted until after the residential vote is counted. I was assuming that in several counties the residential vote should declare one way and the soldiers' vote, sent from Belgium, Flanders or Germany, should change the result of the election while the war is in progress. Would any hon. gentleman say that that would tend to make for unity of thought and harmony of action in the constituency concerned in the matter of the raising of funds to care for the families of the soldiers who are abroad? From the county of Welland about 600 brave men have gone to the front. We jn the county of Welland are loyally, faithfully and industriously doing our duty to look after the families of these men, and intend to continue doing so. I am not afraid of the vote of the young men who have left the county of Wellaind, but assuming that, in some other county, changes are made by reason of the votes which are cast by the soldiers, I say that the condition which would bring about that result is a wrong principle to introduce into the policy of this country at a time when a great war is raging and when every man's mind and heart and soul and interest and industry should be centered on one object: the success of the allied troops and the maintenance of British supremacy. The soldiers at the front cannot possibly know the issues that will be involved in the election. Further, the personal equation in elections counts for a good deal. I do not think
that the right hon. the Prime Minister or the right hon. the leader of he Opposiion should arrogate the vote of the people exclusively to themselves, or to the parties which they represent. Very frequently votes are cast for the representative himself; often the personal equation enters into the election contest more strongly, perhaps, than the policy of a party. How can the man at the front know for whom he is voting? He has to vote for a Government, or an Opposition, or an independent candidate. He does not know who will represent him in Parliament. Probably if he knew the Government candidate he would not vote for him; probably if he knew the Opposition candidate, though the voter might be a Liberal, he would not vote for him, thinking that the candidate would not be fitted to represent him and his views in Parliament. I contend that the soldier under these conditions would vote in absolute ignorance of the situation. I defy any gentleman in this House to say that any soldier has ever asked to have a vote. The Minister of Justice was asked a question in that respect, which he has not yet answered. Will the Prime Minister, if he can, state one instance in which the soldiers have asked that they be allowed to vote. They are going to. the front to fight the battles of Canada and of the British Empire. They are not thinking about votes half so much as the politicians are -thinking about giving them votes. I trust that the politicians are not thinking about controlling the votes after the ballots have been marked. I would not accuse any one of that. But, at this time, when this war is in progress, I say leave this over until another session of Parliament. Then, when we meet together, if the soldiers are still in the trenches and it is thought necessary that they should have votes, let us get together and devise a scheme whereby they can vote intelligently, vote under proper protection, and I for one will aid in that purpose as well as in any other purpose which I consider to be to the advantage of Canada. But at the present time I am opposed to the idea of an election, I am opposed to the idea of flinging the soldiers into the arena of politics, I am opposed to the proposition of bringing about a contention in this country that will break the harmony which now prevails and the unity which now exists. I say, let us go on with one heart, one hope and one endeavour to reach if possible that wealth of freedom which British victory will secure.
