Just a word, (because I realize that the hour is late and much has been said. One cannot have heard the discussion that has taken place on this Bill and read the Bill without being conscious that this committee has laboured long and faithfully to bring about a result which would be agreeable to this House and to the country. The committee was a non-partisan com-rffittee. It was open for any hon. gentleman or anybody else to appear before it and give his views, and apparently until this Bill was brought into this House and the second reading was asked for, the committee made no objection nor was there any difference in the opinion of the committee in regard to the measure now before the House. Where are the hon. gentlemen who represented the Opposition in the House on this committee? They are not here to-night. There has been no complaint from these bon. gentlemen, there has been no minority report, there has been nothing except the appearance of perfect harmony with respect to the provisions of this Bill. I quite approve of all that has been said upon the line of the desirability of observing perfect neutrality in a matter of this kind', - and I second the sentiment expressed by the hon. gentleman who has just sat down (Mr. German), that there should be but one heart and one sentiment and one will behind this war. I say that this very Bill will do all that we can do that we have not already done in the matter of giving our soldiers who are at the front lie art and courage and encouragement of all kinds from this House and from this country. What are we doing? Are these men aliens? They certainly are not, they are British subjects, 99 out of 100 probably are Canadian citizens; and all that this Bill provides is that they shall have the right to vote.	Does any hon.
gentleman in this House believe now that they are not entitled to vote? Because nine out of ten of them are on the list already. The Bill does not go as far as I would like to see. Personally I would like to see it give every man who is fighting a vote whether he be of age or under age. If he is a man performing the functions of a man for our country and our Empire he should have a vote. But the Bill has stopped short at men of 21 years of age and only those vote. What good purpose can be served by putting any impediment or barrier in the way of these men voting?
The hon. gentleman who has just sat down agreed with the spirit and principle 142
of the Bill. His opinion is apparently that this is not the time or the opportunity to deal prudently and in a cool and deliberate manner with it. His opinion is that there should be a Bill of this kind at another session. Then, of course, if a Bill of this kind is at any time passed either at this session or at a future session, it must be in contemplation of an election, otherwise it is useless waste paper. A Bill of this kind, if passed, must contemplate its being used in the election. If one were to look for any reason why the Opposition in this House is opposed to this Bill it would be very difficult to find any concrete argument that has been made by any of ithese hon. gentlemen either individually or as a whole. The hon. gentleman who has just sat dowm is in favour of the principle of the Bill and would favourpassing it at another session. The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) says: Oh, yes, let us pass this Bill but only in so far as it will apply to soldiers who have not gone to the war. I understood that to be his argument.

Oh, no, I do not wish to be understood in that way at all. My objection to the Bill was that the provisions in regard to the soldiers who had not gone to the front were not suitable to the case; that they lent themselves absolutely to improper handling.

It comes to the same thing very largely, he would give votes to those who have not gone to the war if that were done then when they went to war some provision of this kind would have to be made giving them a vote.

I do not object to those
who have gone to the war having votes, but I wish to see proper safeguards as to the method of voting.

That comes down to the great body and burden of opinion on the opposite side; it is a matter of detail. Everything that has been said by way of criticism on the second reading of this Bill could be dealt with and properly dealt with in Committee of the Whole, if the hon. gentlemen who are expressing these opinions are honest and sincere with them. But we find, that a good deal of criticism on this Bill comes from those who see evil in it. We know the old motto, evil be to him who evil thinks, "Honi soit qui mal y pense." That might very well be applied to much of what



has been said against this Bill. I wish to point out what is known to hon. gentlemen in this House, that of all classes of the community who poll their votes faithfully the soldiers stand at the top of the list. I know of no element or part of the community that values its vote more than the military, either the regular soldiers or the volunteers. But we find that in a measure and in a certain sense this very principle is now adopted and applied. As has been said by the right hon. leader of the Opposition, there is no Franchise Act now in Canada as a whole. There was one, but there is none now. Each province has its own law. In the month of June, when the registration for the voters' lists takes place for Dominion or Provincial purposes, if the soldiers are in camp, as they frequently are in that month, they register themselves by the thousands simply by making affidavits very similar in principle to the affidavit called for by this very Bill, or by having comrades make affidavits on their'behalf, so that they are now advanced to at least one-half of the privileges which this Bill gives them, they have, by the law of Ontario-and I fancy this is fairly general throughout the Dominion-the right to register although they are not at the place of registration, in the way I have indicated. What is the use of talking about qualifications nowadays and saying this Bill provides no qualifications? We all know that manhood suffrage to-day prevails throughout Canada and that is all that this Bill contemplates. Every man of 21 years of age who is a British subject and resident a certain time in any community is entitled to vote. So we are by this Bill merely giving manhood suffrage, which is the law to-day practically throughout Canada, to the people who are now entitled to vote, and the only difference between what the law is now and what ft will be after this Bill becomes law is that those who are away on active service shall be permitted by some lawful means to transmit a vote into the ballot box and have it counted on election day. The hon. member for Edmonton was very apprehensive about corruption. He was one of those who saw bogies everywhere. But I should like to point out to him that under this Bill the ballot papers will be sent by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to the office of the Canadian High Commissioner in London, who in turn will send them to the proper officer or officers who will give the necessary papers to each volunteer entitled to vote. Every safe-
guard has been provided for, from the time the ballots leave Ottawa until they gdt back. Every precaution has been taken for .ensuring secrecy. The hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) was was anxious as to the counting of the votes afterwards, and he referred to the case of New Zealand. In New Zealand the votes did not arrive for some days after the poll was held. But no such condition could arise under this Bill, for it provides that the votes shall tfe counted on polling day. I should be very sorry to see what the hon. member for Welland has in his mind's eye, namely, the civilians voting one way and the soldiers another. The people of this country are all one, whether soldiers or civilians. Nine-tenths of the soldiers are civilians anyway, who have gone to fight for the Empire from patriotic and manly motives. They will come back to their ordinary vocations with the honours and prestige that attach to men who have been engaged in a noble cause for their country in time of need. The hon. member for Bruce (Mr. H. Clark) reminds me that every vote has the same value whether it is a civilian's or a soldier's. The vote of the civilian should be worth 100 per cent, and so should the vote of the soldier; and the soldier's vote will be worth 100 per cent under this Bill. A great deal has been said to-night about liberties, British institutions, democracy and so forth. But where would democracy be if it were not for the soldiers who are fighting the battles of the country at the front? Who, I ask, is entitled to greater consideration at the present time than these men who are preserving the liberties and freedom of this country? And I am referring not only to our own soldiers, but to the men from all parts of the Empire, the Old Country included. It seems to me that if the soldiers of any part of the Empire are entitled to a vote or to any great consideration it is the soldiers who have gone from Canada. I do not desire to belittle the efforts of men who have gone to the front from other parts of the overseas dominions, hut Canada, of all the dominions, is the only one that has no material interest in this war. Her only interest is loyalty to the Empire and to herself. All the other dominions have as neighbours German colonies by XI p.m which they have been menaced, and it is only natural to expect that alter the war these German colonies will form part of the nearby British Dominions. It is quite possible anyway. But the

soldiers of Canada have gone from loyalty to the Empire and to Canada, loyalty to liberty and to everything that is right and proper in mankind.
On referripg to my notes I am afraid I have attributed a remark to the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) which was made by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley). I think it was the hon. member for St. John who was in favour of giving a vote to the soldiers who hereafter go to the war, but not to the soldiers who have already gone. What are we to make of this patchwork of opinions from the Opposition side of the House? One hon. gentleman says they should all have votes, another says that none of them should have votes, another says give half of them votes. What harmony is there in that? I think some of the criticisms of the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition were trifling, if he will permit me to say so. One great objection that he had was that we were creating a franchise. I can recollect as a boy, and my right hon. friend can recollect better than I can, when we had a whole week's open- vote at election time. Was it desirable to change that practice? I think so. And shall we not change our practice from time to time as democracy progresses? Are we to stick forever to a certain method of voting? Surely not. Suppose that we are creating a franchise, which I deny, what evil is there in that? I see no harm in it. I do not think my right hon. friend's objection will appeal to many hon. gentlemen in this House or out of it. Then he likened the soldiers to railwaymen or fishermen or lumbermen whose vocations take them away from home, but who have a permanent residence and a vote in Canada. I should like to point out to my right hon. friend that these men he speaks of are all entitled to vote; they can return to their homes on election day. But the soldier cannot do that, and that is just the difference between the two classes. Another reason that the right hon. gentleman gave for not giving soldiers votes was that they were being well treated already, and he pointed out that they were to have pensions. Surely every civilized country in the world treats its soldiers well, and gives them pensions. That is not an over-humane act. Surely it is the least we can do. I do not think that the people of this country will consider that in giving votes to the soldiers we are treating them magnanimously.

So far as I can sum up the opposition to this Bill it is this: hon. gentlement opposite trust nobody, not even the soldiers. They are afraid that the soldier will not exercise his franchise with that secrecy and propriety which is ordinarily required in the polling of votes. As I have pointed out, the Bill provides a complete chain of safeguards from the time the ballots leave the office of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery until they return to Ottawa. No reasonable objection has yet been made. The Bill is founded on motives of propriety, and I believe the people of this country will demand it.. Furthermore, I believe that the soldiers who have left the country understood that they were going to be given an opportunity to vote; so that in passing this Bill we are doing no more than carrying out the spirit of what was generally believed to be an implied agreement entered into between the public of this country and the men who are fighting at the front. That is, that they shall have every good treatment that can .be given to them and an opportunity of voting was certainly considered to be something that they would enjoy. I appeal to hon. gentlemen to pass this Bill and to do the proper thing. If there is any detail of the Bill that can be improved the time and place to do it is in committee. Let the Bill leave committee in such shape that it will be agreed to by both parties and I believe it will meet with the approval of every person in the country.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonell) has made reference to some hon. gentlemen on this side of the House who were members of the committee who considered this measure. I do not know that I would have risen were it not that my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) desired me to say, owing to the fact that he was called away this morning, that he did not consider this measure as it was submitted to the House a proper solution of the problem as to how the soldiers should have their votes polled and that had he been here he would have voted against the measure along those lines. It is a very peculiar measure. In the face of the greatest war that was ever waged, in view of the demands that are being made upon every citizen in the Empire and upon every man with a drop of British blood in his veins, hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House turn aside from the consideration of their re-

sponsibilities as British citizens, and as having to do with the Government of Canada, and the part which Canada has to play in this Empire, and sit down and try to devise some method by which votes may be polled. This is purely an election measure. ''There is no precedent for it. The idea that a Government should provide for going into another country where the enemy are engaging in battle with our sons to hold a poll has never been suggested . anywhere. You will search the history of England in vain to find any precedent for the action which is now being taken. We are having this done here for the first time. Were it not for the fact that hon. gentlemen are intending to have an election we would not have this Bill before us at all. You see it on the face of the Bill itself. The first section creates a franchise and the second provides that the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, shall immediately send to the office of the High Commissioner in Great Britain a certain number of ballots. It says that he shall send them right off and, the language being peremptory, this is a duty imposed upon the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery which he must immediately fulfil. Why is it that we are to have an .election? The right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) intimated that because of the conduct of the Opposition, because we ventured, to criticise the Government in connection with the purchase of boots, and because of something that was happening in the Public Accounts Committee, although he had not thought about an election he was now thinking about it. Since the 16th day of February I have been sitting in the committee appointed for the purpose of investigating the supply of boots to the soldiers but I am not sitting in that committee on account of any action on the part of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. It is on account of the right hon. gentleman's own action. He moved the committee and declared it to be necessary. Therefore, why should he complain? If things come out in that committee why should he complain about it? Does he suggest that the hon. gentlemen who happen to compose that committee are to sit there and register his decrees m regard to the question which the committee has to deal, that we are to cease to perform our functions as members of Parliament and members of that committee? Why? Hon. gentlemen behind him were deliberating as to how, in the midst of this great war there could be some political scheme devised in 
regard to votes and that is why they were not doing anything in regard to boots or criticising anything that had been done.
My right hon. friend intimated on the day that the address was debated on the opening of this session of Parliament that every hon. member of this House and the country at large were entitled to the fullest information with regard to all expenditures of a military character. When, adopting his own suggestion, there were referrered to the Public Accounts Committee expenditures for military purposes, my right hon. friend proclaims that because hon. gentlemen have been performing their duties as members of Parliament they have been doing something which is trespassing upon the: position which the Government occupy and doing something which, warrant my right hon. friend, in the face of this war, in plunging this country into a general election. There is not much use in discussing the question of where he personally stands upon this matter of a general election. Every one who has been through an election knows that these things are in the hands of the fates.
But if my right hon. friend wants to divide up this country, if he wants to stop recruiting, if he wants to stay the hand of generosity, if he wants to chill the response to the appeals which are being made to the patriotism of our people in every part of the country, if he wants to paralyse the efforts of those who are trying to do all they can for Belgium and the wives and children of the men who have gone to the front, if he wants to turn the people in every hamlet from the peaceful avocations which they have undertaken for the purpose of doing their part in dealing with the situation and doing their duty to the Empire, he will bring about this internecine struggle which will have as a result the tearing asunder of the good feeling which exists and which is contributing so greatly to the cause that all British subjects have so much at heart-if, I say, my right hon. friend wants to do these things he can get offended at what was done in the Public Accounts Committee and the Boots Committee.
My right hon. friend does not respond to the appeal which was made by my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) and he foregoes the opportunity of putting himself on record as being the big man in this country. The time will come when the people will estimate him at his true worth. It is because there has been all this talk about a general election that we have this

Bill. The second clause provides that the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery shall send ballots across the ocean at once for that particular reason. What is the use of discussing the abstract question as to whether soldiers should have votes or not in the way in which the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) did? The soldier who is a citizen of this country has a right to vote; there can be no question about that. Who can question that, and why should we take up the time with platitudes abhut Parliament wanting to provide for his voting? But this fantastic measure of the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) is another _ thing altogether. There is a great deal of difference between the abstract proposition that a soldier who is a citizen of this country should have a vote and the method by which the Minister of Justice proposes to enable him to vote. In the first place, this measure is altogether so unique in its character, having regard to the war situation, that one might well ask that why is it that over in the Imperial Parliament, which is sitting just now, we have never heard that the. great statesmen who are considering this war problem have proposed any scheme by which the men who live in the British Islands, and who are now across the channel fighting for the Empire, shall record their votes in a general election? Why is it that we have never heard of it? Nobody has ever suggested the possibility of it. Therefore, why is this measure introduced at all? If we are not going to have a general election, as my hon. friend from Welland says, we do not need this Bill.
If we are going to have a general election, then the soldiers are entitled to vote if their votes can be recorded under proper safeguards and under proper conditions. Parliament since Confederation has time and again taken up days and weeks and months deliberating questions of the franchise and of the proper method of safeguarding the manner in which the voting of this country shall be carried on. My hon. friend proposes to dispose of those safeguards with one fell swoop. It does not matter to him that we have no regard to what Parliament has done in the past, whereby even in the quiet hamlets of this country it has provided for the greatest possible secrecy and honesty in polling. He says: We are going to provide a scheme here absolutely unique and novel in its character, because we want a general election, and we are going to have this measure passed whether you like it or not; If you say anything, you are disloyal and you do not want the soldiers to vote.
This was the text of my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) to-night. If it was not, I do not know the English language. It is time that full-grown men in this country, who have reached the position of being representatives of the people, should give up reiterating in this House speeches which they make only in localities where they presume upon the ignorance of the audience they are addressing. If they would make fewer of such speeches and more attempts to consider cold facts, instead of hurling across the floor from time to time taunts that hon. gentlemen on this side are disloyal, because we do not see eye to eye with them on every proposition they may bring forward, it would be better for the dignity of this Parliament and more for the honour of this country, and, as British citizens and parliamentarians, we would have more pride in ourselves if we looked at questions in that way. That is the way in which I -would like to look at this proposition to-night. Shall our soldiers who are fighting for their country have an opportunity of exercising their franchise? I say, yes, if you can provide honest and proper methods by which those votes can be dropped into the ballot box, without disarranging the whole electoral machinery of this country, without violating all-the canons of the election law, without disregarding every principle which has characterized British parliamentary Government ever since we have had parliamentary government. Why was it that in the days of the Crimean war, and during all the various wars of the last three-quarters of a century, the English Parliament never passed a measure of this character? My hon. friend the Minister of Justice this afternoon read the provisions of a measure which he said had passed the second reading in the English Parliament, and he went on to say that because that Parliament was so busy the measure was never heard of again. If that is the way in which the statesmen who guide this Empire carry on its affairs, it is time we found it out. If they are too busy to pass measures of the greatest possible importance in the interests of the country, then they are not performing their duty. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice knows full well that that is not the reason, and that the reason why the measure was not passed is because the mature judgment of the Imperial Parliament in considering this question was that it was absolutely impracticable. I presume this Bill will pass from its second reading to the Com-

mittee of the Whole, in which each one of the details can be discussed; but the hon. -member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), who discussed this matter with his usual earnestness, appealed to the House to do one thing -to put the Canadian people in the position of saying: Although we do not expect that any of these votes will ever be recorded in Flanders, or Belgium, or Germany, we shall be able to say that we did what we could to give our soldiers an opportunity to vote. That is a very nice thing to be able to say; but let me point out that, if we have any responsibility here as public men, when we are endeavouring to place upon the statute books of this country any measure dealing with such an important question as amending the Dominion Election Act, we are not doing so because we want to be able to say to some one else that we tried to do the best for them, although we could not effect anything. If we cannot put on the statute books a measure that is absolutely workable in every respect', having in it all those safeguards which Parliament in previous years has -always regarded as being -absolutely essential to the proper recording of votes in this country, what is the sense of putting a measure on the statute-book which will enable us to say we did what we could?
Is the hon. member in favour of the principle of the Bill?

I am in favour of giving votes to our soldiers if we can provide the proper means of doing so and the proper safeguards. This measure does not offer a possible, even a plausible condition by which that can be done. When *we come to discuss the question in its details, the anomalies and difficulties in regard to the measure can toe very readily pointed out. Therefore it seems to me that we are discussing on the second reading, not the details of the measure, because they will be discussed later on, but the wisdom and tihe advisability of putting on the statute-lbooks in this year of grace, 1915, this peculiar legislation which has never before seen the light in all the long past of the parliamentary government of this Empire. This legislation should not be put upon the statuteJbook, because the right hon. gentleman, who is responsible to the people of this country for the advice which he gives His Royal Highness, knows as well as I do that if he throws Canada into the throes of an election contest, he produces a condition under which will be utterly destroyed all those feelings of

unity and of devotion to the flag which today animate the Canadian people to a greater degree than ever before in our long history. He will stop recruiting; he will disarrange all the conditions, and of course he will have to take the responsibility. It is because my right hon. friend is thinking of having an election that we have this measure. If he were not thinking of having an election, we would not have this Bill at all, and therefore, I say on the second reading of this Bill that it is totally unnecessary, utterly uncalled for and without the slightest justification. When it passes to the Committee of the Whole, as I assume it will, I shall be prepared to discuss the details, and point out at greater length what seem to me to be the anomalies of this measure, but do not let it be understood that hon. gentlemen on this side are opposed to any man who happens to wear the King's uniform having a vote.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: You have said so several times.
Who has?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. -Clark).
The hon. member for Red Deer can speak for himself in regard to that.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is trying to speak for him.

My hon. friend from Red Deer, if I understood him aright, pointed out the anomalies of the men who are fighting in the trenches in Flanders going and recording their vote, and he said that they should follow Kitchener's principle. He argued that the men in Flanders were thinking more of fighting the Germans than of voting.
The hon. member for Red Deer has a son in the trenches.

In the garrisons at Halifax, Sydney and Canso, there are something like 1,200 men, 300 of whom come from Charlottetown and Prince Edward Island generally, and four or five hundred from New Brunswick.
These men cannot leave the garrison to go to vote. They are farmers' sons, many of them men of substance in their several provinces. Would it toe just or right to deprive these men of the franchise?

These men will not he deprived of their franchise unless my hon. friend's leader wants to bring on an election this year. My hon. friend the casuist from Portage la Prairie, the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen), will hardly be able to distort the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) into an intimation of a policy on the part of the Liberal party to prevent the soldiers from having votes. As to that, I wish to say that the hon. gentleman belongs to the school on the other side whose particular business seems to be to throw out imputations on the score of loyalty and patriotism. I do think that, as the rising hope of the Conservative party, as he is, he ought to be a little more ambitious to rise to higher lines than to indulge in such claptrap as that which, if he must use it, should be used only in the backwoods of his constituency. It is not worthy of the hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think it is out of order to speak of the utterance of an hon. member as unworthy.

Mr Speaker, of course I bow to your ruling in regard to that; but I would point out that the language which one has to use to characterize actions of that kind must be more vigorous than ornate. I reiterate that, as I understand the views of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, we hold this measure as entirely unnecessary, unless hon. gentlemen opposite are going to have an election. That is the preliminary question at the basis of this whole measure. The soldiers who are abroad, like the soldiers who are at home, as Canadian citizens should have votes, if those votes can be recorded with due regard to the safeguards which are thrown around elections in this country. And this Bill does not provide such safeguards.

It is not my intention at this late hour to occupy much of the time of the House, but I feel it to be my duty to express my reasons for opposing this Bill. Let me say at once, I am strongly in favour of giving the soldiers votes, but I am in favour of giving them votes when they come back victorious from France and Germany. As has been said, if this Government does not intend to have an election, there is absolutely no need for this Bill. If we grant that, we must acknowledge that this is nothing but a political measure. It is offered here with the idea of winning votes in this country
from the friends and relatives of the soldiers at the front; it is offered here with the idea of affording the Government party from one end of the country to the other an opportunity to go forth and wave the flag as they have done so often before. I do not like to impute motives of this kind against any Government, but I consider it perfectly clear that this Government are glad that we are opposing this Bill. We have evidence of that from the gentlemen on the other side who have already spoken, because, without exception they have accused the members of the Opposition of being opposed to the principle of a vote for the soldiers. We on this side have without exception stated that we are not opposed to the soldiers voting but that we are opposed to the provisions of this Bill which do not safeguard the secrecy of the ballot or the rights of the voters.
It is possible, in fact it is probable, that if this war should continue, I myself shall be at the front. I have already offered my services to Colonel Baker when he was forming the 5th Mounted Rifles, and although I was not accepted, I should like to say to the Minister of Militia that at any time he requires my services or would like them, they are absolutely, at his disposal. I have had some experience in military life, and I feel perfectly sure that if I ever land in the trenches, be it in Belgium, or France, or Germany, the very last thing I shall want to bother my mind about will be an election in Canada. Like the men who are there now I shall have on my mind greater things than that. Those men are busy day and night in defence of this country, in defence of this Empire. They will not have time or disposition to read party literature, or to hear political discussions from their officers; nor will their officers if they fulfil their duty, have time to collect ballots or discuss politics with the soldiers.
If this Bill passes, will the soldiers have to vote?

I should imagine, Sir, that
under some of the officers, they would.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman would name some of those officers. If I may be permitted, I should like to say that an hon. gentleman who would cast a slur like that upon officers ought to be willing to name them.

As I was saying I 'feel that if I get over there, I shall not care one jot whether this Government is returned or

whether this Government is defeated. I shall expect if I am there, that this Government will do its duty to this country as I shall be doing mine.
I shall not expect them to waste their time in the political strife which would be involved in a general election. They will have quite enough to do if they devote their energies and abilities to carrying out the tremendous task which is now imposed upon them; if they direct their energies towards seeing that contracts are honestly and faithfully carried out and that the evildoers, grafters, and political heelers have no opportunity of wrongfully obtaining the money of the people of Canada.
I am not in favour of the details of this Bill; I do not think that the proposed method of obtaining the votes of the soldiers is such as to carry out the objects of the promotors of the Bill. When this Bill is considered in committee, its details may be more fully discussed. If the right hon. Prime Minister i$ sincere in the remarks which he made to-day with regard to voting by the soldiers, why does he not declare that there shall not be an election until the war is over, or until the term of the present Parliament expires? If he should do this, he would show his absolute sincerity; he would give evidence of the fact that he puts his country above his party, and that he really believes that the soldier should have a vote. I quite fail to see how, under this Bill, the soldiers would be enabled to vote for any particular representative. It is all very well to say: vote for the Government or vote for the Opposition; but it should be remembered that many voters vote not for the party, but for the man. There is no hurry for the passing of this Bill. The Prime Minister has said tonight that an election has not been decided upon; that the matter has not been discussed. I think it would be reasonable, therefore, to expect the Prime Minister to explain to this House how it is that he allows the hon. Minister of Justice to bring down a Bill which can only have in view the holding of an election this year.

speakeroldname: Mr. H. H. McLEAN (Sunbury and Queens):
speechtext:
I do not intend at this late hour to take up the time of the House by restating the arguments that have been advanced in favour of the principle of this Bill, or in giving at length the reasons why I am in favour of votes for soldiers. I wish simply to place myself on record as being strongly in favour of

votes for soldiers. When the Bill is under consideration in committee, I shall be able to discuss its provisions at greater length, and, perhaps, to go fully into the details of the Bill.

I wish to endorse what has been said by the hon. member for Mississquoi (Mr. Kay). I have two sons who are engaged in this conflict; my eldest son is with the second contingent in St. John, and my youngest son is with the Mounted Rifles in Sherbrooke. While I am desirous that the soldiers of our Dominion should be enabled to cast their vote, unless that can be done in a reasonable way and with all proper safeguards, to my mind we had better leave well enough alone. There is a .good deal in what has been said by the hon. gentleman that the soldiers will not know the issues of any election that may be held. Further, I am afraid that undue influence may be brought to bear upon the soldiers in the trenches. We were assured to-day that canvassing would not be allowed, but we are aware of the fact that there is an indirect means of canvassing a voter. I do not see how it would be possible to prevent literature from getting into the hands of the soldiers. During the election of 1911 I practically received a letter appealing to me as a Liberal-that letter was sent broadcast throughout this country, and was signed by R. L. Borden-to vote Tory and save Canada for the Empire. Is it not possible that a similar letter may be sent, appealing to the Liberals to sustain the Government, along the lines of the speech delivered by the right hon. gentleman in the debate on the budget? Portions of that speech, reflecting on the Liberal party, have been used by the press of the Conservative party as campaign literature. I am afraid that this matter will come down to active partisan politics, and it would be a great injustice to the people of Canada to take active partisan politics into the trenches. I think it would be unwise to have an election while the war is in progress.	And if we are
not to be called upon to exercise our franchise, why is there the need for the Bill now before the House?	It
seems to me that we might very well follow the example of the United Kingdom and keep these matters out of active politics. A remark was made by the Minister of Finance during the Budget debate which I was

sorry to hear. It was to the effect that however much loyalty my right hon. friend who leads His Majesty's loyal Opposition exercised at the present time it would be a long time before the people of this country would forget what he had done-referring to the Naval Service Act. To my mind that was uncalled for and I think the right hon. gentleman might very well have retorted to the Minister of Finance that it would be a long time before the people of Canada would forget the fact that when the right hon. gentleman had behind him unanimity of opinion in the Dominion of Canada upon the establishment of the naval service the Conservative party threw that question into active politics. So I say now it would be better, if at all possible, to leave this mat- . ter over and let us hope that the soldiexB will have a vote in due time. I would go so far as to say that if the war is not concluded in 1916 I would ask the Parliament of the United Kingdom to extend the duration of this Parliament so that we might have no election until the war is over and then our soldiers, I hope a large majority of them at any rate, will return to exercise their franchise in this young nation, a nation that to me is a greater nation in a way than the nation to the south of us. There are features in which our system of Government excels that of our neighbours to the south and I say we would do well if possible-although this is a matter entirely in the hands of the Government-to avoid an election during the continuance of the war.
When the Bill is considered in Committee of the Whole I shall have some remarks to make on its details-I notice, for instance, that no provision is made for the case where two candidates of one party may be running in a constituency with no candidate for the Opposition. A by-election was called in Terrebonne where two Liberal candidates ran on an issue on which the Liberal party were divided, and there was no Conservative candidate. It is quite possible that a similar case might occur.
I am heartily in favour of granting a vote to every Canadian citizen, especially those who are absent from Canada fighting for the protection of our homes and of the greatest young nation, shall I say, and for the greatest Empire that the world has ever seen.

There is not now that unanimity among the members on the other side of the House that seemed to prevail before six o'clock
this evening. I listened to the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) and one could only understand from his statements that he was determinedly opposed to giving soldiers votes, while the gentlemen who have followed lately have seemed to veer in a contrary direction; in plain parlance they are letting themselves down as easily as possible.	My reason for rising
to	support	the	Bill	is that I
have the honour and pleasure of representing a riding that adjoins the constituency of North Simcoe. The member who represents that riding (Mr. Currie) is not here to-night owing to the fact that he is in the firing and not in the talking line. One result of his going to the front as he has done has been that he has taken with him from the riding of North Simcoe the pick' of the young men of that riding. They are business men, men who have left their businesses behind; they are farmers' sons who have their rights in that riding, they are intelligent men who know everything as to the issues to be put before the people just as well as we who nfay be hereon the spot. Then I ask why should not these men have votes. To say that they will not know the issues is idle. They are not unintelligent men and to say that they will not know the candidates is equally idle. The hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) dwelt a great deal on the personality of the candidates. These young men will receive letters from their friends, they will receive the public press of the country; and long before polling day they will know of the candidates in their ridings. One reason for which hon. gentlemen oppose the Bill was told by the hon. gentleman from Missisquoi (Mr. Kay) and that is that the Bill is so popular in the country that it will attract votes of Liberals who are not away, who are resident in the country and will be here at the time of the election. There can be no mistaking his words, their purport was that every man who is in the fighting line and his friends left in Canada, Liberal or Conservative, will be voting for this Government because it is giving the vote to the soldiers here. I tell the hon. gentleman that many men will vote for that reason.

I think the hon. member misunderstood me. I said the desire of this Government was that they should get the vote of the friends of the soldiers who are in this country. I did not mean that they will get them.	,

With all due deference, I think the hon. gentleman's fear is that they will get them too. This is a popular measure in the country and hon. gentlemen apprehend that; and I think that is what the hon. gentleman had in his mind at the time. So far as the personality of the candidate goes, every soldier who votes over there will know exactly the candidates on either side in the constituency where his vote will be ultimately recorded. The hon. member for Missis-quoi being not only an hon. but a gallant gentleman, I think casts rather a reflection on the officers who are in the lines. Is it to be said that a man who will risk his life over there-the hon. gentleman does not seean to be doing that at present although he is a major in the force-
I do not wish to sail under false colours, I would say I am only a lieutenant.
Well, there are many lieutenants over there and there is still room for one.
The hon. member has offered his services.

Hon. gentlemen opposite say that officers will canvass the soldiers. Well, it is not our fault if the bulk of the officers who have gone to the front from this House are Conservatives. Surely the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie), who is in the firing line to-day, cannot be blamed for being over there. Nor is it any more reprehensible that the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Carrick), who is also at the front, should be over there. If the hon. member for York, N.B. (Mr. McLeod) is at the front, he is not to be blamed for that; and the hon. member for Brome (Mr. Baker) will be over there by June at all events. Surely the hon. gentleman should not complain if all the officers have come from this side of the House. I think that is all the more to their credit.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that all the Canadian officers at the front are Conservatives? I can tell him that there are as many Liberal officers as Conservatives.

I was speaking of the members of this House who are officers in the Canadian forces. I was not speaking of the officers on the whole staff. All I can say in regard to these officers who have gone from the House of Commons is that

the country will admire them more than if they had remained at home.	'
I would suggest that my hon. friend s statement will not make for unity of feeling in this country, and certainly it will not help the patriotic funds.

The hon. gentleman has mentioned that point before. We have had elections before in this country, but after the elections people have gone back to their vocations just as usual; and surely the same thing would happen if an election were held now. I think the hon. member for Welland is looking through a glass very darkly when he says that if the Conservative party should win in an election this coming summer, the bowels of compassion of the people all over this country would be closed, so that they would not give a dollar, when requested, to the Red Cross or any other patriotic fund. The people of Canada, Liberals and Conservatives, will not be so small or so narrow as to stop contributing to the patriotic funds so long as the money is required, simply because one party or the other has been returned to power.
